News.title: Family plea after dad found dead on school field and e-bike pulled from canal
News.content:
Family plea after dad found dead on school field and e-bike pulled from canal

The family of Neil Thompson, who was discovered dead on the grounds of a school in Wolverhampton, have issued a heartbreaking appeal on what would have been his 46th birthday

View 4 Images The body of Neil Thompson - known as Chuck - was discovered at Smestow Academy by an 11-year-old girl (Image: West Midlands Police / SWNS)

The family of a man found dead at a school have made a fresh appeal so they can have a place to grieve and remember him.

‌



Detectives believe they may be a step closer to solving the tragic mystery of how beloved dad Neil Thompson was discovered dead on the playing fields after his e-bike ended up in a canal. The body of the 45-year-old was found at Smestow Academy in Wolverhampton on January 19 by a horrified 11-year-old girl as she prepared for a PE lesson.

‌



The investigation took another twist after the water-damaged bike was later removed from Smestow Canal and left propped against a bridge. Now, on what would have been Neil’s 46th birthday, his family want the person who hauled the bike from the water to come forward.

‌



View 4 Images Police have released an image of the bike which was hauled from the canal (Image: West Midlands Police / SWNS)

Police share new information eight months after man found dead on Wolverhampton school field by young girl READ MORE :

Questions remain over death of dad found on Wolverhampton school field by pupil after he went out on e-bike READ MORE :

The force released pictures of the rust-covered e-bike and speaking on behalf of his bereaved relatives, West Midlands Police detective sergeant Amie Petford said: “His family are now asking the person who got the bike out of the water gets in touch so that they can have a place where they can go to grieve.

“The bike was rusty and appeared that someone had pulled it out of the canal and left it by a bridge at a lock so it is likely it would have been near there, but his family are hoping to know exactly where so they can lay flowers.”

‌



Following his death earlier this year, Neil's family paid tribute, saying: "Our beautiful son, brother, father and friend Chuck, very much loved in the community of fishing, his one true love. His love for life and funny stories touched the lives of so many people."

View 4 Images A young girl found the beloved dad at her school in January (Image: Anita Maric / SWNS)

An inquest into his death has heard that he died from aspiration of blood caused by traumatic facial injuries and a serious head injury and officers now believe he may have suffered the devastating injuries when he crashed his e-bike.

‌



Police believe he left home on his bike at around 8.17pm on January 18 to visit a friend. He set off for home at around 1am the following morning, with CCTV capturing him riding along a canal towpath at 1.26am.

A dog walker later photographed him in the grounds of Smestow Academy at around 7.15am after spotting him while walking through Smestow Valley Nature Reserve. Police believe Neil was still alive at that point, but what happened in the hours between remains a mystery.

View 4 Images Police at Smestow Academy, Wolverhampton (Image: Anita Maric / SWNS)

‌



A post-mortem examination found significant injuries to the left side of his face, evidence of a traumatic brain injury and a fracture around the left eye socket. Consultant pathologist Dr Brett Lockyer said the injuries were consistent with blunt-force trauma and suggested Neil could have suffered them in a heavy fall, but could also have been assaulted.

However, police now believe he died as a result of injuries suffered when his e-bike crashed into the canal.

The father of the 11-year-old girl who discovered Neil's body previously revealed how the youngster was left "really shaken up" by the ordeal. He said: "My daughter phoned her mum up, screaming, and told her that she found a dead body by the goal posts on the field.

Article continues below

"She's only 11 years of age. They went out for PE and it was very foggy. It's terrible what she's had to see."

News.title: Royal Family live: Moment Harry ignores question about Earl Spencer’s explosive book after Palace hits back
News.content:
King Charles made clear his concerns about AI in a speech in Scotland on Thursday.

Speaking to AI leaders, he said: "I must say, I am enormously grateful to you all for stepping away from your busy lives and making the journey to this rather remote, but uniquely special corner of Scotland, at Dumfries House.

"This place is perhaps particularly meaningful to me, as it has become something of a living laboratory for what I have referred to – in a book I co-wrote some sixteen years ago – as the philosophy of Harmony, which emphasises the balance, order, and relationships between ourselves and the natural world – a central truth to creating a future in which we are a part of Nature, not apart from it.

"If Harmony has any relevance to today's discussions, it is perhaps as a reminder that innovation must always be considered within the wider systems upon which all depend. As you gather for what, I hope, you will find to be fruitful conversations on the rapid development of Artificial Intelligence, I can only pray that this philosophy goes some way to arming you with the unique perspective needed to reconcile the enduring needs of humanity, with the extraordinary capabilities of these new technologies.

"Ladies and Gentlemen, we might readily agree that the development of AI – its substance and its pace - are both intriguing and deeply concerning in equal measure. AI is already showing its immense capacity to improve and save life – for example, in the field of life sciences and medicine. Yet, those who have created these technologies are now increasingly warning that AI risks developing darker capacities – perhaps even to take life. In this regard, if I may say so, there seems urgency in adequately considering the existential dangers of such technologies falling into the wrong hands, and being used in potentially catastrophic ways. Surely, we need sufficient means of control before it is all too late?

"Those in our world who value deeply our humanity and its vital moral component are anxiously seeking your reassurance that we will not lose control of our destiny, or our souls…

"So, today, I want to ask two simple questions, building on the message I sent to the United Kingdom AI Safety Summit in Bletchley in 2023:

"First, how can we harness the benefits of AI, with safety at its heart? And, second, How can we build international cooperation and consensus to achieve this, so no Nation is left behind - but the human race is left in place?

"This may sound hyperbolic. I have long thought it is just enlightened realism…

"While these are simple questions, I fully realise that the answers will require all the intellectual excellence – and, crucially, the emotional excellence which separates man from machine – which is represented in this room.

"In other words, as I have said, our humanity must remain sacred.

"The decisions taken at this formative time will shape the world inherited by future generations. And so, the task before you is not merely to advance technology, but to ensure that it remains firmly in the service of humanity, community and the natural world. As we embrace what is new, we must not lose what is timeless.

"I can only applaud those of you who are so deeply committed to harnessing Artificial Intelligence for good, so that we might see a future where human potential remains boundless, whilst technological development is carefully curated to enhance our success. I am most grateful for the presence in this room of many of our greatest technological minds, and indeed, for the thoughtful stewardship demonstrated by those gathered here today as you consider the fundamental principles that should – and must – guide the development of Artificial Intelligence in the years ahead.

"I very much look forward to returning to hear the conclusions of your productive – and I hope harmonious! – discussions later on today."

News.title: Police had email proving 'Putney Pusher' suspect was innocent, family claim
News.content:
Police had email proving 'Putney Pusher' suspect was innocent, family claim

Nicholas Brandram's sisters said they provided evidence to detectives that the wealthy banker could not be the 'Putney Pusher' but officers ignored it before he took his own life

View 3 Images Nicholas Brandram, 44, took his own life this week (Image: Family Handout/PA Wire)

An email allegedly proving the innocence of the prime suspect in the "Putney Pusher" case was ignored by police before he killed himself, his sisters have claimed.

‌



Nicholas Brandram, 44, was arrested in June, nine years after a jogger shoved a female pedestrian in front of a bus on Putney Bridge in west London.

‌



The wealthy banker was found dead at his home on Tuesday, while still under police investigation.

‌



His sisters Alexia Hicks, 40, and Sophie Voelcker, 45, claimed that the army veteran provided police with evidence that cleared him, including an email sent 18 minutes after the 2017 incident.

Describing his arrest, Ms Hicks told the BBC on Friday: "My brother woke up to a large handful of police officers wearing armed vests and with a film crew on the doorstep from the media.

"So, this came completely out of the blue, off effectively an allegation which must have been either malicious or mistaken."

‌



View 3 Images A CCTV still of the 'Putney Pusher' (Image: SWNS.com)

The sisters said it was "ridiculous" that Mr Brandram was ever made a suspect, as he did not match the description of the pusher.

They said: "We provided evidence very quickly to show that this did not look like our brother. He had a withered leg from an injury sustained back from when he'd been in the army.

‌



"The victim had apparently reported that the attacker had had brown eyes. Our brother had very clear blue eyes.

"He had a prominent military tattoo on his forearm, which understandably would have been visible because the runner was wearing a T-shirt."

They also said their brother lived in Notting Hill, a few miles from Putney, at the time of the incident.

‌



The sisters said he sent an email from his work account while in his Bond Street office around four miles from the scene at 8.13am on May 5, 2017. The jogger was last seen by his victim at approximately 7.55am that morning.

View 3 Images Mr Brandram's family claim he was innocent

They told the BBC: "He was unable to send emails outside of his desk...I provided an email from our brother at 8.13am which we know he sent from his Bond Street address.

‌



"For those who don't know London, to go from Notting Hill Gate to Bond Street is miles and miles from Putney Bridge. He had no connection to Putney Bridge at the time."

In further criticism of the Met's investigation, the sisters said Mr Brandram never received DNA test results.

They said he "willingly" provided a sample two months ago in an effort to clear his name and pleaded with police to speed up the results.

‌



The sisters said detectives had told their brother they did not know when the work would be completed prior to his death.

Paying tribute to him, they said he was warm, enthusiastic and charming.

They said: "He was a gentleman. He was our very, very, very loved brother and uncle, father, son. He was a real family man and we've always been a very close family and didn't deserve any of this happening to him."

‌



Mr Brandram was arrested after detectives were said to have spoken to someone who had been close to him.

The Metropolitan Police said that the investigation was continuing. Chief Superintendent Dan Knowles said on Thursday that "further investigative work" was taking place.

Mr Knowles added: "Our thoughts are with Mr Brandram's family and friends at this deeply distressing time."

Article continues below

The force has referred itself to the police watchdog over its contact with Mr Brandram.

Last week, the Met confirmed he had been released under investigation.

News.title: DWP PIP changes update as 'timeline' explained for 'all customers'
News.content:
DWP PIP changes update as 'timeline' explained for 'all customers'

The Department for Work and Pensions (DWP) has issued an update with new changes now in effect

View 3 Images Sir Stephen Timms has this week explained changes being made that will affect PIP claimants (Image: Parliament TV)

The Department for Work and Pensions has issued an update on an important PIP timeline that will affect all claimants as new changes take effect. The department says the reforms will improve day-to-day accessibility for people claiming the benefit.

‌



Personal Independence Payment (PIP) can help cover additional living costs if you have a long-term physical or mental health condition or disability and struggle with certain everyday tasks or getting around due to your condition. You can receive PIP even if you're working, have savings or are claiming most other benefits.

‌



Changes outlined in Parliament this week come as the number of people claiming Personal Independence Payments (PIP) in England and Wales has reached a record high, according to the latest figures. As of July, just over four million people were entitled to claim the benefit - a rise of 7%. An MP asked the department "what the timeline is for expanding the digital application option for Personal Independence Payment to all eligible claimants".

‌



View 3 Images (Image: Mike Kemp, In Pictures via Getty Images)

In reply, Sir Stephen Timms - Minister of State (Ministry of Housing Communities and Local Government) (Equalities) - set out what is happening and how claimants stand to benefit from the changes. He said: "Through the Health Transformation Programme, we are expanding digital services for Personal Independence Payment customers.

"Over 90% of those making new PIP applications can now submit their health information online after starting their claim by phone. This is benefiting customers by removing postage times and increasing accessibility. We are continuing to extend this option to all customers and, by the end of the Programme, customers will be able to view application progress and report a change of circumstances online, reducing their need to call the enquiry line."

‌



Health Transformation Programme and Health Assessment Service

His comments, issued on Thursday, come just after a new update was released from the government released this week saying that the Health Transformation Programme (HTP) "is modernising Health and Disability benefits over the longer term. It is transforming the entire Personal Independence Payment (PIP) service, aiming to introduce a simpler application process, including an option to apply online, improved evidence gather and a more tailored journey for customers."

The government claims the Health Transformation Programme changes aim to "build trust in our services and decisions, and create a more efficient service for taxpayers." The programme is developing a new Health Assessment Service and long-term transformation of the Personal Independence Payment service, officials say.

The Health Assessment Service (HAS) covers Personal Independence Payment and certain specialist benefits, incorporating new IT and streamlined procedures. The latest update from the government released this week states: "The HTP has been developing the new HAS at a small scale initially in the Health Transformation Area (HTA).

‌



"There are currently two HTAs located in London and Birmingham. Within these HTAs , new PIP applications as well as reassessments and award reviews are processed in-house for a select number of London and Birmingham postcodes. Universal Credit (UC) Work Capability Assessments (WCA) and Employment Support Allowance (ESA) WCA were previously handled in these HTAs but, from 16 May 2025, all referrals were permanently redirected to external assessment providers."

Applying for PIP

According to Citizens Advice, unless you have a terminal illness, you'll typically need to undergo an assessment to complete your Personal Independence Payment (PIP) application. It's a chance for you to discuss how your condition impacts you - it's not a diagnosis of your condition or a medical examination.

Currently, the DWP will attempt to conduct the assessment by reviewing your medical evidence and speaking with you over the phone or via video call. It's important to submit your medical evidence as quickly as possible.

‌



View 3 Images Millions of people in the UK claim PIP (Image: SEAN GLADWELL via Getty Images)

If the DWP cannot assess you over the phone or via video call, they will invite you to a face-to-face medical assessment. If you are concerned about being assessed over the phone, you can have someone aged 16 or over join the call with you. They can participate in discussions and take notes.

PIP consists of two parts - a daily living part for those who need help with everyday tasks and a mobility part. The latter is for those who need help to get around.

Article continues below

The government guidance says that whether you qualify for one or both parts, as well as how much you might get, "depends on how difficult you find everyday tasks and getting around". To apply for PIP, visit the gov.uk webpage on the subject.

The Timms Review is currently speaking to people across the UK in a series of meetings as part of a review about the benefit. The review, launched after a Labour rebellion ended Sir Keir Starmer's attempt to cut the welfare bill by reforming PIP, is designed "to ensure that Personal Independence Payment (PIP) is fair and fit for the future in a changing world". The review's findings are due this autumn. For more on the Timms Review, visit the gov.uk web page on the topic.

News.title: 'Everything is harder when you’re hungry' – the kids praying for free school meals
News.content:
“When parents can’t afford school meals, we often see the kids come in with a jam butty and a packet of cheap crisps, maybe some squash,” the Reverend Sandra Jones is saying.

“Buying a loaf and some jam is so much cheaper than paying for lunches – but it doesn’t give children what they need. It means everyone isn’t equal, given the same start and chance. Free school meals would do that for kids.” Of all the attempts to lobby the Labour Party conference, which starts at the end of next week, the Reverend Jones may be leading one of the most unique.

The morning the conference opens, on Sunday 27th September, she will lead a call to prayer on behalf of hungry children up and down the land – from the heart of Andy Burnham’s constituency, Makerfield. Rev Jones will be leading the prayers at St Thomas’s Church, where the Prime Minister is a member of the food pantry, which helps people access good, affordable food.

The former deputy headteacher who leads five churches in Wigan, is hoping the power of prayer will move politicians to act. “Those packed lunches make financial sense, but it doesn’t give children what they need,” the campaigning clergywoman says, when we visit her at St Thomas’s, an imposing red-brick gothic church in Ashton-in-Makerfield. “When I was a teacher, I’d see that in the afternoons – children who weren’t able to learn or listen as well as they could.

‌



“We want all children to have a good, nutritious meal at least once a day without parents having to worry. Too many parents are just above the threshold when it comes to qualifying for free school meals, and they’re often being pushed further into poverty.” Churches across the country can order special packs to remember free school meals in their prayers on Sunday 27th.

Schools to cut down on sugary puddings and deep fried foods in major meals overhaul READ MORE :

Tesco announces free fruit for a week for certain customers in new update READ MORE :

View 4 Images Reverend Sandra Jones to lead a call to prayer at Labour Conference (Image: STEVE ALLEN)

Meanwhile, the National Education Union’s ‘No Child Left Behind’ campaign will have a stall with children from Monksdown Primary School, at the Labour Party’s official conference ‘Sunday Service’ at St James in the City. The campaign, led by teachers, parents and a coalition of 370+ civil society organisations and public figures, urges the Government to extend Free School Meals to all primary school children in England. The way it's done in London and in Wales already.

Sophia Henderson, aged 10, is already a veteran campaigner, having previously travelled to Downing Street to talk to ministers about free school meals. Now she’ll be heading to St James’ to try to catch Labour delegates. “It’s important because we need to be able to do our best,” she explains. “All children deserve it, to have good food.

‌



“You can’t learn when you’re hungry – everything is harder when you’re hungry. But lots of parents can’t afford to pay for the lunches, especially if you have two or three children. If they are free you can save £500 a year for each child – and you can use that to pay your bills.”

Her schoolfriend, Amber Smith, nine, is in Year 5, and will be joining the Labour Party Sunday Service too. “We want the government to understand why we need to do this, to help kids and parents,” Amber says. “I know myself it’s really important to get a good meal. It helps me learn, but not everyone gets it at the moment, and not everyone’s family can afford it and that’s not fair.”

4 View 4 Images Sophia Henderson, 10, is a veteran campaigner for free school meals (Image: Supplied) 4 View 4 Images Amber Smith, nine, will join the Labour Party Sunday Service (Image: Supplied)

‌



In Ashton-in-Makerfield, we also heard from north-west mums who think free school meals are key to lifting cost-of-living pressures on families. “Both me and my partner work – him full-time and me part-time,” Katherine, a mum-of-two from Wigan, said. “So, we’re not entitled to free school meals.

“We find it a struggle to keep our kids' school meals accounts topped up. I top them up £3 a day so £15 for the full week per child. It’s a struggle paying, and I find myself giving my child grief all the time when he goes over the £3-a-day limit I set for him – but it's unaffordable on top of all the other bills. It feels like us workers get punished – even though most weeks we struggle like we don't work.”

Priscilla, another Wigan mum, says free school meals would make a huge difference. “Particularly with the rising cost of food and bills, it would take away some of the financial pressure,” she says. “It would also give parents peace of mind knowing their children are receiving a healthy, nutritious meal at school, while ensuring that no child feels different or excluded.”

Mum Rachel says parents are hit with one cost after another. “We already have to pay for before and after-school clubs just to have the luxury to remain in employment,” she says. Then there are all the holidays where we need to pay £100+ per week per child just to be able to stay in work. And then school meals on top.”

‌



Lindsay, a Wigan foster carer points out that, under the current system, looked after children do not qualify for free school meals. I’m a foster carer; every penny we receive is spent on giving our children amazing experiences,” she says. “In the past we always received free-school meals for our looked after children – a huge weight lifted financially and mentally.

“Now it’s either a rushed packed lunch in a morning or being chased by school to top accounts up. They need at least £5 a day to get something substantial and that adds up very quickly.”

A Department for Education spokesperson said: “This government is giving free school meals to every single child from a household that claims Universal Credit – a historic step backed by over £1 billion in funding that will lift 100,000 children out of poverty. This is alongside the removal of the two-child limit, which taken together, is set to lead to the largest reduction in child poverty in a single parliament, since records began. That is alongside broader action give people the breathing space they need including expanding childcare, rolling out free breakfast clubs across the country, cutting back on uniform costs and cutting energy bills.”

View 4 Images Dan Munro, Youth Mission Enabler at St Thomas in Ashton and part of the campaign (Image: STEVE ALLEN)

‌



Dan Munro, 34, works with young people and schools in the area. St Thomas’s with Rev Jones. “When I go in to school I see young people who haven’t had anything to eat all day,” Dan says. “It’s very sad but not that unusual. When we run activities in school where there is food provided, you notice the ones who always get there first – to make sure they get something to eat, in case the food runs out.

“Even if it’s just chips they will be there. Often young people will ask can they take something home for a brother or sister too - so you know there are other young people who are hungry at home. Giving children one free, good meal a day makes a huge difference to their lives, their learning, their health, their behaviour. As a society it feels like the very least we can do.”

The story of the loaves and the fishes is central to Christian teaching, and organisers say they hope the church’s intervention on Free School Meals will offer space “to reflect on the steps we’d like the new Government to take to promote justice, dignity and equality”.

Rev Jones is praying that “together, we can build a future where no child goes hungry and all children break bread together in the dinner hall – free from stigma and shame.”

News.title: NHS says 20 women had breasts removed unnecessarily as hundreds of cancer patients suffer significant harm
News.content:
Women had their breasts unnecessarily removed at an NHS trust which outsourced cancer surgery under a “pay per patient” deal.

Denise Howarth is one of 20 women told by the County Durham and Darlington Foundation Trust (CDDFT) they were given mastectomies unnecessarily.

The 51-year-old is one of 1,472 breast cancer patients treated at the trust between January 2023 and February 2025 whose treatment was identified for review after a decade of ‘systemic failures’ was identified. From 514 cases reviewed by the trust so far, 315 patients have been found to have suffered harm, including 77 who were significantly harmed. One patient is known to have died.

View 6 Images Denise during her hospital treatment

‌



Private hospitals accused of ‘profiteering’ after demanding more NHS cash in Government deal READ MORE :

Denise, a mother-of-two, said: “They called me at home to say I needn’t have had my breast removed and it was something which really knocked me off my feet. I was just in shock, then ended up in tears on the phone.

“An apology is not enough. This is life-changing. I’ve lost so much confidence. I feel robbed of the person I was before. As a woman, losing a breast has a huge impact on you.”

The trust is now considering reviewing all breast cancer surgeries dating back to 2015 affecting 5,390 procedures.

View 6 Images Amir Bhatti ran NHS breast cancer surgery at the trust as well as being a director at the private clinic

‌



The scandal could have profound implications for outsourcing treatments to private clinics - widespread across the NHS - as an independent review identified a “clear financial incentive” to carry out more operations.

Steve Russell, who has recently taken over as the trust's chief executive, said payment per service is not uncommon in the NHS but said he had ended the practice for breast cancer services at his hospitals. He told the BBC: "We recognise there was a conflict of interest that wasn't managed properly."

Mr Russell said he apologises "unreservedly" for the harm the trust caused, adding: "There are no words I could use to convey how personally distressed I am. What happened was utterly unacceptable."

View 6 Images The trust's newly-arrived CEO Steve Russell says he apologises 'unreservedly' for the harm caused (Image: BBC)

‌



Denise has since found out her surgery was carried out by Cathedral Surgical Services which was one of two privately run clinics contracted by the trust.

Amir Bhatti was the trust’s Consultant Clinical Lead in Breast Surgery at the time - as well as a director at the private clinic which carried out surgeries on Saturdays for the trust.

An external review said this agreement created a “clear financial incentive” linked to “higher patient throughput”. Mr Bhatti was restricted from performing breast cancer surgery by the trust last February.

View 6 Images Amir Bhatti in a previous interview with the BBC

‌



Denise, and other patients, have since been interviewed by Durham Constabulary as part of an investigation to establish if any criminal offences have occurred. She said: “Now, knowing what we know about these clinics and how they were set up, and how many people have suffered from poor treatment, it all feels so wrong. I feel betrayed, hurt and angry at what has happened to me.”

Catriona Dunbar, 41, of Stanley, County Durham, was diagnosed with breast cancer in June 2023 and has been interviewed by police about her treatment. She received a letter of apology from the trust for a lack of informed consent before surgery, lack of proper post-op dressings and taking three months to confirm test results on whether the cancer had returned.

Ms Dunbar, who is represented by Hudgell Solicitors, said: "The letter is full of apologies but there is no accountability. Nobody is doing the right thing and taking ownership for what has happened to so many women."

Denise had been diagnosed with grade 1 slow growing cancer in 2023 after discovering a lump in her breast. She initially underwent a lumpectomy, then a mastectomy, as well as eight rounds of chemotherapy and radiotherapy.

‌



View 6 Images Denise Howarth is among hundreds who were harmed

She was told by the NHS in September 2025 that she could have been offered a second lumpectomy rather than full breast removal. This option had never been discussed with her. She has instructed Hudgell Solicitors to represent her in taking legal action against the trust.

Denise said: “I fear I will never be the same person again, although I have tried to be strong. Friends are very kind, they praise me and tell me I look great and say how strong I am, but the reality is it’s a huge struggle. I’ve broken down many times.

“I find it difficult to choose clothing I feel comfortable and happy in, and it worsens at this time of year as I can’t really wear the summer tops with straps, I always need to wear a T-shirt.”

‌



View 6 Images Surgeon Amir Bhatti's picture on the wall at the hospital (BBC)

Denise is also critical of the post-operative support offered to her, which has meant that she has never had reconstructive surgery. She said: “I asked many times at my reviews about breast reconstruction, but I was told it was too soon, and that I would need major surgery.

“I mentioned that I didn’t feel in the right head space [for that] at that time, but I’d not ruled it out completely. I then got a letter saying I’d turned it down, which was not the case at all.”

She added: “I’ve always been one to keep quiet, but I feel I need to be vocal on this. I feel we all do, all the women who have been affected and harmed. We are stronger together.

‌



“We need people at the trust, from management to the consultants, to be held to account. This simply should not be happening to one person, let alone hundreds as it has.”

When approached by the BBC about the story, Amir Bhatti said: “I remain committed to the ongoing trust investigation and it would be inappropriate for me to discuss this whilst proceedings are ongoing."

Steve Russell said in a statement: "We are deeply sorry to the women and families who have been harmed and let down by failings in our breast services.

"We recognise the profound impact this has had and have been clear that there were opportunities when, as a trust, we should have listened more carefully and acted sooner. Significant changes have since been made to the breast service and are bringing improvements for patients.

‌



"Our dedicated support line remains available to anyone with concerns about their breast care on 0191 333 2126 or at cddft.breastservices@nhs.net."

News.title: Women told breasts removed needlessly as NHS trust finds more than 300 suffered harm
News.content:
Pam Brown from Durham was an NHS patient who underwent a mastectomy in 2022 at Spire Hospital in Washington, where one of the outsourced private clinics was based.

As with Denise and Jo, Pam does not know who carried out her operation. Bhatti was the consultant overseeing the care of all three women.

As far as Pam knows, her mastectomy was necessary. But the scars left behind - both physical and psychological - have deeply affected her.

We have shown photographs of Pam's scarring to Liz O'Riordan, a former breast cancer surgeon. She describes them as "awful" and says she has never seen anything like it: "That's not acceptable at all. I'd have brought her back for revision surgery."

Concerns were also raised last year in a report by the Royal College of Surgeons (RCS) that breast cancer cases had not been discussed properly in multi-disciplinary team meetings (MDTs).

These meetings are designed to ensure treatment plans are reviewed and challenged by surgeons, radiologists, pathologists and cancer specialists - before major decisions, such as mastectomies, are made.

There was little evidence the trust's breast unit was contributing to MDTs, and decisions about patients' cases were being made based on the unchallenged opinion of individual surgeons, according to the RCS report.

Outdated practices at the trust that did not meet guidance on best practice included a high rate of "re-excision" (repeated procedures), low uptake of breast reconstruction immediately after mastectomy, and operations that may have been carried out "too quickly".

The Aubrey review also suggested patients were potentially treated by locum consultants who were not competent, and noted that Bhatti had repeatedly raised concerns about trust delays in obtaining vital diagnostic equipment.

CDDFT says it is co-operating fully with the investigation by Durham Police and the National Crime Agency - and is sharing information when requested.

But for the women whose breasts have been wrongly removed, it is too late.

"You can't put a breast back," says O'Riordan. "These are lifelong disfigurements, and it's horrific." Breast cancer surgery, she says, "has some of the tightest guidelines and protocols, and you should have the same treatment wherever you are, private or public, in any part of the UK."

The Department of Health and Social Care says its thoughts are with the women and families affected but it is not able to "comment further on those past failings while the current investigation is ongoing".

It adds that the trust is working urgently with NHS England, the Care Quality Commission and independent experts to address what happened "and to ensure that all future patients receive safe care".

We approached Amir Bhatti about the concerns raised. He said: "I am grateful for the opportunity to respond, but I remain committed to the ongoing trust investigation, and it would be inappropriate for me to discuss this whilst proceedings are ongoing."

News.title: Woman tells BBC of trauma after unnecessary breast cancer surgery
News.content:
Twenty women underwent mastectomies unnecessarily while being treated for breast cancer, an NHS trust in north-east England has told the BBC.

They were among hundreds of patients who came to harm during treatment at the breast unit of the County Durham and Darlington Foundation Trust (CDDFT).

The admission comes in the wake of revelations about serious failures in the unit, as reported by the BBC last year.

Steve Russell, who has recently taken over as CDDFT's chief executive, says he apologises "unreservedly" for the harm the trust caused.

Denise Howarth is one of several women who have been told by the NHS that their breast was removed unnecessarily.

The BBC's health correspondent Sharon Barbour has this report.

Read more on this story.

News.title: Our brother did not match description of 'Putney pusher', suspect's sisters tell BBC
News.content:
The sisters of the man suspected of being the so-called "Putney pusher" have told the BBC their brother was innocent, and accused the Metropolitan Police of being "negligent and reckless".

Nicholas Brandram's sisters gave BBC Radio 4's Today programme a list of reasons why they believed their brother could not have been the jogger who pushed a woman into the path of a bus on Putney Bridge, west London, in May 2017.

Brandram was found dead on Tuesday evening and his family said he "took his own life after months of immense pressure" caused by the Met investigation.

The Met said it recognised the "strain that being subject to a police investigation" could cause, and that a mandatory referral had been made to the police watchdog.

Brandram's sisters Alexia Hicks and Sophie Voelcker told Today presenter Justin Webb their brother's mental health had been deteriorating in recent months and that "every day was becoming difficult" while he was under police scrutiny.

They said it was "ridiculous" their brother - a banker and former army officer - was the suspect because:

His identity did not match the profile of the pusher, saying their brother had a withered leg from an old army injury and a prominent military tattoo on his forearm

The victim reported the attacker had brown eyes but their brother had blue

Their brother lived in Notting Hill, had no connection with Putney and they had evidence to suggest he was in his Bond Street office at the time of the attack

He willingly provided a DNA sample to the Met to speed up the inquiry but never received results, despite pleading with police to speed them up

"It's out there on the internet what the so-called Putney pusher looked like. We provided evidence very quickly to show that this did not look like our brother," the sisters said.

"Nine and a half years ago when the incident occurred, there'd been absolutely nothing connecting our brother to the attack.

"So this came completely out of the blue, off effectively an allegation which must have been either malicious or mistaken."

News.title: MI5 accepts it gave evidence based on lies in neo-Nazi spy case
News.content:
The hearing follows a damning official report, published in July, which concluded that MI5 gave evidence based on "lies" to three courts while defending a violent neo-Nazi spy whose abuse was uncovered by the BBC.

The report, by the then deputy investigatory powers commissioner Sir John Goldring, heavily criticised a series of senior MI5 figures and their organisation.

He found that one senior MI5 spy - known as Officer 2 - lied repeatedly, while another - Officer 3 - misled his own colleagues and lied about what he was told.

He also found there were "serious and systemic failures in MI5's conduct" throughout the case.

Sir John's investigation was ordered by the prime minister in September 2025 after MI5's explanations about what happened were rejected as deficient and unreliable by the High Court.

In court on Friday, Otty announced that "MI5 accepts without reservation" Sir John's findings, including about the actions of individual officers and "systemic failure" within the organisation itself. Until now, MI5 had only offered apologies for giving "incorrect" evidence.

He said MI5 "fully accepts and acknowledges the gravity of the issues raised" and they must never happen again.

He added that MI5 had committed to a major programme of reform under the leadership of director general Sir Ken McCallum.

Otty argued against contempt of court proceedings being brought, saying it would not be in the public interest given the detailed Goldring investigation, MI5's apologies, and its commitment to a programme of reform.

He said Officer 2 had resigned from the service and that Officer 3 had been suspended and was facing disciplinary proceedings, which could lead to his dismissal.

The court will hear legal submissions later on Friday from barristers for the BBC and Officers 2 and 3.

The case centres around an MI5 informant known as Agent X, a foreign neo-Nazi misogynist who used his security service role as a tool of abuse.

He coercively controlled his partner, known by the alias Beth, and attacked her with a machete. MI5 then helped him go abroad to continue intelligence work while under police investigation.

The government took the BBC to court in 2022 in a failed attempt to block its investigation into X, but won him legal anonymity. Beth then sued MI5 at the Investigatory Powers Tribunal, and in 2024 she sought a review of a ruling at the High Court.

Arguing for secrecy in all three courts, the security service told judges that it had always stuck to its core secrecy policy and never told anyone whether X was an agent, including me - as the BBC journalist who had investigated him. The courts were told this in a sworn statement from a senior officer, a deputy director called Witness A.

The courts accepted MI5's arguments. This meant Beth and everyone else was banned from ever officially being told X was an agent and denied access to the key evidence. She was left at a serious disadvantage and may have lost the case.

But what MI5 said was untrue.

MI5 had in fact disclosed the man's agent status in phone calls to me, as it tried to persuade me not to investigate him in 2020.

Officer 2 had tried to cover up for the man, falsely saying he was not an abusive misogynist nor a real extremist.

Following the court decision, in late 2024, I challenged MI5 and said they had lied to the courts. MI5 aggressively maintained its position that its "neither confirm nor deny" policy (known as NCND) had been maintained until I produced evidence proving it was untrue, including a recording of one of the calls with Officer 2.

Because of the BBC's revelations, two official inquiries took place which absolved MI5 and its officers of deliberate wrongdoing, claiming the false evidence was down to mistakes and poor memories.

But, in July 2025, a panel of senior High Court judges ruled that the investigations carried out by MI5 suffered from "serious procedural deficiencies" and that "we cannot rely on their conclusions", leading to Sir John's investigation and Friday's hearing.

News.title: War may be coming. Are we psychologically ready?
News.content:
If the UK suddenly found itself at war, would you know what to do? Do you know what would be expected of you?

The government wants us all to start preparing for severe disruption to our lives. It wants us to stockpile canned food and drinking water, strengthen our civic resilience, and plan for the possibility of war.

Work has begun on the government's so-called "war book", which hasn't been updated in decades.

The UK's most senior soldier has sounded the alarm. The Chief of the Defence Staff Sir Richard Knighton this week said the threat from Russia meant Britain was living through the "most dangerous" period of his 35-year career in the armed forces.

But what is the threat? In 1940 the danger of a German invasion of the UK was very real. But the chances of Russian tanks rolling up Whitehall are surely negligible.

"It's not the tanks you need to worry about," says historian Margaret MacMillan, author of War: How Conflict Shaped Us.

"It's the cutting of cables on the ocean floor. It's the hacking into systems on which so many things depend. The possibility for asymmetric war, for cyber war, is growing by leaps and bounds."

But are we ready? After 80 years without war on our own soil, are we, as a society, psychologically prepared for it? Are we ready to approve large increases in defence spending, and for the sacrifices that that might entail in other areas of our national life? Or does the threat seem too far-fetched to be real?

News.title: British woman rescued in Malawi shootout that left four suspected kidnappers dead
News.content:
A British woman who was kidnapped in Malawi nearly a week ago has been rescued in a police operation that left four suspected kidnappers dead and a senior police chief wounded.

Nusrat Osman, 47, was freed on Thursday during an operation on the outskirts of the southern city of Blantyre, police said.

Officers exchanged gunfire with the suspected kidnappers, who police said were armed with an AK-47 rifle and a pistol.

"The criminals got shot and were rushed to the hospital where they succumbed to the injuries," the Malawi Police Service said in a statement.

Deputy Inspector General of Police Noel Kayira, who was involved in the operation, also sustained gunshot injuries and is being treated in hospital. The police statement said he was in a stable condition.

Osman was reunited with her family following the rescue and was also taken to hospital for treatment, and for physical and mental health assessments, local media reported.

Osman's younger brother, Shobi Jiwa, praised the Malawian police for securing her release, telling the UK's Sun newspaper that the family was deeply grateful for the force's efforts in investigating the kidnapping.

He also paid tribute to Kayira, the police chief who was shot during the rescue operation, describing him as the family's "hero" for putting his own life at risk to save her.

Police have not identified the four suspected kidnappers who were killed and have not provided further details about how officers located the group.

Osman was abducted by four unidentified men in Blantyre's Mount Pleasant neighbourhood on 11 September.

Police said she had been driving home when the men blocked her vehicle, forced her into another car and drove away.

Her disappearance prompted a major search operation, with authorities offering a reward of 30 million Malawian kwacha ($17,000; Â£12,500) for information leading to her rescue and the arrest and conviction of those responsible.

Osman, who is from Leicester in the UK, has lived in Malawi for several years and works for an auditing firm. She is married and has two young children.

The UK Foreign Office earlier told the BBC that it was aware of reports that a British national had been abducted in Malawi and was in touch with local authorities.

The case had puzzled investigators because police said there had been no known ransom demand or communication from the kidnappers following her disappearance.

Her family had made emotional public appeals for her safe return, describing the disappearance as deeply distressing and urging anyone with information to contact police.

The kidnapping also caused concern among Malawi's business community and British nationals living in the southern African country, where abductions of foreign nationals are relatively uncommon.

Police have not disclosed a possible motive or said whether they believe other people were involved.

They said investigations were continuing to establish the full circumstances surrounding the kidnapping and the subsequent rescue operation.

Authorities have urged the public to remain calm while the investigation continues.

News.title: New wild cat species discovered - with only one known living member
News.content:
A spotted cat from the forests of Bolivia has been confirmed as a new species.

The small feline, about the size of a domestic moggy, went under the radar because it was confused with other wild cats that share similar spots and stripes.

But DNA studies show the cat is actually in a class of its own, highlighting how much remains unknown about some of the world's most elusive mammals.

Scientists hope the discovery will draw attention to the conservation of tiger cats, a group of small wild cats found in South and Central America that receives far less public attention than their larger cousins like lions, leopards and tigers.

News.title: US fans with Ed Sheeran tickets left torn over Macklemore controversy
News.content:
The snowballing controversy over pro-Palestinian rapper Macklemore being dropped as a support act for Ed Sheeran has plunged the tour into crisis and left concert-goers in the middle of the fraught Israel-Gaza debate.

Fans who spoke to the BBC - including those who have tickets to see Sheeran's next show - have been split since Macklemore was dropped from the Loop Tour this week after his "free Palestine" protest on stage.

All of Sheeran's opening acts have since quit in solidarity.

"I'm still torn," Damien Given told the BBC on whether he would attend Sheeran's show on Saturday, calling the artist's response disingenuous. Another fan called it a "no-win situation".

Since the controversy blew up earlier this week, ticket prices, external for his remaining shows in the US, Mexico and South America have dropped, as calls for boycotts spread.

Sheeran has responded, saying he's been "appalled by the conflict between Israel and Palestine", but would not be drawn into a political debate.

News.title: Charles 'sounded giddily elated' after Diana died, Earl Spencer claims
News.content:
Earl Spencer, brother of Diana, Princess of Wales, has claimed King Charles "sounded giddily elated" when he called him after her death in 1997.

In a controversial book about Diana, he alleged the then-Prince Charles sounded like a "lottery winner" after the news.

Buckingham Palace strongly pushed back on Wednesday against the credibility of the book after an initial extract claimed Charles had said of Diana: "We'll forget her soon enough."

A spokesperson said: "While we do not comment on books as a matter of principle, His Majesty is mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgment and colour memory in ways others do not recognise, even many years after such a loss."

The latest claims are once again highly personal in their attacks on King Charles and the royals, interpreting their motives in a very harsh light.

The evidence is Earl Spencer's own recollection of conversations about that emotional time around his sister's death, almost 30 years ago.

What remains to be seen is how the public might respond to the allegations, whether they might support this book as a new and different Spencer perspective, or whether they might feel it to be inappropriate to be sharing such private disputes.

Representatives of Prince Harry have said they do not want to comment on the book and Buckingham Palace has pointed back to its response from Wednesday, when it rejected the account of Prince Charles in the wake of Diana's death in Paris.

News.title: Family of Jagtar Singh Johal say Scot detained in India has been granted bail
News.content:
The family of a Scottish Sikh activist who has been locked up in India for almost nine years without conviction have said he has been granted bail.

Jagtar Singh Johal, from Dumbarton, was arrested in 2017 in connection with alleged terror offences.

He was arrested for his alleged role in a series of targeted killings of religious and political figures.

His family said they were still waiting for the details of what will happen next but are "relieved" by the Indian court's decision.

The 39-year-old was acquitted last year in a case in which he was accused of financially supporting terror group the Khalistan Liberation Force (KLF), which has carried out attacks in the Punjab region.

But he still faces federal charges lodged by the Indian authorities.

Johal's imprisonment was recognised by a UN panel as arbitrary detention in 2022 and he has claimed to have been tortured.

Indian authorities have previously denied the torture claim and have repeatedly maintained due process is being followed.

He was arrested in the Punjab region just weeks after his wedding in the country.

His supporters say he was targeted for blogging about alleged human rights abuses against the Sikh community in India and was coerced into signing a false confession to participation in the killings.

His brother Gurpreet Singh Johal has lobbied successive governments calling for his brother's release.

News.title: Badenoch says she is instructing lawyers to challenge government after Tory-run council's 94% tax hike
News.content:
Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has said she has brought in lawyers to potentially challenge the government over local funding cuts, after a record council tax rise in one of her party's flagship local authorities.

She told BBC Newsnight the proposed 94% hike in Wandsworth, a south-west London borough run by the Tories, was "outrageous" but that "they're not doing it because they want to".

Badenoch said the Conservative Party had "instructed lawyers" to see if an Â£84m-a-year government funding cut, which Wandsworth Council has blamed for the increase, can be blocked.

The government said it was "fixing an outdated funding system so funding goes where need is greatest".

Wandsworth has long had one of the lowest council tax rates in the country, with an average Band D property currently paying just over Â£1,000, compared to above Â£2,000 in an increasing number of London boroughs.

But this would nearly double with the planned Â£958 rise.

There has been heavy criticism since the move was announced in a council meeting on Tuesday. A final decision is to be made early next year.

Changes to the funding formula for councils announced last year will see money redistributed from some council areas to others. Wandsworth Council said it stood to lose Â£84m annually in funding by the end of the next three years.

Commenting for the first time on the row, Badenoch accused ministers of seemingly "taking money from areas that don't vote Labour and giving it to places that do vote Labour".

"I think it is outrageous that Wandsworth Council is having to put up council tax.

"But they're not doing it because they want to. It is because the government has taken away 40% of their funding.

"So we have actually instructed lawyers, as the Conservative Party, to see if we can challenge the government on this decision."

News.title: Healey to ask EU finance ministers to let UK into Made in Europe scheme
News.content:
The chancellor is to warn the European Union (EU) not to lock the UK out of its scheme to protect industries from unfair Chinese competition.

John Healey will push for closer UK-EU partnerships on tech, defence, and manufacturing at a meeting of EU finance ministers in Dublin on Friday.

But he will call on the EU to design its "Made in Europe" programme in a way that deepens ties with the UK "rather than erecting new barriers", Treasury sources told the BBC.

Officials said Healey will tell European finance ministers it is important to "learn lessons" after talks collapsed last year for Britain to join an EU defence loans scheme.

That dispute centred on how much money the UK would pay to join.

The "Made in Europe" policy, officially called the Industrial Accelerator Act (IAA), is currently being considered by the bloc and aims to protect EU manufacturing with restrictions on goods from outside countries.

There is concern in government the scheme could lock British firms out of European supply chains.

Treasury officials said Healey wanted to reduce the economic impact of Brexit and build closer ties with the EU, but not at any cost to the UK.

Former UK trade negotiator Sir Crawford Falconer said the EU's original plan would have allowed free trade partners - such as the UK - to be included in the scheme but a subsequent proposal recommended limiting membership to EU nations.

Sir Crawford said that caused "everyone to hit the panic button," adding: "If we weren't able to complete on equal terms, it would put the viability of some of our production facilities at risk."

Earlier this year, the Nissan car company said: "EU and UK manufacturing are deeply intertwined, and restricting eligibility for public support to EU only assembly would damage competitiveness, disrupt integrated supply chains, and undermine Europe's EV transition."

Healey said: "The next chapter of Britain's growth story will be written in more places.

"To me, closer ties with the EU means British businesses â wherever they are based across the UK â get better access to both the supply chains and the customers they need to grow."

Healey will use the meeting in Dublin to focus on tech firms, defence companies, and manufacturing.

"The chancellor wants to make sure nothing holds them back," a Treasury source said.

It comes after a reset summit with the EU was delayed after Sir Keir Starmer's resignation as prime minister.

Treasury sources now expect that to take place in November.

Healey's meeting in Dublin comes after it emerged earlier this week that he is in discussions about joining a global investment bank aimed at raising more money for defence spending.

He is considering a bid to join the Defence, Security and Resilience Bank (DSRB), not long after his predecessor Rachel Reeves rejected the idea.

Canada has been leading efforts to establish the bank, which supporters say would enable governments to borrow at lower costs to increase military spending.

Paying for the UK's growing defence commitments is one of Healey's biggest headaches as he prepares for the Budget in October and next year's spending review.

News.title: Sunshine to return to parts of UK with warmer and drier weather on way
News.content:
Don't pack away your summer clothes just yet as warmer and drier weather could be set to return to the UK next week.

Temperatures could reach as high as 25C in parts of England and Wales - several degrees above the average for the time of year.

Forecasts for early next week show an area of high pressure building near the UK. This will largely block Atlantic weather systems, which often bring wind and rain, from reaching the country.

North-west Scotland will see some rain but these systems are not expected to push across the rest of the UK, so this would mean drier weather with lighter winds and higher daytime temperatures for most.

The last few weeks have been very changeable with rain and strong winds in most parts of the UK.

Despite this, the whole of Wales and most of England are still in drought.

After stronger south-westerly winds are due to blow cloud and outbreaks of rain across from the west on Friday, the weather will start to settle down over the weekend.

The northern half of the UK will see a return to sunshine and blustery showers on Saturday, with most of the showers being in Scotland.

The southern half of the UK is likely to be more cloudy and have a muggy feel with the chance of light rain and drizzle.

News.title: UK's 'dismal' Eurovision song choices to be examined by MPs
News.content:
The UK's "dismal" record in selecting songs and acts for Eurovision is to be scrutinised by MPs.

In May, Look Mum No Computer came last with one point. In 2023 Mae Muller finished second from bottom and in 2021 James Newman came last - this time with "nul points".

The act that represents the UK is selected by the BBC, sometimes with a record label or music management company.

The chair of the Digital, Culture, Media and Sport committee, Dame Caroline Dinenage, said: "We want to get to the bottom of who chooses our entrant, on what basis and whether our dismal record of achievement in recent years [Sam Ryder to one side] is the result of bad song choice, weak performance... or something else".

News.title: Fenced-in woman, 81, wins three-year access fight
News.content:
An 81-year-old has won a three-year battle against a council that fenced across a gap in her garden wall her family had used as access for decades.

Helene Ball - a resident of George Road in Matlock, Derbyshire, since 1967 - took legal action after Derbyshire County Council cemented a metal fence panel blocking the 98cm gated gap between her garden and a council car park in April 2023.

A first-tier tribunal has ruled in Ball's favour over the dispute, after she proved use of the gate since the 1960s.

A right of way has now been established, while the council has been ordered by the courts to pay Â£50,000 costs and to ensure her access is not impeded again.

Ball, a retired teacher, told the Local Democracy Reporting Service: "I have taught nine, 10 and 11-year-olds all my life, but I never expected the council to act so babyish, they have been spitting their dummies out of the pram and it has been beyond childish.

"They did everything they could to bully me. They tried to put us off but they messed with the wrong ones.

"At my age you don't know how many years you have left, and this has given me three years-plus of stress but now we have proven they blocked our rights."

News.title: Archbishop of Canterbury withdraws award from Muslim cleric who praised Osama bin Laden
News.content:
The Archbishop of Canterbury has withdrawn an award given to a Muslim cleric who praised Osama Bin Laden.

Hafiz Muhammad Tahir Mehmood Ashrafi received the award for reconciliation and interfaith cooperation from Dame Sarah Mullally last week, on the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 attacks.

Lambeth Palace faced a backlash after it emerged Ashrafi praised Bin Laden - the architect of the 2001 attacks - as someone who had "been fighting for Islam against the Russians, Americans and British", in comments from 2007.

Ashrafi also reportedly said he would give Bin Laden the title Saifullah, which means "Sword of God". He told the BBC his remarks had been "totally taken out of context".

Lambeth Palace now says "comments made by Imam Ashrafi have come to light that have led (us) to reconsider this award and we can now confirm that the award has been withdrawn".

In presenting the award last week, the Archbishop's office said Ashrafi was being honoured for "his outstanding work as an ambassador of interfaith harmony in Pakistan, known for his commitment to promoting religious tolerance".

His award was presented by Dame Sarah in a ceremony that coincided with the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 attacks in the US in which nearly 3,000 people were killed.

Ashrafi told the BBC that his remarks had been "totally taken out of context" and the backlash had been "an unfair campaign" against him.

He said that he was only speaking about Bin Laden in 2007 in response to "the hurt felt by many Muslims" over a knighthood being awarded to the Satanic Verses author Sir Salman Rushdie.

But he defended the comparison he made between an author and a man who was behind the deaths of thousands of people.

Criticism of Ashrafi has gone beyond his comments about Bin Laden.

In giving him his award for promoting interfaith harmony last week, Lambeth Palace had cited the fact that Ashrafi had intervened in the 2012 case of Rimsha Masih, a young Christian girl in Pakistan falsely accused of blasphemy.

But Ashrafi has otherwise been supportive of Pakistan's blasphemy laws that have led to an estimated 2,000 people being prosecuted since the late 1980s.

They include a disproportionately high number of Pakistan's minority Christians and Ahmadis in particular, but many majority Sunni Muslims too.

Ashrafi claimed the blasphemy laws actually "save lives", stopping people taking matters into their own hands.

But Human Rights Watch said last year that "the laws perpetuate religious discrimination and are used to target the poor and minorities in unlawful evictions and land grabs".

The organisation has called on the Pakistani government to urgently reform the laws to prevent them "being weaponised to [...] attack marginalised communities".

New York Knicks star Jalen Brunson will make a guest appearance on Law & Order: SVU this autumn.

NBC announced on Thursday that Brunson is set to feature in the fifth episode of the season, scheduled for broadcast on 5 November. Specific details regarding his role have not been disclosed.

Brunson also appeared on Monday during the opening of the Emmy Awards telecast, which was hosted by Law & Order: SVU star Mariska Hargitay.

Hargitay is a Knicks fan who attended Game 4 of the NBA Finals as New York overturned a 29-point deficit to beat the San Antonio Spurs 107-106, a victory that led the franchise to its first title since 1973. Hargitay and Brunson hugged on court after the game.

Brunson, who plays point guard for the Knicks, spearheaded his team's historic championship win, averaging 28.4 points during the playoffs.

Hargitay, 62, who has starred in Law and Order: SVU for the past 27 years, recently hosted last Sunday’s Emmy Awards. During her opening monologue, she pretended not to know the word “finale,” given that she’s never had one. She also poked fun at Law & Order creator Dick Wolf, joking that wisecracks about his name are unfair as his real name is “Richard Penis.”

Jalen Brunson and Mariska Hargitay attend the "My Mom Jayne: A Film by Mariska Hargitay" ( Getty )

She also spoofed Nicole Kidman’s famous  for AMC cinemas, only to be interrupted by Kidman herself. “Zip it, movie lady,” Hargitay told her. “It’s TV’s turn tonight.”

Hargitay is herself an Emmy winner four times over. She won Outstanding Lead Actress in a Drama Series for Law & Order: Special Victims Unit in 2006 and Best Documentary in 2017 for I Am Evidence.

At the Creative Arts Emmys earlier this month, she won two more Emmys for her documentary about her mother Jayne Mansfield, My Mom Jayne.

Elsewhere, Brunson has also been has also been confirmed a guest host for the new season of Saturday Night Live. The 30-year-old will make his hosting debut on Sept. 26 alongside musical guest Katseye, a pop girl group.

Other basketball stars who previously hosted the show include Charles Barkley, Michael Jordan and LeBron James.

A Powerball player has come forward to claim a prize worth over $1 billion, bought with a $2 ticket.

​The sole winner of the huge jackpot will take home the eighth-largest prize in Powerball history, officials at the Illinois Lottery confirmed on September 15 - a month after the draw on August 12.

​The winner, who has chosen to remain anonymous, revealed that they experienced everything from disbelief to shock after finding out that they had won $1.04 billion.

​“I initially didn’t believe I had won, so I called a family member to confirm it,” the winner said. “Even after claiming the prize, I’m still processing the news and experiencing the full range of emotions that come with winning a billion-dollar jackpot — from disbelief and shock to overwhelming elation.”

​The as-yet unnamed winner also opened up about buying their ticket for just $2.

An Illinois Powerball winner has claimed a $1.04 billion prize, opting for the lump-sum offer of over $450 million ( Getty )

​“I chose a Quick Pick and spent just $2 on a single line of Powerball numbers,” they said. “I never could have imagined that a $2 purchase would lead to a $1.04 billion jackpot.”

​The winner added, “This is truly a blessing, and I’m incredibly grateful for this unexpected and extraordinary opportunity.”

​The Illinois Lottery confirmed that the winner took the prize as a smaller lump-sum payment, instead of the full amount, which is paid over a number of years.

​The lump-sum is valued at around $450.5 million, but that amount is subject to an automatic federal withholding of 24 percent. According to Forbes, the winner could also face a federal marginal rate along with a 4.95 percent tax imposed by the state of Illinois.

​The ticket was purchased ahead of the August 12 drawing at the Hy-Vee Fast & Fresh convenience store in Quincy, Illinois. Hy-Vee Fast & Fresh received a $500,000 retailer bonus for selling the ticket.

​The numbers chosen by the anonymous winner were 4, 26, 66, 67 and 69. The red Powerball number was 9.

The odds of winning the Powerball grand prize are 1 in 292,201,338.00, according to the brand’s website.​

HarperCollins is set to phase out remaining copies of David Walliams’s books after announcing last year that they would no longer publish him.

The book publisher said last year that it had dropped the children’s author following reports that he was accused of behaving inappropriately towards young women. Walliams strongly denies any claims and said at the time that he had not been informed about an investigation by HarperCollins.

HarperCollins has now confirmed that it has dropped Walliams’s backlist, according to The Bookseller. The publication reported that the publisher will gradually phase out stock of Walliams’s books in shops as well as e-book and audio versions available online.

The Independent has contacted Walliams and HarperCollins for comment.

open image in gallery David Walliams with Miranda Hart and Robbie Williams in the TV adaptation of ‘Gangsta Granny’ ( BBV )

HarperCollins has published all 23 of the children’s books written by Walliams, beginning with 2008’s The Boy in the Dress, as well as his short story collections and picture books. They’ve sold over 60 million copies worldwide, while six of them have been adapted for TV.

Those titles – which include bestsellers Mr Stink, Gangsta Granny and Ratburger – have since disappeared from the HarperCollins website, along with his author page.

In December, HarperCollins announced that “after careful consideration, and under the leadership of its new CEO”, it would not be publishing any new titles by Walliams. It came after The Telegraph reported that a complaint from a junior colleague about his conduct lead to other staff members being interviewed and subsequently, he was dropped.

Former employees alleged to the publication that they were advised not to visit his home and to work in pairs when meeting with him.

A spokesperson for Harper Collins said at the time: “HarperCollins takes employee wellbeing extremely seriously and has processes in place for reporting and investigating concerns. To respect the privacy of individuals, we do not comment on internal matters.”

Walliams denied the allegations of inappropriate behaviour, with a spokesperson for him saying in a statement: “David has never been informed of any allegations raised against him by HarperCollins. He was not party to any investigation or given any opportunity to answer questions. David strongly denies that he has behaved inappropriately and is taking legal advice.”

open image in gallery David Walliams released 23 books as well as short story collections and picture books with HarperCollins(Ian West/PA) ( PA Wire )

Days later, the Waterstones Children’s Book Festival axed him from its line-up following HarperCollins’s move.

The actor and comedian rose to fame in the early noughties alongside Matt Lucas with their BBC sketch comedies Little Britain and Come Fly with Me. He became a judge on Britain’s Got Talent in 2012, staying in the role for 10 years but left after a leaked transcript revealed obscene comments he’d made about contestants.

The transcript, leaked to The Guardian in 2022, revealed that during an audition at the London Palladium two years earlier, he called one contestant a “c***” and said of another: “She thinks you want to f*** her, but you don’t.”

At the time, he apologised for the “disrespectful comments” and said that they were part of a private conversation which was “never intended to be shared”. He later sued BGT’s production company FremantleMedia for the leaking of the private remarks, with the matter being settled in November 2023.

At least 15 people have been killed, and dozens more wounded in a bombing at a mosque near a building housing police offices in northwestern Pakistan.

Bilal Faizi, a senior rescue official, said the bombing occurred in Kohat, a district in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province bordering Afghanistan.

More than 30 people were wounded, most of whom were worshippers, he said.

Doctors and officials at the hospital said some of the wounded were in critical condition, raising fears the death toll could rise.

Zulfiqar Hameed, the provincial police chief, said an attacker apparently rammed an explosives-laden vehicle into the mosque, but officers were still investigating.

At least two armed gunmen also attempted to enter the police compound and exchanged fire with officers, local police said.

The victims were taken to a nearby hospital where authorities declared an emergency to handle the influx of casualties. Local police said the explosion was powerful enough to badly damage nearby shops and homes.

open image in gallery Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif condemned the attack ( Getty )

Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif condemned the attack and expressed sorrow over the casualties in a statement issued by his office. He directed authorities to accelerate rescue operations, provide medical care to the wounded and extend assistance to those affected.

Footage posted on social media showed the mosque’s roof had collapsed. Rescuers and residents could be seen pulling injured people from the rubble and carrying them to ambulances.

No group immediately claimed responsibility for the attack, but suspicion was likely to fall on the Pakistani Taliban, formally known as Tehrik-e-Taliban Pakistan, or TTP.

The attack comes a day after a roadside bomb struck a security forces convoy in the northwestern Hangu district and killed six soldiers. Government troops also conducted raids in various areas Thursday and killed 10 militants believed to be members of the Pakistani Taliban, the military and local police said Friday.

Pakistani Taliban have stepped up attacks on police and civilians in recent years. In 2023, a suicide bomber killed 101 people in an attack inside a mosque in Peshawar, the capital of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province.

The group is separate from but allied with Afghanistan’s Taliban, which returned to power in 2021. Pakistan often accuses Kabul of sheltering the TTP and turning a blind eye to cross-border militant attacks. The government in Kabul has denied the allegations.

The Inbetweeners star James Buckley appears to have accidentally let slip a detail about the upcoming third film in a video message for a fan.

Last week, fans were delighted to hear after months of speculation that The Inbetweeners 3 is on its way at Netflix, with all four core original cast members – Simon Bird, Joe Thomas, James Buckley and Blake Harrison – signing on.

Filming has already kicked off, with Buckley, who played chronic liar Jay Cartwright in the Channel 4 series and its two subsequent spin-off films, “leaking” a detail about his character’s fate in a video for a fan.

Following the announcement about the new film, a TikTok user called Sydney posted a video message she’d purchased from Buckley for her loved ones on the video sharing app.

open image in gallery The words 'Cartwright Plant' could be seen in Buckley's video ( TikTok/@sindystarfire )

The clip – presumably purchased on video app Cameo, where Buckley is one of the UK’s biggest earners – showed the podcast host congratulating the couple in question on the news that they are expecting twins.

However, it was Buckley’s outfit that caught fans’ attention; not only was his hair Jay’s shade of blonde and cut into a mullet, but the actor wore a blue shirt and bright green jacket with the words “Cartwright Plant” partially visible on the chest.

In the original Inbetweeners series, Jay’s dad Terry (David Schaal) runs Cartwright Plant Hire, which suggests now that Jay is working for the family business in the new film.

The video was flooded with screenshots of the logo and speculation from fans, leading to the original poster responding: “Oh s*** I feel like I’ve leaked something now unknowingly.”

open image in gallery From L-R: Thomas, Bird, Harrison and Cartwright in ‘The Inbetweeners’ ( Channel 4 )

The Independent has contacted Netflix for comment.

Reports of a new film being in the works first sprung up last year, when creators Damon Beesley and Iain Morris claimed that the Channel 4 comedy, which first ran on E4 from 2008 to 2010, would be returning in some form.

While some fans had feared that the series would instead be rebooted with a new young cast, Netflix instead confirmed that the original Inbetweeners were all returning for The Inbetweeners 3, with production beginning on 7 September.

Beesley and Morris, who are once again writing and directing the franchise, said: ”It’s been super-fun hanging out with our friends again, and we’re going to work hard every week to ensure there are no problemos making this new film for humans.”

The latest movie, which follows on from Inbetweeners box office hit feature films from 2011 and 2014, is expected to be released in 2027. It is not currently known whether The Inbetweeners 3 will be released in cinemas before coming out on Netflix.
