The LRA itself has said the milestone should not be treated as an end in itself. Commissioner General James Dorbor Jallah has said the revenue authority’s performance should ultimately be judged by whether increased collections help finance development and improve public services.

Ngombu Kpawor, a Rehab Community resident, similarly welcomed the milestone but said Liberians would judge it by its effect on schools, hospitals and employment.

“We welcome the $1 billion revenue being raised, but again, we still have doubt as to whether that $1 billion can be used for the upliftment or the improvement of the life of our citizens,” Kpawor said.

He called for investment in public institutions rather than simply distributing money to citizens.

JU Henning Dempster said the government should focus on creating jobs and ensuring that increased revenue eventually improves household incomes.

“What government should do now is to see how the $1 billion can reflect on the local, the time trading,” Dempster said.

He said the milestone would have greater meaning for citizens if they could afford school fees, rent, food and other basic necessities more easily.

Elder Emmanuel Freeman, of Joe Bar Community, questioned whether US$1 billion should be regarded as sufficient given Liberia’s natural resources.

“One billion dollars is not changing lives and the situation in the country,” Freeman said.

He called for greater investment in processing Liberia’s natural resources domestically and expanding economic activity beyond the extraction and export of raw materials.

Freeman also criticized the continued gap between exchange-rate movements and consumer prices.

Not all the reactions gathered by FrontPage Africa were critical. Lavelah B. Kortimai, a motorcyclist, pointed to technical and vocational training programs, road construction, agricultural investment, and what he described as the deployment of 285 earth-moving machines as visible signs that the government is putting revenue to work.

“Everyone is not benefiting,” he said, “but at least some people are benefiting.” Bobby Smith, a local business owner, agreed, citing easier travel to the southeastern counties and a steadier supply of gasoline, rice, and other goods as proof the government is delivering on at least part of its promise — a point Ngafuan himself made during his own tour of the region, pointing to the newly paved road reaching Tappita and the National Transit Authority buses now connecting the Southeast to Monrovia, while acknowledging the area still needs better roads, schools, health care, jobs and transport.

World.title: Liberia: A Coalition of African Civil Society Groups Demands Control of Development Money. But Can They Afford to Say No to Donors?
World.content:
Nana Asantewa Afadzinu, executive director of the West Africa Civil Society Institute, speaks during the Africa at the Centre convening in Accra, Ghana. Credit: Africa at the Centre/WACSI

Summary

A coalition of African civil society leaders are pushing donors to give African organizations and communities more control over development money as traditional foreign aid shrinks. They are also looking to Africans to raise more funds themselves and restrain corrupt money flowing out of the continent.

A growing number of African organizations are rejecting funding agreements that they say do not match their needs.

Leaders say shifting control to African institutions will only work if those institutions are also accountable to the communities the money is meant to help.

By Tetee Gebro, gender and health correspondent with New Narratives

ACCRA, Ghana — When a donor offered money to an organization working in Kenya, it came with an opportunity to expand its work into more communities. For a small organization that needed funding, it might have seemed like an easy decision. It wasn’t.

The donor wanted the organization to expand quickly. The organization said the communities it was already working with needed deeper support before it moved elsewhere. So they made a tough decision.

“They respectfully denied the funding,” said Nafissatou Sene, senior manager of Portfolio Services at African Collaborative, an organization that raises money and funds for African groups working in health, education, gender justice, agriculture and livelihoods.

Sene declined to identify the Kenyan organization because she did not have permission to name it. She said its budget was small and it needed money, making the decision especially difficult, but in the end it decided it had no choice.

“We’re not going to take anything just because it comes our way,” Sene said of the organization’s position.

That kind of decision-making is what Nana Asantewa Afadzinu, executive director of the West Africa Civil Society Institute, said has too often been missing from development in Africa.

“For too long we’ve had development done to us,” Afadzinu said. “We’ve not been in the driving seats of deciding what the solutions should be to our own problems and resourcing them.”

The story has become an example of the kind of power a grouping of African civil society organizations gathered here for the first-ever meeting of African civil society leaders, say they want: the ability to decide what their communities need and insist that donors adjust their requirements to match the communities’ priorities rather than their own.

The three-day conference “Africa at the Centre: Leading Change, Shifting Power” brought together more than 200 civil society leaders, funders, policymakers and development experts from 30 countries, including Liberia. Organizers said decades of development assistance have left foreign donors with too much control over which African problems receive money, how projects are designed and how success is measured. They say this has led to failed projects, lack of accountability, talent diverted from entrepreneurship and job creation, dependency and corruption.

Now, as traditional foreign aid from rich countries shrinks, they are pushing for African organizations and communities to have greater control over development spending by demanding donors listen. But they are also looking to raise more funds from Africans and African governments, and to limit the amount of money that flows out of the continent in corruption and debt payments.

But some at the conference said their proposed solution raises another difficult question: if foreign donors give up power, who in Africa gets it? African governments and civil society organizations have their own problems with corruption, weak accountability and failure to listen to communities. Moving control of development money from foreign institutions to African ones will not necessarily put that power in the hands of the people the money is supposed to help.

Edwin Mende-Cole (far right), executive director of Youth Climate Change Liberia and participants at the Africa at the Centre convening in Accra discuss proposals for shifting greater control over development decisions to African organizations and communities. Credit: Africa at the Centre/WACSI

One Liberian at the conference, Edwin Mends-Cole, said he knows how difficult the first part of that equation can be. Mends-Cole, executive director of Youth Climate Change Initiative Liberia, said small civil society organizations often depend on donor projects to survive. Funding opportunities can be so scarce that organizations adapt what they do to what donors are willing to finance.

“It is hard to say realistically ‘I will not accept,’” Mends-Cole said.

Liberia’s dependence on foreign assistance extends far beyond civil society. World Bank data shows the country received about $563 million in net official development assistance and official aid in 2023, equivalent to two thirds of the national budget. A separate World Bank assessment found official development assistance averaged about 12 percent of Liberia’s gross domestic product between 2022 and 2024.

The limited income of the national government has meant major public services have been left to donors. Donor aid funds at least 50 percent of Liberia’s health sector, for example. But stories of corruption and mismanagement abound, and the government is no closer to standing on its own.

Mends-Cole agrees that donors need to better listen. He said he has seen what can happen when a local organization is able to challenge the way a donor wants to solve a problem.

In 2023, his organization worked on a project under the United Nations Development Programme’s Small Grants Programme to protect biodiversity and mangroves in the Mesurado wetlands. Mends-Cole said the proposed approach focused on educating communities about the need to stop destroying mangroves.

But some people were cutting the mangroves because they depended on them to make a living. Telling them about environmental protection without giving them another way to earn money would not stop the cutting, Mends-Cole said.

“We are on the ground,” he recalled telling the funder. “This approach will not work.” After discussions, he said, the project was changed to include alternative livelihoods.

Mends-Cole said local organizations demanding more power from donors must therefore be prepared to give communities more power too. Before designing a project, he said, organizations should first ask people what problem they need solved. They must be transparent and report to communities on how the funds are spent and results obtained, as well as donors.

West African Civil Society Institute’s Afadzinu said changing the system does not mean simply replacing foreign money. It also means changing who decides how that money is used. She said she wanted to see donors provide more flexible and core funding that allows African organizations to strengthen themselves instead of moving from one donor-designed project to another.

“Don’t help us to continuously depend on you,” Afadzinu said. “Help us to become stronger.”

African countries and organizations must also raise more of their own money, she said, including through local philanthropy, diaspora support, businesses and social enterprises.

Sene said African organizations may already have more power in their relationship with donors than they realize. One organization refusing money may have little influence, she said. Many organizations taking the same position could force donors to listen.

“We cannot give grants or funds to people who refuse to take it from us,” Sene said. “If everybody said no, what are we going to do with the money?”

She acknowledged that completely ending African civil society’s dependence on foreign funding is not realistic in the near future. The immediate goal, she said, should be changing the relationship.

Tendisai Chigwedere of the Flora Hewlett Foundation a Donor at the Convening in Accra

At least one international funder at the Accra gathering is already onboard.

Tendisai Chigwedere of the U.S.-based William and Flora Hewlett Foundation, which was a financial backer of the Convening, said philanthropy has historically held enormous influence because it controlled the money. She said Hewlett is listening to local organizations, giving them more control with long-term partnerships and flexible funding. The Hewlett Foundation said it awarded $631 million in grants in 2024, with nearly three-quarters provided as flexible funding.

“We don’t want you to be boxed into a project,” Chigwedere said. “Allowing you to have general operating support helps you build the institution, build the vision, and work on the agenda… to do the things you need to do.”

Changing how existing donors give money is only one proposal being discussed.

Wanjiru Kanyiha, network coordinator of the Global Public Investment Network, is pushing a model in which African countries would contribute to a common pool according to their ability and participate in deciding how the money is spent. The idea is summed up in three phrases: all contribute, all benefit, all decide.

Under such a system, Kanyiha said, a poorer country such as Liberia would not be expected to contribute as much as a wealthy country but would still have a voice in decisions and could receive more than it contributed based on need.

The model remains a proposal. It has not yet proved that it can replace or significantly reshape the current aid system. Supporters hope to have governments working around one or two pilots by the end of 2028.

After three days in Accra, the West African Civil Society Institute said it will temporarily steward the work after the meeting, coordinate follow-up and help participants continue developing ideas that emerged from the gathering.

In a post-convening reflection, Charles Vandyck, the Institute’s head of capacity development, acknowledged that transferring power from international organizations to African institutions alone would not transform development.

“Redistributing power is not about reversing hierarchies,” Vandyck wrote. “It is about building systems where power is shared, accountability is mutual, and agency is respected.”

This story was a collaboration with New Narratives .

World.title: The Price of a Vote: What Liberia’s Smallest UN Bill Says About Its Biggest Claims
World.content:
Monrovia – There is a number so small it barely registers on the ledger of a $3.45 billion organization: $34,000. It is the least any nation on Earth can be asked to pay the United Nations in a given year — a rate set aside for the world’s poorest countries, Liberia among them. And as of mid-September, it is a number Liberia has not paid.

By Rodney D. Sieh, [email protected]

The amount is almost beside the point. What it represents is not.

By the United Nations’ own public accounting — the Committee on Contributions’ Honour Roll, updated as member states settle their books — Liberia’s regional neighbors have long since closed this chapter for the year. Côte d’Ivoire paid its assessment, a considerably larger $763,551 reflecting its bigger economy, back in March. Sierra Leone paid its own minimum-rate bill, $31,790, on September 9. Guinea followed five days later. As of September 14, 139 of the UN’s 193 members had paid in full. Liberia was not one of them.

It is tempting to read this as a story about capacity — a poor country simply unable to find $34,000. But that reading doesn’t survive contact with the rest of Liberia’s own record. The country met this same UN obligation on time as recently as 2017, paying $25,223 within the 30-day grace window. And at the International Maritime Organization, a separate UN body, Liberia has been anything but delinquent: in both 2024 and 2025, it settled dues of roughly $7.1 million — about 15% of that agency’s entire budget, a sum 200 times larger than what it now owes the UN’s regular budget — promptly and without incident. Liberia’s maritime registry is, after all, one of the largest in the world, and its government has clear institutional reasons to stay current there.

Which makes the lapse harder to explain as a matter of means, and easier to read as a matter of priorities.

That question of priorities sits uncomfortably next to the government’s own recent messaging. Officials have pointed to a milestone: domestic revenue, they say, has crossed $1 billion for the first time. A supplementary budget for FY2026 shows total receipts of $53 million, built on $48 million in World Bank budget support and a $5 million surplus over projections — money the government has been eager to publicize as evidence of fiscal turnaround. Whatever the merits of that broader claim, it is difficult to square a billion-dollar milestone with a $34,000 bill left unpaid to the institution whose Security Council Liberia currently sits on as a non-permanent member for the first time since 1961.

None of this rises to the threshold that triggers real consequences — Article 19 of the UN Charter, which strips a member of its General Assembly vote, only applies once arrears equal two full years of assessments, a bar of roughly $68,000 that Liberia has not yet crossed, and won’t for some time at this rate. There is no indication the country is being sanctioned or singled out. But symbolism has its own currency at the UN, and the Honour Roll — however minor a document it may seem — is precisely where that symbolism gets tallied, name by name, payment by payment.

World.title: Liberia: DNA Links Bon Jallah to Evidence, But Rwandan Expert Says Tests Can’t Show When or How It Got There
World.content:
Forensic report also flags unidentified DNA on toilet paper found at the scene

MONROVIA – A Rwandan forensic expert testified Wednesday that DNA profiles recovered from four exhibits in the trial of former National Security Agency staffer Peter Bon Jallah match his reference sample — but cautioned that the finding cannot show when, how, or under what circumstances the DNA got there.

By Willie N. Tokpah

Pascal Bavugirije, Acting Division Manager of the Biology Division at Rwanda’s Forensic Institute, took the stand as the prosecution’s 12th witness in a trial involving charges of gang rape, statutory rape and kidnapping. His testimony placed an important scientific qualification on one of the State’s central pieces of evidence.

What the DNA Shows

According to a forensic report dated January 22, 2026, autosomal STR analysis produced a single male DNA profile from a white T-shirt, a black T-shirt, and shorts collected from the crime scene, as well as a boxer that police identified as belonging to the alleged victim, Hasat Antoine H.B. Amara. The Rwandan institute concluded that all four profiles matched Bon Jallah’s reference sample and that he could not be excluded as a contributor.

But a fifth item told a different story. Tissue and toilet paper collected from the scene yielded a mixed DNA profile the lab attributed to unknown persons — one that matched neither Bon Jallah nor the alleged victim. Bavugirije said that profile could still be compared against other individuals’ DNA if they were identified and samples were obtained.

A Match, Not a Narrative

Bavugirije was clear about the limits of his findings: DNA comparison cannot determine whether force was used, whether there was consent, when biological material was deposited, or the circumstances that put it on an item. The lab was also not asked to determine whether the material was semen, saliva, blood or something else.

Those limits matter because the charges require proof of specific acts and circumstances — something a genetic match alone cannot supply. When defense counsel tried to press the witness on questions of force, consent and intent, the prosecution objected. Judge Wesseh Alphonsus Wesseh, Sr. sustained the objection, noting that the forensic witness was not the investigator responsible for establishing probable cause.

Chain of Custody in Question

Bavugirije’s laboratory received the exhibits from the Liberia National Police along with the investigators’ own account of where each item came from. The Rwandan team did not collect the clothing itself, nor did it independently verify who owned or wore any of it before submission — a gap defense counsel seized on, particularly around the boxer identified as the alleged victim’s.

The forensic exchange also produced an unusual courtroom moment: after the boxer was entered into evidence, defense counsel asked that Bon Jallah be allowed to stand in the dock for a clothing demonstration. The prosecution objected, arguing the defense would get its chance to challenge the evidence during its own case. Judge Wesseh denied the request, over defense objection, saying the demonstration could wait.

Background

Bon Jallah was arrested in January 2026 after a complaint involving a 16-year-old alleged victim, and has pleaded not guilty to gang rape, statutory rape and kidnapping. The January 22 report was signed by NZARAMBA Gilbert, Acting DNA Specialist; NYIRAMUGISHA Thamar, Acting Director of the DNA Unit; and Bavugirije Pascal.

What’s Next

The forensic testimony leaves the court with two distinct threads to weigh: a documented biological link between Bon Jallah and four exhibits, and an unresolved, unidentified DNA profile from the scene. Neither settles what the DNA presence proves — or doesn’t — about the alleged conduct. That question will now turn on the testimony of the alleged victim and other witnesses, the handling and chain of custody of the exhibits, and how the pieces fit together as the trial continues.

World.title: Liberia: State Rests as Defense Challenges 5,000-Bag Figure, Witness Accounts
World.content:
Monrovia — The prosecution has rested its case against former Foreign Affairs Minister Dee-Maxwell Saah Kemayah and his co-defendants in the Saudi rice trial after 31 days of jury sitting, with the defense expected to begin presenting its witnesses on Friday, September 18, 2026.

By Willie N. Tokpah

The transition comes after prosecution testimony focused on the movement and distribution of thousands of bags of rice donated to Liberia by Saudi Arabia, while defense questioning highlighted gaps between witnesses’ personal knowledge, documentary records and information obtained through investigations.

At the center of the case is a 2023 donation of 29,412 bags of 25-kilogram rice, valued at approximately US$500,000 and intended for disaster-affected and vulnerable communities.

According to the indictment, 11,200 bags were placed at a General Services Agency facility, while 18,212 bags were stored in two National Disaster Management Agency warehouses.

The prosecution alleges that portions of the rice were misappropriated, unlawfully distributed or otherwise improperly handled. Kemayah and the other defendants have denied the allegations and pleaded not guilty.

The 5,000-Bag Question

During Tuesday’s proceedings, an NDMA-related witness testified about his involvement in rice distribution. He personally described receiving or facilitating the distribution of 80 bags to Zota District and 200 bags in Gbarnga, accounting for 280 bags in the transactions he specifically identified.

When asked how he could say that 5,000 bags were not sent to the Gbarnga regional hub, the witness responded, “Because I was there.”

Under cross-examination and re-cross-examination, however, questions emerged about the scope of his personal knowledge and whether his presence at the facility gave him knowledge of every shipment that entered, left or moved through the wider distribution network.

The witness was unable to personally identify the source of the 5,000-bag figure. Questions concerning the documentary basis for the figure also encountered objections.

The issue places emphasis on the distinction between information based on direct observation and figures derived from records or investigations.

Community-Level Distribution

Another prosecution witness, Isaac K. Weede, chairman of the Seven Blocks of Lakpazee Community, testified about the community’s receipt of relief commodities.

Weede confirmed a statement to investigators that he had not received Saudi-donated rice and, to his knowledge, no one from the community had received it.

Defense questioning, however, examined Lakpazee’s decentralized leadership structure. Weede acknowledged that the community consists of seven blocks, each with its own leadership, and that donations could be delivered directly to a block leader before the chairman was informed.

He cited a separate donation of rice and books that was delivered to a block leader identified as Leevah, who subsequently informed him.

The testimony did not establish that Saudi-donated rice was delivered to Lakpazee. It did establish that commodities can enter the community through block-level leaders before reaching the central leadership.

Weede also said substantial donations would ordinarily become known to community leadership because block leaders communicate with the chairman.

Evidence Concerning Kemayah

Earlier testimony from prosecution investigator John Kumeh addressed Kemayah’s response after reports emerged that Saudi-donated rice was allegedly appearing on the Liberian market.

According to Kumeh, Kemayah halted the distribution and established an investigative committee. Kumeh also testified that the committee did not establish that the rice had actually been sold on the Liberian market.

That evidence forms part of the prosecution’s broader case concerning Kemayah’s conduct after the controversy emerged. Whether his actions amount to criminal conduct remains for the court to determine based on the evidence and applicable law.

Political-Motivation Claims

The proceedings have also generated competing claims about the prosecution.

Kemayah and his supporters have characterized the case as politically motivated, while the government has maintained that the prosecution is part of efforts to address alleged corruption and accountability concerns.

Neither characterization constitutes a judicial finding.

Defense Takes Over

With the State having completed its witness production, the defense is expected to begin presenting its case Friday.

The defense will have an opportunity to respond to the prosecution’s evidence, including the disputed 5,000-bag figure, distribution records, community-level accounts and evidence concerning each defendant’s alleged role.

The jury will ultimately have to assess the evidence concerning the quantities received and distributed, the records supporting those movements and the evidence connecting each defendant to the offenses charged.

The defendants have pleaded not guilty and remain presumed innocent unless proven guilty according to law.

World.title: Liberia: Crisis Rocks Union as Row Over Secretary General Deepens Amid Resignation and Rescindment of Decision
World.content:
Monrovia – Liberia’s umbrella body for musicians is in turmoil. The Musicians Union of Liberia (MULIB) is embroiled in a deepening leadership crisis that has paralyzed its activities, divided its National Executive Committee, and left the Union with two men laying claim to one of its most strategic offices – Secretary General.

By Emmanuel Weedee-Conway

There is a complete misunderstanding among members of the leadership over governance, constitutional interpretation, and administrative procedure, a rift that has now spilled into the public domain.

Documents and internal executive chats obtained by FrontPage Africa (FPA)News Paper show a breakdown in cohesion that has led to counter decisions, accusations of constitutional violations and confusion among the general membership.

The flashpoint is the resignation and later attempted return of the Union’s elected Secretary General, Zubin L. Cooper.

According to official communications, Cooper tendered his resignation on June 24 in a message addressed to MULIB President Mustapha A.B. Swaray.

In that message, posted in the MULIB Executive Chat, Cooper wrote: “This decision has not been made lightly. However, after careful consideration, I have concluded that, due to increasing professional and personal scheduling commitments, I am no longer able to dedicate the time and attention required to effectively carry out the duties and responsibilities of the office as prescribed by the Union’s constitution and governing framework.”

He also cited concerns about limited progress on key initiatives.

But in a dramatic twist on July 23, Cooper wrote to the National Executive Committee to withdraw his resignation, saying he had reorganized his commitments and was now able to fully serve.”

Since submitting my resignation, I have taken the opportunity to carefully reassess my professional and personal commitments. I am now in a position to fully dedicate the time, energy, and attention required to effectively discharge the duties and responsibilities of the office of Secretary General.”

The reversal came too late. Two days later, on July 25, President Swaray, in an Independence Day message to the MULIB family, announced the appointment of Alfred Gabriel Flomo, alias Legendary Super 7, as Acting Secretary General effective immediately.

“This appointment became necessary following the resignation of the former Secretary General, Zubin Cooper, due to his busy schedule which could no longer permit him to effectively handle the affairs of the Union. In view of the strategic nature of this office, the position could not remain vacant for a long period,” Swaray wrote.

That appointment has now set the stage for a constitutional showdown.

In a detailed response to FPA on September 15, the embattled Secretary General has pushed back, denying that he ever formally resigned.

Cooper argues that what is being treated as official resignation and withdrawal letters are merely WhatsApp messages with no legal standing.

“What is being referred to as ‘documents’ showing my resignation are, in fact, WhatsApp messages and not official; signed, stamped, or notarized communications. Under Liberian law and standard administrative practice, a resignation from a position of this nature requires a formal written communication, not an informal electronic exchange,” he pointed out.

“In that WhatsApp conversation, I stated an intention to resign and indicated I would follow up with a formal written letter, as administrative procedure and, separately, common Ministry of Labor practice would require. That formal letter was never submitted.”

He applied the same argument to his withdrawal: “I did not withdraw a resignation, because none was ever submitted. There is nothing to withdraw. What I did was signal my intention not to follow through with my earlier stated intention to resign.”

Cooper is also challenging the legality of the Acting Secretary General appointment. He contends that the MULIB Constitution and Bylaws (2025, notarized) only provides for interim appointments on the Board of Directors under Article 9.2.2(e) and has no comparable provision for the National Executive Committee.

He noted that under Article 9.3.1, the Secretary General is an elected officer, and under Article 7, replacement can only be done through a National Congress process.

“My status remains that of the duly elected Secretary General of MULIB,” he insisted, asking the leadership to cite the specific provision relied upon.

The second front of the crisis involves allegations that Cooper abused his office to front for non-members to obtain Liberian Service Passports.

At issue is a June 14, 2026 letter to the Director General of the Liberia National Tourism Authority (LNTA) requesting Service Passports for a MULIB delegation to an Independence Day Cultural Celebration in Europe.

The delegation listed included Mr. Joseph Junior Teah – Vice President for Operations, Joseph S. Kemoh (J Boy De Prophet) and Houstin S. Gblah (Double H), an artist manager.

Critics alleged Cooper attempted to secure a Service Passport for Double H, a non-member.

Cooper denied fronting, saying the request was centered on J Boy De Prophet, a member, who was traveling with his manager, which he described as standard practice.

He said the letter emanated from his office as mandated by Articles 9.4 and 10.4 of the Constitution, which gives the Secretary General responsibility for official correspondence and public relations, with the President duly copied.

He, however, admitted that Double H was not a registered, dues-paying member at the time.

“Double H was not, at that time, a registered, dues-paying member in the Union’s formal records,” Cooper asserted.

“This needs context, however: the current leadership took office roughly a year and a half ago, and in that time no new membership drive has been conducted.

On the specific paralysis, Cooper blamed a minority within the Executive for failing to adhere to the Constitution:

“The Union has effectively been at a standstill since the elections — not because of anything I have done, but because certain members, the same ones taking WhatsApp messages to the press as though they were official documents, have failed to adhere to the Union’s rules and Constitution… cherry-picking individual sections and combining them in ways that produce interpretations the document was never intended to support.”

He rejected the label that he is embattled, claiming the majority of members still recognize him.

“I am not embattled. The majority of MULIB’s members recognize me as the Secretary General they elected and voted into office,” he noted, adding he is willing to sit with anyone but warned that continued constitutional violations would force the Executive Committee to issue votes of no confidence and call a National Congress to resolve the matter.

As it stands, the Union risks operating with two Secretariats, with Flomo acting on the authority of a presidential appointment and Cooper holding onto his elected mandate.

There is a reported call for an emergency National Executive Committee meeting and possible intervention by the Board of Directors to avert a total collapse ahead of key programs for Liberian musicians.

World.title: Minister Ngafuan Says Increased Revenue Means Greater Capacity to Deliver for Liberians
World.content:
Monrovia – The Minister of Finance and Development Planning, Augustine Kpehe Ngafuan, has clarified that Liberia’s achievement of the US$1 billion domestic revenue threshold should not be interpreted as a claim that the country’s longstanding development challenges have been solved.

Minister Ngafuan said the milestone should instead be viewed as an indication of increased fiscal capacity, giving government greater room to respond to the pressing needs of citizens and finance national development priorities.

Speaking on the OK Morning Rush on Thursday September 17 in Monrovia, Minister Ngafuan explained that all of the country’s problems will not be solved because it crossed the US$1 billion threshold, but said the capacity to address the pressing issues has improved with the size of the budget.

The MFDP Minister made the clarification while reflecting on Liberia’s recent revenue performance and the broader implications of increased domestic resource mobilization.

According to Minister Ngafuan, the significance of crossing the US$1 billion threshold goes beyond the figure itself, noting that stronger domestic revenue provides government with a broader fiscal base from which it can support critical national priorities, including infrastructure, healthcare, education, social services, public-sector operations and other development interventions.

He cautioned the Public that increased revenue should not create the impression that every challenges facing Liberia can be addressed immediately.

Rather, he said, the additional fiscal space creates an opportunity for government to progressively tackle those challenges through improved planning, responsible spending, stronger institutions and effective implementation of development programs.

The Minister’s remarks underscore the importance of ensuring that increased revenue translates into tangible improvements in the lives of ordinary Liberians.

He stressed that the ultimate value of revenue mobilization should be measured not simply by how much money enters government accounts, but by how effectively those resources are converted into public services and development outcomes.

For the Ministry of Finance and Development Planning, the Minister noted that the revenue milestone represents part of the government’s broader effort to strengthen domestic resource mobilization and reduce vulnerability to unpredictable external financing.

He emphasized the need for a stronger domestic revenue base as an important component of fiscal sustainability, noting that Liberia’s development ambitions require adequate and predictable resources.

The Minister further stressed that the achievement should be seen as a foundation for doing more, rather than as an endpoint.

For citizens, the broader expectation is that improvements in revenue collection will ultimately be reflected in better roads and public infrastructure, improved access to quality healthcare and education, stronger social protection and expanded economic opportunities, something the Minister said the government is tackling.

World.title: Liberia: Three years in, Rep. Wongbe’s Development Record is Challenging Nimba’s Party-driven Politics
World.content:
In Nimba County, where political survival has traditionally required a party card, Rep. Wongbe is betting his future on something else entirely: a paper trail of finished schools, clinics and contracts

NIMBA COUNTY – There is a version of Nimba County politics that has held for a generation. Influence flows through party structures, and party structures flow through a handful of dominant personalities. It is the version built by the late Prince Yormie Johnson and carried forward, in different form, by the Movement for Democracy and Reconstruction (MDR), the organization that still counts the majority of the county’s sitting lawmakers among its ranks.

By Selma Lomax, [email protected]

Representative Taa Z. Wongbe is the exception the model was not built to accommodate.

Elected in 2023 to represent District Nine, Wongbe took his seat in the 55th National Legislature not as an MDR candidate, not as a coalition pick, but as an independent who defeated an incumbent by more than 2,300 votes — 6,538 to 4,209, according to the National Elections Commission.

Three years on, his political survival is being tested less by the ballot box than by a quieter question whether a lawmaker with no party machine behind him out-perform the machine itself?

Wongbe’s answer, so far, has been to substitute infrastructure for ideology.

His constituency office’s 2026 report lays out seven priority areas — education, infrastructure, health, economic empowerment, energy, youth and sports, and social cohesion — and documents engagement across eight communities during the legislative break alone.

It’s an approach less about grand political theory than about a working theory of representation that a lawmaker who shows up between elections earns more durable loyalty than one who shows up only for them.

That theory is being tested against Nimba’s geography as much as its politics. District Nine’s communities are separated by roads that make basic services a daily negotiation rather than a given, and it’s against that backdrop that Wongbe’s project list has to be read — less as a monument-building exercise, more as an attempt to close gaps that have existed for decades.

Classrooms and Clinics

Two projects anchor the education push. The Volay Public School, roughly 85 percent finished as of early 2026, has become something of a personal checkpoint for the representative, who has inspected the site directly ahead of its planned handover. But the more structurally interesting move came in August 2026, when Wongbe’s office partnered with the Luminos Fund Liberia to launch an Accelerated Learning Program across nine District Nine public schools — a program aimed squarely at children who have fallen behind or dropped out, built around foundational literacy and numeracy rather than new buildings.

The district’s office committed roughly US$6,360 to stipends and transport for a dozen volunteer teachers going through the required training, a relatively small outlay for what is, in effect, an attempt to intervene in a problem no construction project can fix on its own.

Healthcare has followed a similar dual pattern, a physical renovation paired with a service gap being addressed directly. The Zuatown Clinic has been completed, the Mehnla Clinic is about 80 percent done. At Graie, a maternal waiting house is under construction — a facility designed for pregnant women who would otherwise face long, often dangerous journeys to reach care as delivery approaches. It’s a modest-sounding project with an outsized purpose in a rural district where distance itself can be a health risk.

Power, Signal and the Search for an Economic Identity

If schools and clinics represent the district’s present needs, electricity and telecommunications represent its bid for a different future. The “Light Up District 9” initiative, formalized in August 2026 through a Memorandum of Understanding with BNE Development Corporation, aims to extend energy access into communities that have functioned without it for years.

Agriculture may be where Rep. Wongbe’s ambitions run longest. During a development tour through Zekepa, Guoiton, Blamein, Mehnla and Graie, he met directly with farmers and cooperatives to discuss market access and productivity — conversations that fit a broader argument he has made publicly: that a district cannot build lasting prosperity on government jobs and political patronage alone

A parallel push to secure an Orange telecommunications tower reflects the same logic in 2026, connectivity is not a convenience but an economic precondition, tied to everything from mobile banking to emergency response.

Agriculture may be where Rep. Wongbe’s ambitions run longest. During a development tour through Zekepa, Guoiton, Blamein, Mehnla and Graie, he met directly with farmers and cooperatives to discuss market access and productivity — conversations that fit a broader argument he has made publicly: that a district cannot build lasting prosperity on government jobs and political patronage alone.

His personal investment in a farm in Graie Township, alongside emerging engagement with the North Carolina–based Green Rural Redevelopment Organization, suggests an attempt to position District Nine as a genuine agricultural contributor to both Nimba and Liberia’s food security goals, not merely a recipient of aid.

The Small Interventions

Not every line item is a headline project. A women’s microloan initiative continues to support small-scale economic activity. A sponsored knockout tournament in Kwendin, and support for District Nine teams at the Inter-District Peace Tournament in Ganta — complete with jerseys, footballs, and cash incentives for participating teams and goal scorers — reads, on its face, like modest constituency spending.

But in a district where organized youth activity is scarce, these interventions function less as sport and more as social infrastructure: one of the few settings where young people from different communities regularly interact.

A community town hall project in Kwendin — backed by cement, zinc, steel rod and cash contributions from Rep. Wongbe’s office — has also become a case study in the harder part of constituency work: follow-through. When residents raised concerns about the pace of construction, Wongbe committed to closer monitoring, an episode that illustrates both the risk and the discipline required of projects announced with fanfare and expected to be finished quietly.

What the Ledger Doesn’t Yet Show

A more complete accounting of Wongbe’s tenure would include the voices of the people these projects are meant to serve — market women, farmers, parents whose children are now in the Luminos program, families closer to a functioning clinic than they were three years ago.

That reporting has not yet been done here, and any such testimony belongs in the story only once it has actually been gathered, attributed to real people who can be identified and, if necessary, contacted for verification. Their assessment — distinguishing what the representative’s office reports from what residents actually experience — would tell a fuller story than any list of completion percentages can.

Legislator, Not Just Builder

Wongbe’s footprint in Monrovia has extended beyond constituency work. In February 2024, a communication he brought to the House helped trigger scrutiny of electricity supply problems and financial questions at the Liberia Electricity Corporation.

A more complete accounting of Wongbe’s tenure would include the voices of the people these projects are meant to serve — market women, farmers, parents whose children are now in the Luminos program, families closer to a functioning clinic than they were three years ago

He was a visible player in the 2024 speakership contest, chairing the strategic committee that backed then-Speaker J. Fonati Koffa. And in November 2025, he introduced two pieces of proposed economic legislation: a National Community & MSME Stimulus Bill seeking US$10 million for grants to small businesses, farmer groups and women-led initiatives, and a Liberia Future Generations Extractive Savings Fund Act proposing that 10 percent of extractive revenues be set aside in a long-term national savings mechanism.

Neither bill’s fate is yet decided. But together they suggest a lawmaker trying to connect what he sees in District Nine’s villages to policy debates in the capital — an attempt, at minimum, to be more than a construction manager with a legislative title.

The Machine He Didn’t Join

None of this happens apart from Nimba’s political arithmetic. The MDR’s weight in national politics grew substantially after April 28, 2023, when Joseph Boakai named Jeremiah Kpan Koung — then MDR’s standard-bearer — as his running mate on the Unity Party ticket, fusing MDR’s Nimba-based organization to what became the winning presidential

campaign. The Carter Center’s report on the 2023 elections documented just how central Nimba, and the tensions surrounding it, had become to that race.

Koung is now Vice President. MDR still holds the majority of Nimba’s legislative seats. And Wongbe’s decision to stay outside that structure inevitably reads as a political statement whether he intends it as one or not — particularly as allies describe a rise in hostile media narratives they attribute to his refusal to align with the party.

That characterization has circulated, but it remains an allegation rather than a documented fact, absent evidence identifying who is actually producing or funding any specific attack. What can be stated plainly is the structural contrast that an independent lawmaker operating inside a county where nearly every other seat answers to a party apparatus he has chosen not to join.

2029 Is Already in the Room

With the next general election still three years away, Nimba’s political map is already shifting under the surface. MDR has clear incentive to consolidate its Nimba base — its 2023 alliance with the Unity Party remains the foundation of a governing partnership it has every reason to protect.

But the county’s politics are no longer a single storyline. Senator Samuel Gongben Kogar, Representative Musa Hassan Bility of the Citizens Movement for Change, and Garrison Yealue of the opposition Congress for Democratic Change each represent distinct currents pulling at Nimba’s political identity — and Senator Kogar’s own expulsion from MDR is a reminder that party loyalty in the county is neither permanent nor uncomplicated even for those who hold the party card. District 9’s uniqueness: There are 78 towns and villages, border five counties, and are Liberia’s largest electoral district by land area. That scale is central to understanding our development challenges.

Cultural diversity: Our district is home to three principal tribes: Gio, Mano and Gbi. This diversity is an important part of our identity.

Development philosophy: Wongbe approached District 9 almost as a small country requiring an integrated development plan. My focus is connecting education, healthcare, agriculture, infrastructure, energy and economic opportunities.

Project updates: Volay Public School has been completed and dedicated. Dorbor town will be dedicated in October. Please update that section and the conclusion. We can also provide updated project figures.

5. Roads: Roads and bridges remain Wongbe’s biggest challenge and an area where he hasn’t delivered. According to many in the district, this deserves honest attention because connectivity is fundamental to everything else we are trying to accomplish.

Electoral history: FrontPage Africa gathered that District 9 has never re-elected an incumbent lawmaker. Against that shifting field, Rep. Wongbe’s central wager is that voters will eventually judge him on delivery rather than affiliation.

The Record, Contested

It would be incomplete, and inaccurate, to present that wager as uncontested. A 2024 report by In Profile Daily documented criticism from the NYDO over alleged interference by Wongbe in a road development project in the district — a reminder that his record, like any lawmaker’s, has drawn scrutiny as well as praise.

Democratic accountability requires exactly that kind of friction; a representative’s standing should rest on more than the account his own office publishes.

The Real Test Ahead

Ultimately, the measure of Rep. Wongbe’s independence will not be settled in press statements or social media disputes. It will be settled in whether the Volay school opens on schedule, whether the Luminos program actually lifts outcomes for children who had fallen behind, whether the maternal waiting house in Graie reduces real risk for real women, whether “Light Up District 9” reaches homes that have never had power, and whether the farmers he has met with gain the market access they were promised.

For now, Wongbe occupies a genuinely unusual position in Liberian politics, an independent lawmaker inside one of the country’s most tightly organized political counties, testing whether a development record can substitute for a party network. The next election will be less a referendum on which party controls Nimba than a test of whether that substitution actually works.

World.title: Two die in Chinsali fatal road accident
World.content:
A Fatal Road Traffic Accident has claimed two lives on the spot while two others are nursing serious injuries at Chinsali General Hospital.

Muchinga Province Police Commissioner Lubinda Mayamba confirmed the development in a statement made available to the media in Chinsali today.

Mr Mayamba said the road traffic accident occurred yesterday at around 13:00 hours at Chipunga Village along the Great North Road in Chinsali District of Muchinga Province.

The Provincial commanding officer noted that involved was a stationary Howo Sino truck and trailer bearing registration numbers T834 EEM and T321 EFD loaded with 13 bundles of copper, a property of Stunner’s Company Limited and a Toyota Hilux double cabin bearing registration number GRZ 167 EA a property of the Road Development Agency (RDA) with five (5) passengers on board.

He said the accident happened when the driver of the Toyota Hilux was overtaking improperly and in the process hit a Howo Sino truck and trailer, which was parked off the road, on the left side and lost control of the motor vehicle.

“The truck had earlier incurred a damaged rear right part of the trailer and damaged two right rear tyres, which was parked on the left side (yellow line) off the road into Northern direction which was in custody of Kayumba other names not known believed to be Tanzanian national and is currently at large while his passenger Maxon Mushya aged 26 of Serenje who escaped unhurt,” the police commissioner added.

Mr Mayamba further explained that the Toyota Hilux which was being driven from South into the Northern direction by Mannnaseh Mwenya ,40, of Chiwanda area in Isoka District had its front part extensively damaged.

He further identified other accident victims as Exildah Mutale aged 41 of Chimbele Village in Senior Chief Nkula Chiefdom,who sustained multiple bruises on the head,right hand, painful chest and general body pains and Chrispin Bwalya aged 51 of Kapili village under Chief Nkweto’s area in Chinsali District who sustained a cut on the head and suspected fractured left arm and general body pains.

Mr Mayamba said the injured accident victims are currently admitted to Chinsali General Hospital where they are receiving treatment while two adults, whose details are not yet known but, one male and one female, who died on the spot, have since been deposited to Chinsali General Hospital Mortuary awaiting possible identification and postmortem examination.

He said both vehicles are still at the accident scene.

The Commissioner explained that the driver of a Toyota Hilux reported himself to Isoka Police Station where he is detained for causing death by dangerous driving, while investigations into the matter have been instituted.

World.title: Malindi leaves ZRL
World.content:
Zambia Railways Limited (ZRL) Managing Director, Cuthbert Malindi, has left the company following a mutual separation agreement with the Board of Directors.

According to a statement made available to the media by ZRL Board of Directors, the separation took effect on September 17, 2026.

The Board has appointed Company Secretary Mwendabai Bulaya as Acting Managing Director.

The Board has thanked Mr Malindi for his leadership, commitment and contribution to the company during his tenure.

The statement also reads that the appointment of an Acting Managing Director is aimed at ensuring continuity in the management and operations of ZRL.

The Board further states that it will communicate further developments regarding the company’s leadership in due course.

World.title: US Commends Zambia for Peaceful August 13 Elections
World.content:
The United States has commended Zambia for holding successful and peaceful elections on August 13, 2026. The praise came from Eugene Park, Executive Director to the Deputy Under Secretary of the United States Air Force for International Affairs, during a courtesy call at the Ministry of Defence in Lusaka on Thursday. Mr Park said the American government is proud of the peaceful elections and of the Zambian people. He also reaffirmed the strong bilateral ties between the two countries and pledged continued support for the Zambian military.

“Zambia is a priority country for the United States. We have had over 60 years of bilateral relations. We are ready to work with you and support the modernisation of the Zambian military,” Mr Park said.

Mr Park commended Zambia for taking the lead in international military engagements. He cited the hosting of the Africa Land Forces Summit in 2024 as one example. He also pointed to the African Air Chiefs Symposium, which Zambia hosted this year. Both gatherings brought senior military commanders from across the continent to Lusaka.

Ministry of Defence Acting Permanent Secretary Milicent Mwenda said defence and security cooperation between Zambia and the United States is growing every year. She said Zambian military personnel have had opportunities to train in the United States. Mrs Mwenda also thanked Washington for infrastructure it recently handed over at the Kenneth Kaunda Peace Training Centre in Lusaka. She said the facilities cost millions of dollars.

“We wish to thank the American government for the various infrastructure they recently handed over at the Kenneth Kaunda Peace Training Centre in Lusaka. That infrastructure cost millions of dollars and we appreciate so much,” Mrs Mwenda said.

World.title: Mushipi speaks on new role as National Athletics Coach
World.content:
Newly appointed Interim National Head Coach Sydney Ackim Mushipi says his appointment is a moment of great honour and humility and a call to serve the nation.

Reacting to his appointment by Zambia Athletics at its Executive meeting on 12th September, Mushipi said he receives the role with discipline, loyalty and patriotism.

“It is a moment of great honour and humility. To be entrusted by Zambia Athletics to lead our national team is not just a personal achievement, but a call to serve the nation,” Mushipi said.

“I feel the weight of the responsibility, but also the confidence that comes from years of preparation – from Zone VI Games to Youth Olympics, Commonwealth Youth Games and All Africa Games. I am ready to serve.”

Mushipi said serving as National Youth Director and Development Manager was a foundation which taught him where the future lies – in the youth.

He described the transition as a natural progression from building the base to leading the top.

“It means continuity. The athletes I nurtured from Mauritius 2013, Nanjing 2014, Samoa 2015 and Ndola 2023 are now seniors. Now I have the opportunity to complete their journey from junior promise to senior podium,” he said.

“For the national team, it means a seamless system where development and high performance are connected.”

On his plan for the national team, Mushipi said: “We will not change everything, we will improve our system.”

He outlined professionalizing the high-performance approach with science-based training for sprints and hurdles, his speciality, but extended to all events.

“As Ex Manager of Africa Athletics Development Centre Lusaka and World Athletics Lecturer, I will bring international standards to our coaches. A competitive nation needs competitive coaches,” Mushipi said.

“Our goal is simple: move Zambia from participation to podium at Region 5, Africa Games, Commonwealth and World level.”

Mushipi said he fully aligns with the President’s vision of Catch Them Young, describing it as the only sustainable future.

He unveiled a four-fold plan:

a) Schools Activation: As former Head Coach for International Schools of East and Southern Africa in Mozambique, Ethiopia, Uganda, he will strengthen inter-schools and provincial talent identification.

b) ZAHPC Lusaka Hub: Use the Africa Athletics Development Centre as national talent centre for early development.

c) Coaches in Communities: Train and deploy CAA and ZA Lecturers to every province to catch talent at 12-15 years.

The fourth pillar is expected to focus on retention and transition pathways.

Mushipi holds World Athletics Level 3, World Athletics Coaching Diploma and Sports Science Diploma from Mainz University, Germany.

World.title: Zambia’s maize reserves hit record 3.1 million tonnes
World.content:
Zambia’s maize reserves hit record 3.1 million tonnes

The Food Reserve Agency (FRA) is holding a record 3.1 million tonnes of maize in national strategic reserves. Executive director Justin Chuunka says this puts Zambia “beyond secure” on food for the first time in the country’s history.

Mr Chuunka announced the milestone yesterday during a tour of the Kabuyu satellite depot in Kazungula District, Southern Province.

“Countrywide we have more than three million tonnes and it has never happened in the country where we have three million tonnes, meaning that in terms of national food security, we are beyond secure,” he said.

The stockpile is made up of 1.7 million tonnes bought from farmers since May and 1.4 million tonnes carried over from the previous year. The agency procured 1.6 million tonnes in the last marketing season.

This year’s season runs from May 1 to October 31, so the FRA is still buying. Grain is being bought from farmers and stored at the same time as a buffer against bad weather.

Mr Chuunka said the reserves showed the country’s strengthened capacity to guarantee food availability and protect citizens against hunger. He assured Zambians that they would not face hunger-related deaths, and stressed the FRA’s role in managing the national strategic reserves.

To protect quality, the agency has sent its property director to optimise storage space, while officers on the ground handle the grain. The maize now arriving has been graded as top-tier white maize.

The FRA chief praised farmers at Kabuyu for running the depot themselves and creating jobs in their community.

The Kabuyu satellite depot committee zoned the surrounding areas and organised farmers into delivery schedules to keep deliveries orderly. Mr Chuunka urged satellite depot committees across the country to adopt the same community-driven approach to improve operations and bring in more farmers.

Kazungula District Commissioner Elias Siamibila said the committees were set up to give communities the responsibility and authority to run depots on their own.

“The community is able on its own to manage all these activities, and all power is actually vested in the community. That is the essence for which the satellite depot committees were established,” Mr Siamibila said.

Livingstone District Commissioner Eunice Nawa joined the delegation.

The record harvest has stretched the depot’s operations.

Depot chairperson Teddy Mulambo said Kabuyu handles about 2,000 bags a day from five agricultural camps. A shortage of empty grain bags has slowed buying, and an estimated 20,000 bags are still sitting with farmers. He appealed for new bags to be supplied urgently before the rains.

Jimmy Maiba, who chairs the Musokotwane camp agriculture committee, said the high yields meant farmers needed more satellite depots to sell their maize easily.

In Luapula, Provincial Permanent Secretary Prudence Kangwa gave figures for the province. As of September 10, the FRA had bought 3,161,326 bags of 50kg each there, worth K1.096 billion.

Of that, K328.2 million had been paid to 15,575 farmers out of 59,529 captured, she said.

The FRA’s figures match a regional assessment by the Alliance for a Green Revolution in Africa (AGRA).

AGRA’s August 2026 Food Security Monitor says Zambia remains relatively food secure, with most of the country in the minimal food insecurity category. Several SADC countries face worsening conditions in the October 2026 to January 2027 lean season, and Zambia’s position contrasts with theirs.

The report records a 12.7 per cent fall in maize prices from July to August, as harvest arrivals improved supply in markets. Bean prices fell 5.9 per cent and rice 4.2 per cent.

AGRA warns that vulnerable households in parts of western, southern and eastern Zambia could still come under stress. It says market supplies and household purchasing power need to be protected.

The report also warns of a threat from the weather.

“The anticipated persistence of a strong El Niño poses a major threat,” AGRA said.

It warns of below-average rainfall, higher temperatures, lower crop and livestock output, less farm work and falling household incomes in the 2026/27 season.

Zambia’s neighbours are in a weaker position. In Malawi, maize prices rose 3.5 per cent in August and beans 5.8 per cent as supplies stayed tight.

Maize prices in Mozambique fell 2.0 per cent, but AGRA says food insecurity remains a concern there because of climate shocks, conflict and supply disruptions. Zimbabwe faces worsening conditions in deficit areas despite an above-average national maize harvest.

AGRA says surplus producers such as Zambia can help ease regional food prices. It warns that disruptions to production, transport or trade could quickly spread shocks across borders.

Mr Chuunka has gone on to tour other satellite depots in the region. Buying continues until the end of October.

World.title: Haimbe to represent Hichilema at UN General Assembly
World.content:
Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation Minister Mulambo Haimbe will represent President Hakainde Hichilema at the 81st Session of the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA81) in New York. There he will deliver Zambia’s national statement and seek support for the Grow Zambia Agenda.

The six-day meeting runs from September 22 to 28, 2026, at United Nations Headquarters. Mr Haimbe will deliver Zambia’s National Statement on the President’s behalf during the high-level segment of the session.

The ministry’s principal public relations officer said Zambia’s participation would be guided by the country’s development priorities and foreign policy.

“Zambia’s participation will be anchored on advancing national development priorities and Foreign Policy objectives, through strengthened partnerships, resource mobilisation, and contribution to global efforts aimed at addressing shared challenges,” she said.

The first appearance since the election

This year’s session is convened under the theme “Restoring Trust, Managing Transformation: A United Nations that Delivers for All”.

The ministry says the gathering gives Zambia a platform to set out its national priorities to the world. It will also be the country’s first appearance on that stage since last month’s vote.

“This session further offers an opportunity to reaffirm Zambia’s longstanding commitment to peace, democracy and stability, against the backdrop of the recently concluded general elections,” the spokesperson said.

Five new diplomatic partners

The ministry expects the trip to deliver concrete diplomatic and economic results, including more resources, wider partnerships and a stronger say on global matters that affect the country.

One result is already scheduled. Zambia is expected to sign memorandums of understanding establishing diplomatic relations with five countries.

“UNGA81 will further provide an opportunity to expand Zambia’s diplomatic footprint and establish new partnerships,” the spokesperson said.

Money, skills and peace-building

The main aim in New York will be to engage international partners in support of the Grow Zambia Agenda.

The delegation will use Zambia’s partnerships to seek technical assistance, development financing and capacity-building investment. That support is aimed at economic diversification, job creation, sustainable development and better livelihoods.

The team will also approach the UN system for technical and institutional support to set up a National Architecture for Peace.

Human Rights Council bid

Zambia will co-host high-level side events on global issues, including the Pact for the Future. The events will cover sustainable development, climate action, development financing, digital transformation and reform of the multilateral system.

The delegation will also host a high-level meeting to rally support for Zambia’s bid for a seat on the UN Human Rights Council for 2027–2029. The ministry says the campaign will set out the country’s commitment to promoting and protecting human rights.

Meetings with the Commonwealth are also planned. They will cover democracy and governance, trade and investment, youth empowerment, climate resilience, sustainable development and institutional capacity-building.

Orders at home

Before leaving for New York, Mr Haimbe gave his senior staff their instructions.

Addressing top management at Charter House in Lusaka yesterday, in his first meeting with them since his reappointment, the minister told staff to familiarise themselves with the Grow Zambia Agenda. He said the ministry’s work must help turn economic growth into jobs and real benefits for ordinary Zambians.

He told senior managers to put efficiency ahead of bureaucracy and make sure government processes do not delay work.

He also urged staff to learn the mandates of other ministries and work more closely with them. That, he said, would help advance the President’s vision and ensure the benefits of growth reach households.

The minister said the Government would be working towards its economic growth targets over the next five years, and the ministry had to keep pace. Efficiency, he said, must come first so that the benefits of the Grow Zambia Agenda turn into better livelihoods.

Mr Haimbe praised the ministry’s two permanent secretaries for keeping it running while Parliament was dissolved.

The Zambian delegation arrives in New York for the opening of the high-level week on September 22. The Human Rights Council bid and the five new diplomatic agreements are at the top of its agenda.

World.title: Musokotwane: second term will be about production, exports and jobs
World.content:
Finance and National Planning Minister Situmbeko Musokotwane says the Government will use its second term to turn the promises of its first five years into higher production, more exports and new jobs under the Grow Zambia Agenda.

Speaking at a press briefing in Lusaka yesterday, Dr Musokotwane said the Government would build on the economic gains of the New Dawn administration’s first term. Its focus now, he said, is to turn those commitments into tangible outcomes for Zambians.

“The promises that were made in the last five years are going to be fulfilled in this second term,” he said.

Production first

The minister said the second term would be marked by higher production across key sectors. That output, he said, would be the base for stronger exports and job creation.

The Government is aiming for large increases in production beyond mining, particularly in agriculture, where the plan includes more maize and sugarcane.

Sugarcane alone is expected to grow by about one million tonnes as the Government works to expand the productive capacity of the economy.

“We are targeting increased production, not only in copper and maize, but also in sugarcane, where production is expected to grow by one million tonnes,” Dr Musokotwane said.

From output to employment

The minister described a chain of cause and effect. Higher output means more goods for the domestic and export markets, and those exports in turn support jobs for ordinary Zambians.

For that reason, he said, the Government’s second-term strategy is about moving beyond policy commitments to actual production.

“If we increase production in these various sectors, exports will increase, and that will create employment for ordinary people,” he said.

A call for support

Dr Musokotwane said the second term of the United Party for National Development (UPND) Government would demand greater effort and commitment.

“This second term is about working hard and ensuring that we deliver according to the expectations of Zambians,” he said.

He called on citizens to back President Hakainde Hichilema and his administration as they work to meet those expectations. The task ahead, he said, is to convert the country’s productive potential into measurable economic opportunities for citizens.

The targets behind the plan

The Ministry of Agriculture has set out the production targets that underpin the minister’s vision.

Agriculture Permanent Secretary for technical services John Mulongoti said the presidential targets for 2031 are 10 million tonnes of maize, three million tonnes of soya beans, one million tonnes of wheat and one million tonnes of sugar a year.

Speaking at the Agricultural Institute of Zambia conference in Lusaka yesterday, Mr Mulongoti said meeting them requires a fundamental shift in how farming is done. Productivity must rise through science, technology and innovation, he said, not just by planting more land.

“Government provides an enabling policy and regulatory environment, while the private sector must bring investment, innovation and commercial discipline,” he said.

Where production stands

The National Union for Small Scale Farmers in Zambia (NUSFAZ) says maize is on course. Secretary general Ebony Lolozi said output reached 3.9 million tonnes in the 2023/2024 season and 5.1 million tonnes last season, while soya beans, wheat and sugar are lagging.

For sugar, NUSFAZ plans to replicate the Kaleya Smallholder Scheme in northern districts such as Mansa and Kawambwa, where sugar mills are under way.

In mining, Konkola Copper Mines has signed a US$498 million contract with China NERIN Engineering Company for a new tailings leach plant in Chingola, with capacity of 70,000 tonnes of copper a year. The company says the plant is part of its contribution to the national target of three million tonnes of copper.

The second-term test

The Treasury chief has set a simple measure for the next five years: more output, more exports and more jobs.

He has asked Zambians to support the Government while it tries to deliver on that plan.

World.title: Nevers chose pension over politics, says Kavindele
World.content:
Former Vice-President Enock Kavindele says Dr Nevers Mumba left partisan politics because it was the only way to keep his government benefits. Dr Mumba’s exit comes as the opposition regroups after the elections and the NRPUP defends its list for the new proportional-representation seats in Parliament.

Dr Mumba resigned as leader of the New Nation Party (NNP) on Tuesday, clearing the way for him to leave active partisan politics.

Mr Kavindele, himself a former vice-president, said the decision came down to benefits. Two former Heads of State, he noted, had lost theirs by returning to the political arena.

“Both Dr Kenneth Kaunda and Dr Edgar Lungu lost their benefits after returning to active politics,” he said.

“I’m not privy to the other reasons Dr Mumba has to quit politics, but obviously, and primarily, it is to do with benefits. He had no way out but to relinquish his partisan involvement to continue enjoying benefits from government.”

Mr Kavindele set out what former vice-presidents receive and said the package was adequate.

“The benefits are okay and enough. It is two motor vehicles, security personnel and 80 per cent of a current serving vice president’s salary, one trip abroad and two local trips fully financed by government,” he said.

He called the package generous compared with what other citizens receive, including people who may have served the country diligently for much longer. He thanked President Hakainde Hichilema for taking the issue of former vice-presidents’ emoluments to Parliament for ratification.

Mr Kavindele said leaving party politics did not mean Dr Mumba had to stay silent on national affairs. He urged him to keep advising and engaging the Government, but quietly rather than in public.

He admitted he did not know all of Dr Mumba’s reasons for quitting, but was in no doubt that benefits were the main one. He also had a wider message for others in the same position. Former presidents and vice-presidents who want to keep their benefits, he said, should stay away from active politics.

Asked about calls for dialogue over the post-election impasse, Mr Kavindele said the law should be strictly followed and allowed to take its course.

NRPUP defends its list

Dr Mumba’s exit is not the only opposition story this week. The NRPUP is defending the list it submitted for the new proportional-representation seats in the National Assembly.

The party, whose presidential candidate was Brian Mundubile, is one of only two that qualified for the 40 seats created under the Constitution of Zambia (Amendment) Act No. 13 of 2025. The other is the ruling UPND.

NRPUP leader Ezra Tembo said the party expects 16 seats in the National Assembly. He rejected claims on social media that Mr Mundubile and his running mate, Makebi Zulu, were not consulted on the list. The two, he said, contributed to it.

The UPND confirmed on Monday that it had also submitted its list. Media director Mark Simuuwe said the ruling party was waiting for feedback from the electoral body.

Seats were shared in proportion to the valid votes each party’s presidential candidate won nationally. Electoral Commission of Zambia (ECZ) corporate affairs manager Patricia Luhanga said the allocation followed “a quota-based formula prescribed by law”.

In the National Assembly, 20 of the seats are reserved for women, 15 for young people and five for persons with disabilities.

The calendar ahead

Candidates from both parties appear before the ECZ today to have their lists validated. The new members register at Parliament tomorrow and take the oath on Monday, September 21. Each must present ZAQA-verified qualifications, a passport and proof of residency where applicable.

Presiding officers will be elected on October 2. President Hichilema opens the 14th National Assembly on October 9.

Dr Mumba will not be part of that new political line-up. He has given up the NNP leadership and, going by Mr Kavindele’s account, kept the benefits of a former vice-president.
