Fox News Digital has reached out to Sullivan, Sanders' attorney and the Plymouth County District Attorney's Office for comment.

World.title: ‘Unprecedented’: Judges reveal behind-the-scenes coordination on Trump immigration cases
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Federal judges in Minnesota tasked with deciding a flood of habeas petitions challenging the detention of immigrants swept up during President Donald Trump's Operation Metro Surge weren't working entirely on their own — behind the scenes, they were regularly consulting one another through running email threads and developing tools to quickly handle recurring legal questions.

The behind-the-scenes coordination among Minnesota's federal bench, revealed in a New York Times report Thursday, included regular meetings, running email threads, an informal spreadsheet created by court clerks showing which judges to turn to with particular legal questions and templates some judges developed to quickly issue orders when similar detention disputes repeatedly came before the court.

The disclosures are fueling questions over whether the judges were colluding on separate cases involving the same Trump administration immigration policies, or simply sharing expertise to manage an extraordinary caseload.

FEDERAL JUDGE TIES ICE AGENTS' HANDS WITH RULING ON WARRANTLESS SOUTHERN CALIFORNIA ARRESTS

"The idea of a running email chain involving a variety of cases — it strikes me as very weird and frankly unprecedented," Robert Luther III, a professor at George Mason University's Antonin Scalia Law School whose work includes federal courts and judicial ethics, told Fox News Digital. Federal judges can and routinely do consult colleagues, Luther said, particularly about procedural or evidentiary questions. But each judge is ultimately responsible for independently deciding the cases assigned to them — a distinction Luther said makes the coordination significant.

The disclosures have also drawn criticism from the Trump administration on two fronts. Department of Homeland Security (DHS) General Counsel James Percival accused the former chief judge who led the district during Metro Surge of "essentially conspiring with his judicial colleagues" to thwart federal immigration enforcement. The Justice Department (DOJ), meanwhile, questioned the decision by sitting judges to give extensive on-the-record interviews about their experience with the administration's immigration operation.

Seven of the district's judges spoke to the Times for Thursday's report, including former Chief Judge Patrick Schiltz, who sat for a 90-minute interview about the court's experience during Metro Surge. Schiltz declined to discuss ongoing cases, according to the Times, but described what happened in Minnesota's federal court as having "created a grave threat to the rule of law."

"It is remarkable that sitting federal judges are giving on-the-record interviews attacking this Administration's policies rather than ruling from the bench," a Justice Department spokesperson told Fox News Digital. "If judges followed the law in adjudicating cases, there wouldn't be an 'overwhelming' habeas caseload. Judges who have made public comments on pending or related matters should consider whether recusal is warranted going forward."

OBAMA, BIDEN JUDGES DRAW FRESH FIRE AS TRUMP'S IMMIGRATION COURT CLASHES HEAT UP: ‘ALMOST IMPOSSIBLE’

But Chief Judge Eric Tostrud, who was himself among the Minnesota judges interviewed by the Times, rejected suggestions that the coordination described in the report compromised individual decision-making. He told Fox News Digital that every member of the bench independently decided the merits of each petition assigned to them, while pointing to an extraordinary surge in litigation — from 12 alien-detainee habeas petitions during all of 2024 to 1,427 through August of this year — and noting that many involved similar or identical, often novel, legal questions.

"The bottom line is that each of us made an independent decision with respect to the merits of each and every petition we were assigned," Tostrud told Fox News Digital.

Tostrud stressed that the judges did not uniformly reach the same conclusions, saying that while some reached the same result on certain legal questions, they "reached different outcomes regarding other legal questions." He said the judges' ability to communicate helped them resolve the cases quickly and thoughtfully, regardless of whether individual petitions were granted.

What exactly the judges were sharing behind the scenes, however, remains unclear. Tostrud declined to disclose the contents of the court's internal working materials, saying documents created by judges and court staff "are not public."

TRUMP ADMINISTRATION'S IMMIGRATION PUSH FUELS ICE'S BIGGEST ARREST MONTH IN AGENCY HISTORY

That distinction could be significant, according to Luther, who said administrative templates are commonplace in federal courts, but drew a line between those and templates touching the substance of a case.

"Templates that deal with administrative matters strike me as entirely appropriate and commonplace in federal courts," Luther said. "Templates for substantive matters — that seems like something altogether different."

The coordination unfolded amid a broader clash between Minnesota's federal bench and the Trump administration over Operation Metro Surge. The dispute came as immigration litigation inundated the district. During the first three months of 2026, Minnesota's federal court received 1,116 habeas petitions, compared with just two during the same period the previous year, according to the Times. Court staff worked 16-hour days, seven days a week, to process the incoming cases.

Patrick Schiltz, who served as the district's chief judge during Metro Surge before taking senior status — a form of semi-retirement — this summer, emerged as a prominent judicial critic of the administration's handling of the operation. In a Jan. 28 order, Schiltz accused ICE of violating nearly 100 court orders during that month and warned that "ICE is not a law unto itself."

OBAMA JUDGE'S PECULIAR TRUMP REBUKE IGNITES FURY OVER 'UNPROFESSIONAL' LANGUAGE: 'EMBARRASSMENT'

The cases cited in Schiltz's January list of alleged violations have largely concluded, according to the Times, which reported that the administration ultimately corrected the issues flagged by the court in many of them.

DOJ said its review of the cases found that in the "large majority" of them, detainees were released on time and no violation occurred, while in most of the remaining cases the department said it ultimately did what the court ordered despite missing an additional deadline.

MASSACHUSETTS' HIGHEST COURT PUBLICLY REPRIMANDS JUDGE ACCUSED OF ENABLING IMMIGRANT TO ESCAPE ICE

Federal judicial ethics rules generally prohibit judges from publicly commenting on the merits of pending or impending cases, but permit judges to explain court procedures and engage in broader speaking and teaching about the law, legal system and administration of justice.

The DOJ argued that judges who publicly commented on pending or related matters should consider whether recusal is warranted. The Times reported, however, that Schiltz declined to discuss ongoing cases, while Judge Nancy Brasel, a Trump appointee who also participated in the interviews, defended judges' ability to speak publicly about judicial independence.

"We are allowed to speak out about judicial independence," Brasel told the Times. "And so we should, in order to keep it."

Luther, however, took a different view of the judges' decision to participate in the interviews.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"Judges should be speaking through their judicial orders, not through their surrogates at The New York Times," he told Fox News Digital.

World.title: Former ‘Alligator Alcatraz’ detainee says he was placed in phone booth-sized cage for 15 hours
World.content:
For around 15 hours, immigration detention officers kept Raúl Suárez Herrero confined in a cage slightly larger than a phone booth, where he feared snakes and endured mosquitoes in the middle of Florida swampland, the former detainee alleged.

Suárez, 59, told José Díaz-Balart in an interview for Noticias Telemundo’s “Ahora 360” that he was forced into the cage, measuring 7 feet, 9 inches high and 4 feet, 3 inches square, for praying out loud for an ill young man at “Alligator Alcatraz,” an ICE detention site.

“I feel like I was in hell,” Suárez later told NBC News in a phone interview from Mexico, where he was deported.

Suárez spoke days after a Department of Homeland Security watchdog confirmed the use of the phone booth-sized cages at the now-shuttered Florida detention camp in a Sept. 11 report.

“The use of such restrictive spaces is highly unconventional and does not align with standards for humane treatment,” the report said.

The DHS Office of Inspector General report documented its inspectors’ findings during an unannounced January visit to the Ochopee, Florida, site.

In December, Amnesty International issued its own report on conditions at the detention site based on interviews with detainees and its own tour of the facility. The organization detailed the use of the small cages and said it amounted to torture.

The facility staff told inspectors that the cages were “calming areas” where immigrants could de-escalate and have time alone and that no one spent more than two hours inside them.

But Suárez told Noticias Telemundo that “they took me there and I spent more than 15 hours inside in that little hole,” referring to the small cage. He said he was forced in around 1 p.m. and taken out at about 5 a.m. “when morning was breaking.” According to Suárez, the cage was in a recreation area where detainees took exercise time. Suárez said he couldn’t stretch out on the cage floor and got little sleep for fear of what might slither into the cage.

“I had to be careful because on the ground there were snakes and you don’t see them. You can’t fall asleep because they can come into the cage,” Suárez said in a video interview.

DHS did not directly address Suárez’s allegations or case in response to questions from NBC News. But a spokesperson rejected “claims that there were ‘inhumane’ conditions” at the immigrant detention center. Those claims are “categorically false” and any allegations of excessive use of force are “FALSE,” the spokesperson said in an email.

“No detainees were being beaten or abused,” the DHS spokesperson said. DHS provides long-standing medical, dental and mental health services, three meals a day that are evaluated by certified dietitians, clean water, clothing, bedding and hygiene products and access to phones to talk with family and lawyers, the spokesperson stated.

Alligator Alcatraz’s standards were consistent with those under other administrations, the spokesperson also said. Further questions were referred to the state of Florida, “as this facility was managed by the State of Florida through the Division of Emergency Management.”

"Alligator Alcatraz" shut down in June. Alon Skuy / Getty Images file

The facility in the heart of the Everglades was built by Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis as part of the state’s push to support President Donald Trump’s aggressive immigration crackdown.

Alex Lafranconi, a spokesman for DeSantis, has dismissed criticism of the small cages. Lafranconi has described the small cages as a confinement area for “violent criminal aliens who have proven they cannot remain peaceful,” and said “we’d make them smaller, if we could.”

Although DHS said the inspector general “indicated” all recommendations have been administratively closed, the OIG said in its report that the administration did not address its 10 recommendations, including that it “discontinue the use of the small metal enclosures to hold detainees for any reason or amount of time.”

The OIG also said that at the time of the inspection, all the detainees were ICE detainees and there was evidence that ICE had some degree of oversight authority and engagement at the facility.

President Donald Trump and then-Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem tour the facility in July 2025. Andrew Caballero-Reynolds / AFP - Getty Images

Originally from Cuba and in the U.S. since he was 12, Suárez was detained by ICE in July 2025 during an ICE check-in.

Before it was recently ordered closed, Alligator Alcatraz had been denounced by multiple detainees and legal and immigrant advocates for its conditions.

The detention facility’s records state the average time people were placed in the smaller cages with metal fencing was 59 minutes and 27 seconds, according to the OIG report. But the OIG said it could not confirm or refute ICE officials’ assertions regarding use of the enclosures or detainees’ allegations they had been denied food or other abuses.

The small cages at the facility were supposed to be a “safe and secure place” where people could “reflect on their behavior choices, manage their emotions, reduce stress, and practice self-directed behavior,” according to the detention camp’s policies, the report stated.

According to detention center records cited by the OIG, 79 people were held in the small cages during the period of July 17, 2025, to Jan. 18, and none were held more than two hours. Detainees in the small cage “may leave at any time by detainee request or per staff directive,” according to the report.

But Suárez was adamant that his confinement was not voluntary and lasted far more than two hours.

“Everybody lied” about the small cages, Suárez said, disputing that he could have gotten out or requested to be let out.

He said he was forced into the cage after praying out loud for a man who had an epileptic seizure as they were waiting to get registered at the detention camp.

Help for the man was taking “too long,” according to Suárez. That’s when he said he started praying aloud, as he used to do at the evangelical church he attended before his arrest.

“I asked God for the young man’s life,” he said.

Suárez alleged two guards then forced him to stand up, asked where he was from and then grabbed him and dragged him “all the way back to where that little cell was.” He said he was kicked in the leg so hard he thought they broke it. “My leg was so big and black.”

“They just dropped me over there and locked the doors,” he said. He said he got no medical treatment for his leg or a medical evaluation after the confinement.

Suárez said his experience has left him psychologically “shattered.”

Suárez was removed to Mexico in February after more than four decades of living in the United States. He was detained on July 16, 2025, when he went to an immigration check-in.

Suárez had been ordered removed from the U.S. in 2000 after serving a prison sentence stemming from a plea agreement on a drug charge. Because Cuba was not accepting U.S. deportees then, Suárez was released and told to check in with ICE annually, a court document states. Cuba has allowed few of its citizens to return after U.S. deportation.

An attorney attempted to get Suárez released from detention. The federal judge had given DHS until late January to remove him or release him, but the judge then extended the government’s time for two weeks. On the deadline date, Feb. 11, DHS deported Suárez to Mexico and the judge closed the case.

“Forty-seven years. They took me to the U.S. as a 12-year-old, when I was a child,” Suárez said. “I was raised my whole life there [in the U.S.]. I’m bilingual and everything. I went to school there and everything. And everything happened from one moment to the next. I still can’t absorb what happened.”

Suárez said he had been a truck driver since he was 17 and had built his own truck driving business with his brother, an American citizen, who died in 2021 from Covid. His father had died in Cuba when he was 3 and his mother, who became a U.S. citizen, died about a decade ago.

When immigration laws were toughened in 1996, making legal residents deportable for certain crimes, he could no longer seek U.S. citizenship, he said.

His mother had urged him to get citizenship, but he didn’t do it, he said.

“I was pretty young. When you are pretty young, you don’t listen to anybody,” he said. He had no other encounters with law enforcement, he said. He said he’d been living a normal life, preparing to buy a house and had a girlfriend.

“Life is changed. I don’t know what is going to happen here in Mexico.”

World.title: White House withdraws Trump’s nominee to lead ICE
World.content:
he White House withdrew President Donald Trump’s nominee to lead ICE, former Oklahoma state trooper Lance Schroyer, according to a notice published Thursday.

The White House did not say in the notice why Schroyer’s nomination was withdrawn.

Immigration and Customs Enforcement did not immediately provide a response about the withdrawal, but a spokesperson said a statement from the agency is forthcoming.

Schroyer’s nomination was blocked by Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., the chair of the Senate Homeland Security Committee, according to a person familiar with the decision, because Paul was unsatisfied with how much information he obtained from the White House about the shootings of two U.S. citizens in Minnesota by federal agents.

The White House has not responded to a request for comment. ICE has not responded to a request for comment about Paul.

Schroyer is a senior adviser to Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, and he was the secretary’s top pick to take over as director of ICE after Todd Lyons’ exit from the position in April.

Lance Schroyer. Department of Homeland Security

Mullin was previously a U.S. senator for Oklahoma and knew Schroyer from that time.

Schroyer has decades of experience working in local law enforcement in the state, but not specifically with ICE.

Trump announced Schroyer’s nomination in a Truth Social post in June, saying, “Lance has firsthand experience getting Illegal Aliens OFF our streets and, just like ME and our Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin, he LOVES the men and women of ICE.”

Acting ICE Director David Venturella is expected to remain in his role leading the agency for the time being, according to an ICE spokesperson.

World.title: Salvadorans with TPS don’t know how long their protections will last
World.content:
HOUSTON — José Palma’s face lights up when he remembers leaving El Salvador in 1998 at the age of 23 for the U.S., with the dream of working, learning English and building a family.

Twenty-eight years later, his life is divided between paperwork, community hearings, and a family full of love and varying immigration statuses: Palma, who lives in Houston, has U.S. citizen children — two of whom are still young — and a wife who’s a legal permanent resident, and he’s a beneficiary of Temporary Protected Status, which allows eligible immigrants from certain countries to live and work in the U.S. without fear of deportation.

As the national coordinator of the National TPS Alliance, Palma has been answering a lot of questions from Salvadorans with TPS: Their immigration protections were set to expire last week, but the Department of Homeland Security announced that Salvadorans will retain TPS protections — including work authorization — for now until an announcement is made at a later date.

But there’s uncertainty among Salvadoran TPS holders about what could come next and what happens now with work permits or driver’s licenses that have expired or are about to expire. Immigrants from countries that have lost their TPS designation, including Haiti and Nicaragua, have lost their work permits and ability to be in the U.S. legally, and they face deportation.

Palma has lived under TPS protection since 2001.

“Everything we’ve built is in danger of collapsing,” he said. “Twenty-five years is not a short time. It’s a lifetime.”

Palma said that amid the uncertainty, Salvadoran TPS holders and their families have been dealing with real consequences: People are being asked not to return to work by their employers, families fear the loss of their health insurance and parents are unsure if they will be able to continue driving vehicles in the United States.

Advising caution

Palma recommended one thing to Salvadoran TPS beneficiaries: “Don’t panic or make decisions based on rumors,” he said.

The Trump administration has said that until it announces a decision, Salvadorans with TPS still have protection, so Palma’s advice is “to rely only on official sources, credible community organizations and established media” for accurate information.

One of the biggest points of confusion, Palma acknowledged, is whether Salvadoran TPS holders can continue working.

“DHS has said that people retain protection, but USCIS guidance for employers indicated that certain automatic work permit extensions were valid until Sept. 9,” Palma said, referring to U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services. “People should keep their USCIS letters, check their myUSCIS account and seek accredited legal advice before assuming which document applies to their case or employment.”

Palma has lived under TPS protection since 2001. Albinson Linares / Telemundo News

For those who have already received warnings from employers, Palma had this advice: “Do not resign or sign any documents you do not understand. Bring any official notifications you receive from USCIS to your employer and ask human resources to check the agency for updates regarding Form I-9. No one should decide the future of your immigration case based on an unverified comment, social media post or phone call.”

Unfortunately, some Salvadoran TPS holders have already been affected. Palma said that people who applied between January and March 2025 to renew their work permits haven’t received them. Some employers have told them not to return to work, and others have told them they can only work until a certain date.

“Driver’s licenses depend on immigration status, health insurance can be cut off and loans can be denied — the consequences go far beyond losing immigration protection or a work permit,” he said.

If the Trump administration decides to end TPS protections for Salvadorans, people don’t have to leave the country within 60 days, Palma emphasized.

“That period is the minimum protection period before a decision can take effect,” he said. “After that, each person must evaluate their case: There may be a family petition, asylum, another legal process or an immigration defense. The recommendation is to seek legal evaluation now and not wait for an emergency.”

What to do in the meantime

Salvadoran TPS holders should be gathering copies of their work permit, TPS certificate, passport, driver’s license, USCIS receipts, birth and marriage certificates, children’s medical and school records, proof of employment, and tax returns, Palma said.

The National TPS Alliance estimates that 170,000 Salvadorans are directly protected by TPS. Albinson Linares / Telemundo News

He also said it’s important to identify a licensed immigration attorney or accredited organization. He urged people not to lie on any forms or submit applications for which they don’t qualify or give money to people who promise to “fix” their immigration status.

Palma also warned against signing documents without understanding them, giving access to bank accounts or personal information to strangers, or trusting a notary as if they were an immigration lawyer.

TPS holders should also avoid any legal problems or issues such as driving under the influence of alcohol, using false documents or committing acts that could jeopardize any future immigration status.

When asked what TPS holders should do if they’re stopped or approached by authorities, Palma said the important thing to do is “stay calm.”

“Bringing a copy of your identification or immigration documents can be helpful. If it’s an immigration officer, don’t sign any papers without knowing what they contain or without speaking to a lawyer,” he said. “Every case is different, but a signature obtained under duress can have serious immigration consequences.”

Temporary status for decades becomes a ‘whole life’

The National TPS Alliance estimates that 170,000 Salvadorans are directly protected by TPS. However, Palma explained that the actual number of people affected is much higher when one includes U.S. citizen children, spouses, employers, churches, businesses and entire communities.

If TPS for Salvadorans is ended, “the impact would be immediate in cleaning, hotels, restaurants, kitchens and construction; there are also Salvadorans with TPS working in transportation, healthcare and professional occupations,” he said.

Palma was asked what he tells people who say that TPS is temporary and beneficiaries should return to their countries.

He said it’s important to understand the history of the program.

“It’s been renewed every 18 months, under both Democratic and Republican administrations, for 25 years. After all this time, we haven’t been given an opportunity to apply for permanent status,” he said. “So, the question is legal, but also moral: If someone has lived in the United States for 25 years with immigration status, is that really temporary? For many, 25 years is a whole life.”

“The least we deserve is the opportunity to continue our lives, as we have done all these years, but with permanent immigration status,” Palma said. “I want Democrats and Republicans to take this issue seriously, reach an agreement and find a permanent solution.”

An earlier version of this story was first published in Noticias Telemundo.

World.title: Driver charged with 2nd-degree murder in L.A. bus crash that news helicopter was covering
World.content:
LOS ANGELES — The woman accused of ramming into a Los Angeles city bus Tuesday has been charged with second-degree murder in the deadly crash, officials announced Thursday.

Bailee Lynn Rios, 36, was arrested Wednesday in connection with the crash, which killed two passengers. While it was covering the tragedy, a news helicopter crashed nearby, killing the reporter and the pilot on board and a pedestrian on the ground.

“What is particularly tragic about this case is that this is a preventable tragedy,” Los Angeles County District Attorney Nathan Hochman told reporters.

In addition to the two counts of second-degree murder, Rios has also been charged with driving under the influence of a drug and reckless driving, according to a complaint.

“She will be looking at a maximum sentence of life in prison,” Hochman said.

It was not immediately clear whether Rios had an attorney who could speak on her behalf.

Law enforcement officials investigate the scene of a crash with a L.A. Metro Bus in Los Angeles on Tuesday. Ronaldo Bolanos / Los Angeles Times via Getty Images

According to police, Rios drove her 2004 Ford Expedition the wrong way down a busy street, ran a red light and hit a car before she slammed into the bus. She was rescued by first responders and taken to a local hospital.

Investigators found drugs in Rios’ car following the wreck, and prosecutors suspect she was driving under the influence, Hochman said.

“She was driving well beyond the speed limit, she entered into opposing traffic because she was approaching a red light where cars were stopped, and she didn’t stop,” he said.

One passenger was fully ejected from the bus and another was partially ejected, police said. Video from the scene in Chatsworth, a neighborhood in Los Angeles’ San Fernando Valley, showed Rios’ SUV partially wedged into the middle of the bus.

The passengers killed in the bus were identified Thursday as Daniel Castillo, 46, and Gage Weida, 31.

In a helicopter high above, reporter Eliana Moreno described the crash as “horrific” on live television.

“This is terrifying,” she said in what would become one of her final broadcasts.

Moreno and pilot George Marciniw were killed when the chopper, providing coverage for NBC Los Angeles and Telemundo 52, suddenly lost altitude and plummeted toward two storage containers.

A person on the ground, Edy Gutierrez Mejia, also died.

NewsChopper 4 was owned and operated by Angel City Air.

The aftermath of a news helicopter crash in Chatsworth, a neighborhood in Los Angeles, on Wednesday. Ethan Swope / AP

The deaths left Chatsworth and the greater Los Angeles community in shock and mourning. Rios’ loved ones said they never could have imagined she would be involved in something so horrific.

“It’s so awful,” her mother, Cindy Rios, told NBC News in a brief phone call Thursday.

Rios’ longtime friend Brad Aragon told the California Post that Rios had struggled with addiction in the past and went to rehab at least once. He confirmed the Post’s reporting to NBC News.

On social media, Rios occasionally posted about being in recovery and battling addictions. Friends left encouraging words and offered help if she needed it.

Hours before the crash, Aragon and Rios had texted each other about planning a visit in October. She seemed shaken by recent events in her life and said she was hanging around with people she knew were toxic, Aragon told the Post.

According to court records, Rios was convicted in 2022 of driving with a suspended license. Previous charges of driving under the influence, drug possession and carrying drug paraphernalia were dismissed.

Hochman said his office is still examining her criminal record. Rios is expected to be arraigned Friday, he said.

She was being held on $4 million bail Thursday.

Weida, one of the men killed in the bus crash, was days away from his parents coming to visit Saturday to celebrate his birthday, Hochman said.

Castillo was a loving father, his daughter, college sophomore Johaunna Castillo, told NBC Los Angeles.

“There’s so many people that cared about him, and every single person drove down to the accident that day, so they could all be with each other,” she told the station. Her father was looking forward to seeing her graduate, she said.

Asked whether the three helicopter-related deaths would be rolled into Rios’ case, Hochman declined to speculate.

“We’ll wait to see what the investigation reveals, and then we’ll make the call at that time,” he said.

World.title: Ohio mother of 16 kids found living in squalid home pleads not guilty to child endangerment
World.content:
The mother of 16 children found living in squalid conditions in an Ohio house has pleaded not guilty to endangering her children, as well as sexual battery of a minor in a separate case.

Elizabeth Siders, 34, appeared in Vinton County court Wednesday for her arraignment. She was arrested June 30 along with her husband, Gary Siders Jr., and her in-laws Gary Siders Sr. and Christina Siders.

Elizabeth Siders pleaded not guilty to 19 counts of child endangerment in the case related to her children. Prosecutors said that the children were found in horrific conditions, in a home littered with feces, and that some of the children were unable to speak.

She also pleaded not guilty to two charges each of sexual battery and unlawful sexual conduct with a minor in a separate case. NBC News has reached out to her attorney for comment.

Siders and her husband were indicted Aug. 21 in the sexual battery case.

The indictments accuse Gary Siders Jr., 36, and Elizabeth Siders of sexual abuse against a minor, who was between the ages of 13 and 16 in 2022.

The indictments indicate the victim was not one of Elizabeth Siders’ children, but they describe her as acting “in loco parentis,” meaning she was responsible for the victim’s care.

She hung her head in court when a judge ordered her Wednesday to have no contact with her children, the minor victim or her husband.

The judge set her bond at $250,000, on top of her $300,000 child endangerment bond. She remained in jail Thursday.

Her defense attorney, Thomas Stolly, told the judge she misses her children and questioned whether she herself is a victim.

“We have an individual in Elizabeth who was married at age 15, who has essentially been pregnant for the better part of two decades, who has never fully gone through any postpartum period,” Stolly said, according to NBC affiliate WSAZ of Huntington, West Virginia.

He said he was concerned about the effects she may suffer given the repeated births and a lack of regular medical care.

The Siders children, ages 1½ to 18, are in state custody.

Stolly previously asked for a competency evaluation for Elizabeth, which was granted last month. The results are pending.

World.title: F-16 fighter jet crashes in residential area in northern Michigan
World.content:
A U.S. F-16 fighter jet pilot safely ejected before the aircraft crashed in northern Michigan on Thursday afternoon, officials said.

The incident occurred in Grand Traverse County when the jet “experienced an incident” during a routine training mission, a spokesperson for the Texas Military Department said.

Michael Kroll, spokesperson for the Michigan Department of Military and Veterans Affairs, confirmed the jet was an F-16 from the Texas Air National Guard.

The pilot is stable and was transferred to a local hospital, Michigan State Police said.

Rescue efforts after an F-16 fighter jet crashed in a rural area near Traverse City, Mich., on Thursday. WPBN

The training mission originated out of the Air National Guard’s Combat Readiness Training Center in Alpena, Michigan, the military department said.

There have been no reports of civilian injuries in the incident, which occurred in a residential area, Blair Township Supervisor Nicole Blonshine said in a phone interview Thursday afternoon.

Blonshine said she did not witness the crash but heard it from her office.

A witness, Nicole Conrad, said her kids noticed the military jet first.

“I hear a big boom, and then I see a colorful parachute and this guy floating down from the sky,” she told NBC News.

Ed Wilson, another witness, said he saw the plane going down, followed by an explosion and black smoke.

“The jet just went straight in with a nose up and disappeared,” he said.

Social media video verified by NBC News appears to show a column of black smoke rising near a home in the area of the reported crash.

A hazardous chemical spill related to the crash led to an evacuation of all business and residential properties within a 1-mile radius, state police said. The order was lifted as of 9:44 p.m.

Air traffic control audio obtained by NBC News describes the declaration of a possible mayday after the plane “may have taken a bird.” It goes on to describe “a lot of black smoke” after it reported “it appears that they may have lost an engine and ejected.”

The Texas Military Department spokesperson said the incident is under investigation.

An F-16 Fighting Falcon is a “compact, multi-role fighter aircraft” that is “highly maneuverable and has proven itself in air-to-air combat and air-to-surface attack,” according to the Air Force.

World.title: 5 steel-toe boots that protect your feet, including picks that don’t scream work boot
World.content:
For casual outings or trips to the gym, sneakers get the job done. But if you work in construction, spend time tooling around a garage or workshop or do anything else that puts you around debris and heavy things, you’ll need a shoe that provides a bit more protection. Steel-toe boots tend to be the go-to choice. In fact, in many workplaces, they are a requirement because they can prevent serious injuries.

“Steel-toe boots reduce crush injuries from blunt heavy objects, stubbing of the toe and lacerations from sharp objects falling on your foot,” says Dr. Adenike Sonaike, a podiatrist and medical director with Baker Street Health in Motion in New Jersey.

I consulted Sonaike and another foot health expert on what to look for in a good pair of steel-toe boots. Then, based on their recommendations, I rounded up highly-rated options from Orthofoot, Cat, Timberland and other brands known for their durability.

The best steel-toe and safety boots of 2026

Using guidance provided by our experts, I sourced steel-toe boots that meet ASTM standards. This is a rating for shoes that pass certain tests pertaining to keeping your feet safe and protected. The boots below also have at least a four-star average rating from hundreds of shoppers or come recommended by experts.

“Orthofeet has some great options,” says Sonaike. “The Granite work boot has a wide composite toe, cushioned heel, arch support and it offers slip resistance.” The upper on these shoes is made from leather and has a coating that makes them water-resistant. The inside is padded for comfort, and the laces are secured with ladder grab notches, which allow you to tighten them or loosen them easily.

These boots have a steel-toe cap and a sole that provides grip on low-traction surfaces. They also have a water-resistant leather upper that is also abrasion-resistant, so they will continue to look good after you’ve worn them a number of times, according to the brand. They almost resemble a nice hiking boot, so if you have to head to an activity straight from your worksite you won’t feel like everyone’s staring at your footwear.

The boots also have an electrical hazard protection of up to 600 volts in dry conditions, according to Cat.

Similar to the boots from Cat, these steel-toe shoes offer electrical hazard protection. They are also heat- and water-resistant and have built-in arch support, according to Timberland. The boots come in six colors and are available in regular and wide widths.

These work boots look a bit more like a hiking boot than most styles. They are water-resistant and also have a moisture-wicking interior that keeps feet dry, even if you sweat. The lug soles provide good traction, and the insole is contoured for comfort, according to the brand. Note that shoppers say that the laces wear quickly and may need to be replaced every few months and these are the most expensive boots on this list.

These work boots have an ASTM-rated steel toe, electrical hazard protection and are water-resistant. They also have a fast-drying lining inside to wick away sweat and a foam cushion insole to reduce foot fatigue, according to Carhartt. They’re available in two colors — both look good with jeans or khakis — and come in regular and wide widths.

How I picked the best steel-toe boots

To round up the best steel-toe boots, I consulted with foot health experts on what to keep in mind when shopping. Here’s what they suggest:

Toe cap: Look for boots that have an ASTM rating for safety footwear, says Dr. Brandon Haghverdian, an orthopedic surgeon at Hoag Orthopedic Institute in Irvine, Calif. This is a rating given to performance footwear, like work boots, that designates that the shoes meet or exceed certain falling and compression tests.

World.title: Sacramento Sikh truck driver survives being stabbed 17 times at Wyoming rest stop
World.content:
A Sikh truck driver from Northern California was stabbed 17 times in an unprovoked attack at a Wyoming truck stop on Sunday, his attorney says.

The Sweetwater County Sheriff's Office in Wyoming confirmed the attack happened just before 3:30 a.m. on Sunday. The driver, a Sacramento man who said he only feels safe sharing his last name of Singh, stopped near the Bitter Creek rest area on Interstate 80 in Wyoming for a bathroom break.

He told attorney and Jakara Movement Director of Legal Services Jasjit Singh that he was first punched in the back of the head in the rest area bathroom. His attacker, another truck driver, didn't speak as Singh repeatedly asked why he was being attacked.

The man began to stab Singh until he was able to push him off and run outside.

A family at the rest area saw Singh's condition after the attack. A father and son followed the suspect, who attempted to drive off in his own tractor-trailer, until Wyoming Highway Patrol troopers arrived.

The family returned to the rest area to help Singh, who called 911. Singh was transported by helicopter to a trauma facility, according to the sheriff's office.

The suspect was located in Rawlins, further east down I-80, by Highway Patrol troopers and taken into custody without incident.

Concern about attack's motive

There is no known motive for the attack at this time and there is no threat to the public, officials said. The investigation is ongoing.

Singh, the driver, is getting support from the Jakara Movement, a California-based grassroots community-building organization that empowers, educates, and organizes Punjabi Sikhs and other marginalized communities.

Jasjit Singh told CBS News Sacramento Thursday there are concerns about why the driver was attacked and whether it was motivated by bias.

The driver was not wearing a turban at the time, Singh said, but he was wearing a kara, which is a metal bracelet traditionally worn by Sikhs. Singh says the victim believes his appearance may have played a role in the attack.

"He feels like that may be part of the targeting," Singh said. "How did this individual choose him? In the middle of the night?"

There has been no official determination from investigators that the attack was motivated by the victim's religion, ethnicity or appearance.

Singh also points to the fact that the attacker was another truck driver.

"What drove this individual to do this? This is another truck driver," Singh said.

The Bitter Creek rest area is along a heavily traveled stretch of I-80 through Wyoming.

Lawmakers respond to unprovoked attack

Jasjit Singh says there have been concerns about the rhetoric coming from Washington and how it could affect South Asian and Sikh truck drivers.

"Now you have this additional fear that as a South Asian or as a Sikh Punjabi Sikh truck driver, you have to deal with these fears on how you look," Singh said.

Singh stressed that the Sikh community has spent decades building relationships with other communities.He is urging people to come together rather than allowing rhetoric to lead to violence.

"We are really begging that folks really come together and realize that we're really stronger together," Singh said. "Nothing should lead to an attack on someone's life."

A sickening reminder that hateful rhetoric will never be just rhetoric.



Words that attack or belittle people over the color of their skin can also incite the most brutal attacks, especially when they are given official sanction.



What an absolute, unmitigated travesty. pic.twitter.com/0SCF2xCyoW — Senator Adam Schiff (@SenAdamSchiff) September 17, 2026

The attack comes days after a social media post from the Department of Homeland Security targeted a specific group of commercial truck drivers and drew criticism from California Gov. Gavin Newsom and other Democratic lawmakers.

The post, which has since been taken down, shows the character Optimus Prime from the "Transformers" franchise facing a man and includes the phrases "America for Americans," "Self-deport or find out" and "Get off our roads, you don't know how to drive, Mr. Singh."

In response to the Wyoming rest stop attack, Newsom's chief deputy director of communications shared a statement with CBS News Sacramento.

"Our thoughts are with this individual and his family during this time. The Trump Administration for over a year has been pushing misinformation to smear an entire workforce and target diverse communities. The President's now-redacted social media post is one proof point — his hateful rhetoric is hurting our communities," Diana Crofts-Pelayo said.

Congressman Raja Krishnamoorthi , an Illinois Democrat, said in a statement that he is "horrified by the brutal attack on a Sikh truck driver who was stabbed 17 times at a Wyoming rest stop. This comes amid rising hatred targeting Sikh and South Asian Americans, with even the Trump Department of Homeland Security recently posting a racist caricature of a Sikh truck driver telling him to 'get off our roads' and 'self-deport or find out.'

"Those spreading this hate, including officials in our own federal government, need to stop. Those who turn it into violence must be held accountable. And all of us need to stand together against both. America must be better than this. I'm praying for Mr. Singh's full recovery and grateful to the family whose quick action helped save his life."

Earlier this month, Krishnamoorthi spoke out against the DHS post, warning that it fueled xenophobia against Sikh and South Asian Americans. He later led representatives, including California's Ami Bera, in demanding action from President Trump.

World.title: Family awarded $40 million after daughter left on freeway by Uber driver is killed
World.content:
Uber was ordered to pay $40 million to the family of a woman killed on an Orange County freeway after a rideshare driver left her on the side of the road.

Carol Normandin and Ken Parker said their 23-year-old daughter, Emily Normandin-Parker, and a friend ordered an Uber after a night out on Aug. 12, 2023. During the ride, Normandin-Parker's friend became sick and vomited in the car. The driver pulled over to the side of State Route 73 and kicked the women out of the car, leaving them on the side of the freeway.

Normandin-Parker was fatally struck by another car as their Uber drove away.

"The reason we're talking is because he didn't take responsibility and neither did Uber," Parker said. "They're still not taking responsibility. We do not want this to ever happen to another mother or another father."

During a five-day arbitration hearing, Uber argued that the driver was an independent contractor under California law and that the ridesharing company should not be held accountable for his actions.

A retired judge acting as the arbitrator awarded Normandin and Parker $20 million each.

In a statement, Uber disagreed with the decision.

"No family should have to suffer the loss of a child, and our thoughts continue to be with the Normandin-Parker family," Uber said. "While we respect the arbitration process, we believe the arbitrator was wrong in holding Uber legally responsible for the tragic events of that night."

After the decision, Uber initially offered a settlement agreement that prohibited Normandin and Parker from publicly discussing the incident, with a provision requiring them to pay $10 million each time they did, according to Panish Shea Ravipudi LLP, the law firm representing the family.

"We turned it down because we would never accept that kind of condition," Parker said. "The case was never about money in the first place."

The family created the Emily Normandin-Parker Foundation to honor their daughter and advocate for stronger rideshare safety regulations.

"In a private car, it's whatever rules they have," Normandin said. "It's whatever they're offended by. I think the whole business model of someone getting in a stranger's car, a stranger to both Uber and a stranger to us, is just dangerous."

World.title: Farmer who voted for Trump says farmers are "all just in survival mode"
World.content:
Matt Bell, 52, has been farming for more than half his life in central North Carolina. He grows soybeans, corn and wheat and raises beef cattle on more than 1,000 acres. But Bell, who voted for President Trump, says soaring prices for fuel, fertilizer, and equipment are hurting his farm and leading some of his fellow farmers to consider calling it quits once this growing season ends.

"I've done this 34 years. I have never worried and stressed like I have the last year," Bell told CBS News in an interview on Wednesday at his farm in Kings Mountain, North Carolina.

North Carolina farmer Matt Bell is interviewed by CBS News chief White House correspondent Nancy Cordes. CBS News

Bell has been forced to make significant changes to his operation as a result of the high costs. He's shifting some of his acreage, trying to stretch out the lifespan of his equipment and producing his own fertilizer. His children have also opened up a storefront where visitors can pick pumpkins and take hayrides in the fall. But Bell is still feeling the pinch.

"We've cut everything we can cut," he said. "The last several years in agriculture have been terrible, and we have, you know, just cut the fat anywhere we could. But we're just getting to the point now there's nothing left to cut. You cannot run without fuel. You cannot run without fertilizer. You have to have that."

Bell says his diesel fuel costs have about doubled since last year

The war with Iran has driven up fuel costs and created supply chain disruptions as the Strait of Hormuz remains under a naval blockade with a limited number of oil tankers allowed through the critical waterway. And the intensifying conflict between Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels and Saudi Arabia and attacks by other Iranian proxy forces on Saudi infrastructure are squeezing global fuel supplies in the Red Sea and contributing to a spike in global fuel costs.

September 2026: North Carolina farmer Matt Bell's equipment runs on diesel fuel, which is about twice as expensive now as it was a year ago.

Fighting in Russia and Ukraine has also limited oil refining capacity, driving up prices further.

Diesel prices nationwide are averaging roughly $6.40 per gallon, according to AAA, nearly double the average price a year ago. In North Carolina Thursday, diesel prices hit their highest recorded average of $6.19 per gallon.

Prices have been so volatile that Bell said the price he's quoted from his distributor in the morning is only valid until the afternoon — when it rises again. He can't avoid the expense — his farm equipment runs on diesel. Bell showed CBS News his combine, which he says now requires about $600 worth of diesel fuel per day. That's more than twice what he paid last year.

Bell said he blew through his yearly fuel budget of $35,000 in August. Now, he expects his total for the year to be closer to $50,000 to $60,000.

"Every piece of equipment on this farm runs on diesel," he said. Without it, his farm wouldn't be able to function.

Tariff impact: "Everything that we touch has gone up"

It's not just diesel prices that are hurting Bell's business. President Trump's wide-ranging tariffs have also driven up costs — and left him and other farmers in limbo as the president continues to threaten to impose more tariffs.

"Everything we're touching, the fertilizer, fuel, chemicals, seed, parts — you know, the whole nine yards, everything that we touch has gone up," Bell said, noting that many of the price hikes resulted from Mr. Trump's tariff policies.

Farmers welcomed Mr. Trump's announcement in May that he had reached a deal for China to buy 25 million metric tons of soybeans from the U.S. annually through 2028. China has purchased significantly more U.S. soybeans in 2026 compared to 2025, but its 10% retaliatory tariff on U.S. soybeans remains in place. China imposed the levy in response to Mr. Trump's fentanyl-related tariffs on China.

Bell said China's soybean tariffs have left the market in limbo: That is, China hasn't increased the prices it's paying for U.S. soybeans, even though everything farmers touch in producing soybeans "has gone up."

In a letter to Mr. Trump on Thursday ahead of his meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping next week, the American Soybean Association called on him to push for the elimination of the 10% tariff.

"I think we've been misled"

Bell initially supported Mr. Trump's policies and even thought short-term price increases resulting from the Iran conflict would be worth ensuring Iran never has a nuclear weapon, one of the president's stated goals of the war.

But he now says the administration has made miscalculations in the war. "We're just being strung along as a country and that's not good," Bell said.

Bell criticized the administration's decision-making around the war, saying, "I think we've been misled."

He also says the administration's agriculture policy is not what he was promised.

"We were sold a bill of goods that agriculture was going to be on the forefront … and there was going to be some policy that would put America's farmers and ranchers first. And right now, that has not happened."

Bell said that while the administration's farmer bailout program sounds significant, "it's not a lot of money."

This November, Bell says he'll be voting for candidates who he says have "common sense," and listen to Americans' concerns.

"I'm a Republican, but I'm probably going to vote a split ticket," he said.

"We are fighting for survival"

Bell said he knows farmers who have been forced out of business as a result of high costs, unable to sustain their business with rising prices.

"I do not want any Americans to feel sorry for the American farmer," Bell said. "I want the Americans to be mad that we have been put in this situation. We are fighting for survival, and we're running out of options."

And he acknowledged it's possible he could also be forced to shutter his farm.

"Money's not the problem, I could care less about the money," he said. "But we take a lot of pride in what we do. You can't put a dollar sign on that. But I can't stay in business under these conditions. Something has got to give."

But asked what he would do if he wasn't a farmer, Bell hesitated: "I don't know. It's all I've ever done."

World.title: Why is a Crystal Lake medical office full of unopened mail, but no employees?
World.content:
Katie Duda noticed an unusual $500 lab test from a provider she said she never heard of on an Explanation of Benefits letter she recently received from her insurer, Blue Cross Blue Shield of Texas.

"Had I been frequently to the doctor getting labs, I probably wouldn't have even given it a second thought," said Duda.

So, she and her mother traced the lab, Niyraa LLC, to a strip center in Crystal Lake and found an office with a sign on the door saying to drop off mail inside. The door was unlocked. No employees were anywhere in sight.

"It looked vacant," Duda said.

Thinking that was strange, they reached out to CBS News Chicago to take a closer look.

A medical office in Crystal Lake that looks like it has never been used, but is apparently billing Blue Cross Blue Shield for patient lab tests. CBS News Chicago

Five times over several months, CBS News Chicago reporter Marissa Sulek and photographers visited Niyraa LLC. They found thousands of pieces of mail, mostly from various Blue Cross Blue Shield entities, addressed to Niyraa LLC sitting in U.S. Postal Service bins on the front desk.

Unopened mail - mostly from Blue Cross Blue Shield - piling up in apparently unused medical office in Crystal Lake. Scott Wilson | CBS News Chicago

We contacted Crystal Lake police, the FBI and U.S. Postal Service Inspectors to tell them all of that mail was there and people's personal information could be at risk.

But every time we went back, the thousands of envelopes were still there. The only thing that changed was that they moved from the front desk to the back, now stuffed in a growing pile of black and white garbage bags.

After we started visiting the office over a period of months, the mail moved from the front desk to a pile of garbage bags in the back. The garbage bags were gone by mid-September. CBS News Chicago

So, who's behind this medical office and what's going on with all of the mysterious mail?

"Mohammed I Quadri" is the name plastered all over the lab's signage outside, inside and on current lab certifications framed and hanging on the wall.

Brittany Serby, who owns the Functional Wellness Clinic a couple of storefronts down, said she's never seen Quadri and is concerned about what might be going on with all of the mail inside the unusual office.

"It was real troubling to learn," she said.

CBS News Chicago contacted the mall owner, who said he hasn't seen Quadri in months, but Quadri still pays the rent.

We also tried several ways to contact the mystery man. We emailed, texted, made phone calls and went to addresses we found that might be connected to him. No luck.

We even waited outside the Crystal Lake lab office one weekday for hours, during a time when it should have been officially open for business. He never showed.

We couldn't find Quadri, but what could really be going on inside this mysterious office with no employees ever around?

For insight into a possible answer, we enlisted the help of a certified fraud examiner and forensic accountant, James Scordo.

We brought him to the office, which was once again unlocked and wide open.

Scordo saw the pristine, clean lab equipment, the same unopened packages of vials and other supplies that had been there for months and the mountains of mail, some envelopes now spilled out onto the floor.

His reaction?

"Oh my God," he said.

His first impression?

"Each one of those could be a potential victim," he said.

Not only could their personal private information be compromised, but Scordo said if the lab tests were never conducted, it could impact each one's medical record and ability to get insurance in the future.

What does he think is going on with all of this mystery mail?

"It appears this is a front for a fraud scheme. I mean, it has all the signs," he said.

Scordo said he believes it could be phantom billing, in which Blue Cross Blue Shield is paying Quadri for services patients aren't receiving. The patients don't even realize their insurer is being billed wrongly for those services.

Serby said she's concerned that no one seems to be doing anything about this wide open office with the mountains of mail.

"It doesn't feel like anything is being done to stop whatever is happening," she said.

We did finally learn that the Postal Service Inspector General is investigating, but apparently had not taken steps to protect the mail for many months, because the mail was always there every time we went back to check.

The FBI also told us they alerted local law enforcement and sanitary crews to make sure those entities knew about the mail in case someone threw it away.

In the past couple of weeks, we received photos from neighboring business owners showing the garbage bags stuffed with mail had been removed, by whom we don't know. However, more mail had been dropped off and was sitting on the front desk.

As recently as Sept. 16, no mail could be seen from the outside, but the door was still unlocked and the sign inviting people inside to drop off mail was still taped to the door.

We also contacted Blue Cross Blue Shield who said they can't comment on any provider relationships.

World.title: FBI investigation thwarts "mass casualty attack" from man accused of ISIS allegiance
World.content:
A Pennsylvania man planned to carry out an ISIS-inspired "mass casualty attack" before an FBI investigation thwarted him, according to federal law enforcement officials.

Speaking at a press conference Tuesday, federal officials said Jonathan Kramer, 21, of Valencia, had pledged allegiance to the Islamic State of Syria. He was arrested Saturday outside of a hotel in Cranberry Township, around 25 miles north of Pittsburgh, with a rifle, ammunition and dozens of knives in his possession.

Suspect shared "radical ideology"

Richard Evanchec, special agent in charge for the FBI's Pittsburgh field office, called the planned attack an "imminent threat of violence inspired by ISIS."

"Let me be clear about this threat: Jonathan Kramer demonstrated a sustained devotion to the Islamic State of Syria," Evanchec said. "He recorded a pledge of allegiance to the same. Following that pledge, he made efforts to spread their propaganda and shared ways to kill all in the name of a foreign terrorist organization."

United States Attorney Troy Rivetti said it became clear that Kramer, a 2023 Mars Area High School graduate, was moving forward "with his radical ideology." But officials didn't elaborate on any specifics surrounding the alleged planned attack, including when or where it might have occurred.

Timeline of arrest

On the morning of Sept. 12, federal agents said they watched Kramer leave his home, carrying a backpack. He got into an Uber and went to a Walmart in Gibsonia. In the parking lot, they say he met another person and took something from the trunk — a long black bag that agents say could hold a rifle.

He then took an Uber to a hotel in Cranberry Township, where they said Kramer paid $450 in cash for a week. He then went to Dunham's Sports, where agents said they watched him at the firearms counter.

When he returned to the hotel, the FBI moved in and arrested him.

A photo shared with KDKA shows Jonathan Kramer at the hotel in Cranberry where he was arrested. (Photo: KDKA)

Investigators said a search of Kramer's hotel room and home led to the discovery of a semi-automatic rifle, loaded rifle magazines, a rifle scope and boxes of ammunition, along with 30 knives and a note. The note told people not to look for him, saying "I cant live In constant Fear," according to court paperwork. The FBI said he had roughly 190 rounds of ammunition.

The FBI said it also found social media correspondence that led investigators to believe an attack was being planned.

"This defendant made repeated attempts to encourage and coordinate violence through encrypted platforms such as advising others on attack methods, discussing chemical poisons, vehicle attacks, drone delivery explosives and firearms-based assaults," Evanchec said.

Authorities thank public for help

Rivetti referred to the FBI investigation that led to Kramer's arrest as being "covert."

"We want to thank the individual who first reported this defendant's dangerous and troubling behavior, as well as the other individuals who agreed to speak to law enforcement this weekend," Rivetti said.

Rivetti said that the cooperation of the public in investigations is key for law enforcement to be able to "prevent horrific crimes from being committed in our community."

"We hope this prosecution serves as a stark reminder to everyone of the importance of vigilance," Rivetti said.

Federal charges have been filed against a Pittsburgh-area man accused of plotting an attack in support of ISIS. KDKA Photojournalist Fred Williams

U.S. Congressman Mike Kelly (R-PA), whose district includes Butler County, said in a statement that he commends the diligent work of the FBI and law enforcement for apprehending Kramer before he could potentially follow through with an alleged attack.

"This disgusting, hate-filled extremism has no place in our nation," Rep. Kelly said.

Kramer has been charged with one count of receipt or transfer of a firearm or ammunition knowing or having reasonable cause to believe such firearm or ammunition will be used to commit a felony or a federal crime of terrorism.

During a federal court appearance in Pittsburgh on Wednesday, Kramer waived his preliminary examination hearing. He was shackled at his hands and feet and in a red jumpsuit. He was stoic and showed no emotion.

A date has not been set for Kramer's next court appearance.

World.title: F-16 from Texas crashes in Michigan, evacuation order lifted
World.content:
An F-16 fighter jet crashed in Grand Traverse County, Michigan, on Thursday, triggering an evacuation order along part of County Road 633, the county's emergency management said.

Grand Traverse officials said the plane went down near County Road 633 and Blair Townhall Road and that traffic in the area was shut down. Blair Township Supervisor Nicole Blonshine said she did not believe anyone on the ground was hurt or that any homes were damaged.

A spokesperson with the 149th Fighter Wing of the Texas National Guard confirmed that the pilot ejected and is in stable condition. They are currently receiving medical treatment. Michigan State Police, which is assisting the Grand Traverse County Sheriff's Office, says no other injuries were reported.

"A 149th Fighter Wing, Texas Air National Guard F-16 Fighting Falcon was on a routine training mission from the Air National Guard's Combat Readiness Training Center, in Alpena, when it experienced an incident earlier this afternoon," the Texas Military Department said in a statement.

Air traffic controller audio obtained by CBS News Detroit suggests the plane may have "taken a bird."

The crash remains under investigation.

Emergency management initially issued a shelter-in-place order covering County Road 633 from Jefferson Place to Blair Townhall Road. Officials had instructed those in the area to stay indoors, close their windows and vents, and follow instructions from emergency personnel.

An evacuation order is in effect at about 5 p.m. local time within 1 mile of the site. Anyone in that area is urged to evacuate away from the intersection of County Road 633 and Jefferson Place. Shelter is available at Kensington Church (6880 Secor Road in Traverse City, Michigan). Emergency management says Kensington Church and the American Red Cross are assisting impacted residents.

Officials lifted the order sometime before 10 p.m., saying impacted residents can return to their homes. However, some residents, including those of the Glacier Pond subdivision, will not be able to return home. Emergency management says those residents have been contacted by first responders.

Munson Healthcare in Traverse City says it is the local decontamination site after first responders and community members were exposed to a hazardous chemical called hydrazine. Anyone who was within 1 mile of the crash site and are symptomatic should seek medical attention. Anyone who is asymptomatic is advised to monitor for signs such as coughing, wheezing or trouble breathing and should seek medical care if they notice the symptoms.

World.title: Holdout juror in Lindsay Clancy trial says he "didn't have any doubts"
World.content:
The lone holdout juror in the high-profile Lindsay Clancy murder trial said he "didn't have any doubts" about what he believed was Clancy's criminal responsibility, providing his account of the jury's deliberations.

"I didn't have any doubts," juror Michael Desronvil said in a statement obtained by CBS News through his representative, Ray Marcel. "As I tried to explain different possible theories during deliberation, I kept getting cut off as if I had doubts based on the evidence present."

"Based on all the physical evidence, key witnesses, and what the prosecution presents, I thought it was enough proof that she knew exactly what she was doing and planned," his statement read.

The jury remained deadlocked on Sept. 4, the seventh day of deliberations, after not coming to a unanimous decision about whether Clancy was criminally responsible for killing her three young children at their Massachusetts home in January 2023. Clancy had pleaded not guilty to first-degree murder in the deaths of 5-year-old Cora, 3-year-old Dawson and 8-month-old Callan. The judge declared a mistrial after the hung jury could not reach a verdict.

Paula Devlin, a juror in the murder trial, told "CBS Mornings" last week that jurors spent several days seeing if they could convince the holdout juror, who believed Clancy should be found guilty of murder, to come to their side, but he would not budge.

"We all worked together. And I don't know if it was to convince him to start with," Devlin told "CBS Mornings" co-host Gayle King. "We all worked together to convince ourselves once we got to that point where it was 10 to 2. I felt very bad for them because they felt attacked. And there is no way to not do that."

Attorney Edward Andrew Paltzik announced on social media that he is now representing Desronvil, saying that Desronvil is "safe and sound at an undisclosed secure location in a rural area of Northern New England."

The holdout juror has been subjected to widespread criticism online in the wake of the mistrial.

"Rest assured that the evil people who have so viciously attacked this American Hero and Champion of Justice will be held accountable to the maximum extent of the law and beyond," Paltzik said in a post on X.

CBS News recently reported that the holdout juror was accused of domestic violence in 2021. Police in Brockton, Massachusetts, said he was accused of grabbing his wife by the throat and throwing her into a dresser during an argument. He pleaded not guilty to a count of domestic violence assault and battery, and the charge was later dismissed, according to court records.

CBS News legal analyst Caroline Polisi said the key question is whether Desronvil disclosed the allegation on his juror questionnaire. But with a mistrial already declared, it's unclear whether the issue will have any impact on the case going forward, she said.

Clancy admitted to killing her three children, but jurors could not agree on whether she should be held criminally responsible. Several jurors and Clancy's defense attorney said the jury was divided 11-1 in favor of finding her not criminally responsible, citing evidence of her mental illness.

Judge William Sullivan declared a mistrial after the jury reported being deadlocked three times.

District Attorney Timothy Cruz has not yet announced whether the state will retry Clancy. The next court hearing is scheduled for Sept. 29 at Plymouth Superior Court.
