World.title: ‘Tell Matura, I got 10… months’: Prince Copious sentenced for burglarizing attorney’s home but Audrey says ‘he should have gotten more’ because her stolen gun was never recovered
World.content:
‘Tell Matura, I got 10… months’: Prince Copious sentenced for burglarizing attorney’s home but Audrey says ‘he should have gotten more’ because her stolen gun was never recovered

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Attorney Audrey Matura says the sentence handed down to her former handyman, Prince Copious, for burglarizing her home was too lenient, particularly because her licensed firearm remains missing and has never been recovered.

Copious was sentenced Thursday to 18 months in prison after pleading guilty to burglarizing Matura’s Chetumal Boulevard residence in April 2025. After credit for 224 days already spent on remand and other deductions, he has 10 months and 16 days left to serve.

Matura told Breaking Belize News that she believes the punishment amounts to little more than a slap on the wrist given the circumstances of the burglary.

“The sentence was lenient given the fact that he stole a licensed firearm which he refused to say where it is, other than to say to me he took it to Belmopan,” Matura said.

She also said that at the time Copious pleaded guilty, he was already on remand in connection with another burglary.

Matura further alleged that Copious had a lengthy antecedent history involving burglary and theft charges, but said many of those matters were never concluded because of repeated court adjournments and frustrated victims.

“His antecedent history shows many charges for burglary and theft but the court process so slow and frustrating that many of those cases were never heard as victims got tired of the adjournments,” Matura said. “That is why he had gotten away with so much and has graduated from petty theft to bigger items.”

Those claims relate to allegations and charges described by Matura and do not, by themselves, amount to convictions.

Matura said she had hired Copious to perform maintenance and handyman work at her home and business, placing him in a position of trust. Police later alleged that surveillance footage showed him using a makeshift ladder to access the second floor of her home through a bathroom window.

Among the property reported stolen was Matura’s 9mm Ruger pistol valued at $3,500, a magazine containing seven live rounds, jewelry, cosmetics, a knapsack and knives belonging to her son. The stolen items were valued at more than $6,000.

Matura said the firearm remains her greatest concern because it has never been recovered.

She also previously told reporters that while Copious was in police custody, he admitted the burglary to her and allegedly provided information about other persons to whom he would take stolen property. Matura said she recorded that conversation and was disappointed that police did not use the information to more aggressively pursue the missing items and firearm.

Copious initially pleaded not guilty following his arrest but changed his plea to guilty on August 11, 2026, after his trial had already begun.

As police transported him to prison Thursday afternoon, Copious reportedly waited until cameras stopped recording before calling out a message for Matura: “Tell Matura, I got 10,” before pausing and adding, “months.”

He will now serve the remaining 10 months and 16 days of his sentence at the Belize Central Prison.

World.title: Deovan Hall shot dead while riding home from event in Corozal; police seek two suspects
World.content:
Deovan Hall shot dead while riding home from event in Corozal; police seek two suspects

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Police are seeking two suspects following the murder of Deovan Hall, who was shot multiple times while reportedly heading home on his bicycle in the San Antonio Village area of the Corozal District Wednesday night.

Police responded to reports of a shooting and found Hall’s lifeless body near a field along a feeder road with multiple gunshot injuries.

Initial investigations indicate that Hall had attended an event and was riding home when he was approached by persons in the area. Police say there appeared to have been a struggle before Hall was shot.

Hall was pronounced dead at the scene.

Police say Hall had previously been arrested for minor offences, but investigators have not confirmed whether his past encounters with the law have any connection to his murder.

Two suspects are being sought as the investigation continues.

World.title: 20-year-old Anthony Perry gunned down on Louise Bevans Street; police point to ongoing rivalry
World.content:
20-year-old Anthony Perry gunned down on Louise Bevans Street; police point to ongoing rivalry

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Police believe an ongoing rivalry involving persons in the Louise Bevans Street area may be behind Wednesday night’s murder of 20-year-old Anthony William Perry in Belize City.

Perry was walking in the area when he was approached by a gunman who opened fire, striking him. He was rushed to the Karl Heusner Memorial Hospital but was pronounced dead on arrival.

Police say Perry was known to authorities and that investigators believe the murder stems from an ongoing rivalry involving persons from the area. Investigators are currently seeking two suspects and are reviewing surveillance footage that may assist the investigation.

No one had been detained in connection with the murder at the time of Thursday’s police briefing.

Perry’s age, full name and the location of the shooting were also independently reported Wednesday night by Breaking Belize News, which reported that he was shot on Louise Bevans Street before being taken to KHMH.

World.title: Honduran scrap-gold dealer allegedly lured to Faber’s Road and shot dead for money
World.content:
Honduran scrap-gold dealer allegedly lured to Faber’s Road and shot dead for money

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A Honduran national who regularly purchased scrap gold in Belize City was allegedly lured to the Faber’s Road area Wednesday evening before being shot and killed after a demand for money, police say.

Police responded to the shooting at around 6:20 p.m. and found 42-year-old Dennis Guevara suffering from gunshot injuries. He was rushed to the Karl Heusner Memorial Hospital, where he later succumbed.

According to investigators, Guevara routinely purchased scrap gold from people in the area and had reportedly been contacted by someone who asked to meet him there.

Police say that during the meeting, the person allegedly demanded money from Guevara before shooting him several times.

Authorities have not yet confirmed whether robbery was the motive for the killing.

Investigators are reviewing surveillance footage from the area and are working to identify and locate suspects.

World.title: U.S. Ambassador André Bauer personally delivers school bags to students in Santana Village
World.content:
U.S. Ambassador André Bauer personally delivers school bags to students in Santana Village

By Breaking Belize News Staff: United States Ambassador to Belize André Bauer personally handed out backpacks filled with school supplies to primary school students during a visit to Zion Park Methodist Primary School in Santana Village on Thursday.

Bauer was joined by locally employed staff of the U.S. Embassy in Belmopan for the distribution, which also included supplies for teachers. In photographs shared by the Embassy, the newly appointed ambassador is seen interacting directly with the children and handing backpacks to students.

The Embassy described the initiative as part of its continuing commitment to education and opportunity across Belize.

Thursday’s donation continues a years-long pattern of U.S. Embassy support for Belizean students. In 2022, the Embassy provided 500 backpacks containing school supplies to students of Carmelita and Santa Martha Government Schools in the Orange Walk District.

In 2016, the Embassy donated more than 150 backpacks to a back-to-school drive for children in residential care facilities; records from that initiative indicate then-Deputy Chief of Mission Adrienne Galanek participated in the distribution rather than then-Ambassador Carlos Moreno.

And Bauer is not the first U.S. ambassador to personally get involved in handing the bags to Belizean children. In January 2023, then-Ambassador Michelle Kwan personally distributed backpacks and school supplies during a visit to San Jose Government School in Orange Walk. News 5 reported Kwan describing the experience of “passing out school supplies, backpacks to the students,” while the Embassy’s contribution of school supplies was valued at approximately US$8,000.

Bauer was sworn in as U.S. Ambassador to Belize in August and recently began his assignment in the country.

World.title: International News: U.S.-Mexico trade talks advance
World.content:
International News: U.S.-Mexico trade talks advance

By Zoila Palma: U.S. President Donald Trump and Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum spoke by phone Wednesday as the two countries continue negotiations aimed at reaching an agreement on trade, according to a U.S. official and a person familiar with the conversation.

The call comes as Washington and Mexico move closer to an agreement on the future of the U.S.-Mexico-Canada Agreement (USMCA).

The two sources offered differing descriptions of the conversation.

The person familiar with the call, who spoke anonymously, described it as “so-so” and said new topics were introduced during the discussion, creating some uncertainty.

A U.S. official, also speaking anonymously, described the conversation as “constructive” and said the trade negotiations remain active and are moving in a positive direction, Politico reports.

Mexican officials believed the two sides were nearing an agreement addressing concerns surrounding the USMCA, the North American trade pact signed during Trump’s first term, according to the person familiar with the call. The ongoing review has involved increasingly detailed negotiations between Washington and Mexico over the future of the agreement.

The fourth round of formal U.S.-Mexico discussions has been rescheduled for September 28 and 29 in Washington. The talks follow a third round in July between Mexican officials and U.S. Trade Ambassador Jamieson Greer, where both sides reported progress on areas including automobiles, steel and aluminum, agriculture, labor and economic security.

World.title: Trees, Climate action and conservation: Ministry brings sustainability to Independence Day parade
World.content:
Trees, Climate action and conservation: Ministry brings sustainability to Independence Day parade

By Zoila Palma: The Ministry of Sustainable Development will join Belize’s 45th Independence Day celebrations in San Ignacio and Santa Elena, highlighting its efforts to promote a healthier, more resilient and sustainable Belize.

The Ministry will participate with an Independence Day float showcasing its departments, programmes and national initiatives.

Featured initiatives will include the One Million Trees Campaign, the “Bin It” campaign promoting responsible waste management, climate action and resilience, and water conservation.

The float will also highlight efforts in biodiversity and protected areas, the Carbon Market and the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs).

Through the initiatives, the Ministry aims to raise awareness about environmental stewardship, responsible resource management and the importance of building communities that can adapt to a changing climate.

World.title: ‘Mommy, them want me turn cruff”
World.content:
BICKERSTETH, St James — The lament of a 10-year-old student struck a chord with residents Thursday after thieves ransacked Bickersteth Primary and Infant School, making off with computers and tuck shop supplies in the fifth break-in there in just seven years.

“Mommy, them people yah want me turn cruff,” was how the boy reacted to news of the break-in, his mother told the Jamaica Observer.

The mother, who asked not be named, said her son, a grade five student, cried on the verandah of their house as he was told that school would be closed on Thursday and Friday because of the crime.

“I told him ‘Son, you nah turn cruff, we will stand with you’,” she related to the Observer.

Cruff is a Jamaican colloquial term for individuals who are deemed lazy, lack ambition, or have poor social etiquette.

The mother is among parents and residents who are now expressing anguish over the situation at the school.

“I usually send him out before me, but he has to stay home with his sister today,” the distraught mother said.

On Thursday morning, school administrators turned up to see windows and doors at the school pried open and items missing.

“They ripped the grill out the wall, broke the window and came in,” Principal Robert Gordon said. “Not even [Hurricane] Melissa did a job like that, the place was ransacked.”

Category 5 Melissa left widespread destruction across western and south-western parishes last October.

Principal Gordon said Thursday’s early morning break-in was the fifth in seven years.

“Last year, this time, they broke into the school twice, but that individual was held. We lost some equipment as well — computers and food items,” Gordon said.

He speculated that the robbery may be connected with others committed in western Jamaica in recent times.

“Based on what is happening now and the series of schools — Bogue Hill, Retrieve, Anchovy — it seems like they are just going through and hitting schools in a series,” Gordon said.

A man who gave his name as Anglin, described the break-in as disheartening.

“I have four daughters and all of them went through here. The last one was head girl at Anchovy, one got 11 subjects at Mount Alvernia, but this is the ground where it all started,” he said.

“This is heartbreaking, man,” he added.

On Thursday, following an emergency meeting of the school board, several members of staff were seen engaged in cleaning-up activities while listening to gospel music amid the sound of power tools as work was ongoing to replace a damaged window.

“We are trying to fix back as best as possible, even though it might be temporary, but we want to secure the area from the elements because rain may fall and the entire area is ripped out and we don’t want the office to be compromised any further,” Principal Gordon told the Observer.

“The gentleman that is working now is a community person; he’s from the area, his children came to school here. We called him, he dropped what he was doing, and he’s here and we are very appreciative of that,” Gordon said, adding that the school will be closed for the rest of the week while they work to sort things out. However, online classes will be held.

“One of the things we looked at is the impact it will have on the students seeing the school ripped apart and that could have a long-term impact on their mental psyche,” the principal explained.

“We said, ‘Okay, let’s sort of fix back the school in a way, because these children are very young, they are very impressionable, and we have to be mindful of what they see’,” he added.

“We have spoken to the teachers and we have asked them to send out work for the students to do virtually,” he revealed.

On Wednesday, Education Minister Senator Dr Dana Morris Dixon acknowledged that schools, particularly in western Jamaica, are being plagued by break-ins since the start of the academic year.

“The west has gone through a lot of trauma for us to be dealing with theft of computers for these schools and these children, it is really heartbreaking,” she lamented during the weekly post-Cabinet news briefing.

She said the series of robberies has resulted in her reaching out to the national security minister and police commissioner for assistance.

World.title: ‘It’s a fallacy’
World.content:
ROBINSON... we’re far from being in a good position in the economy

Opposition spokesman on finance Julian Robinson has dismissed as a “fallacy” the rosy picture of the Jamaican economy presented by Finance Minister Fayval Williams during Wednesday’s post-Cabinet media briefing.

Among other things, Williams noted that the rate of recovery from the fallout caused by Hurricane Melissa, which destroyed large swathes of south- and north-western parishes last October, was 18 months ahead of earlier projections by the Planning Institute of Jamaica (PIOJ).

However, Robinson is pointing to inflation running at nearly eight per cent and a $30-billion tax revenue shortfall as signs of a struggling economy.

In a video released by the Opposition People’s National Party (PNP) on Thursday, Robinson suggested that the finance minister was merely trying to put a positive spin on the situation. He reminded that in the last quarter the Government’s own projection for revenues was $28.7 billion lower than projected.

“It’s important to note that these projections were done in March 2026, which is after Hurricane Melissa, so they would have factored in Melissa and they would have made their projections,” he said.

Robinson pointed out that the revenue shortfall of nearly $30 billion forced the Government to go back to the market to borrow $30 billion but the Administration was unable to raise the full amount.

“To give this impression that the economy is doing great is really a fallacy,” he declared.

The Opposition spokesman also highlighted what he described as the cost of living pressures facing Jamaicans. He cited that at nearly eight per cent, inflation was “way above the Bank of Jamaica (BOJ) target range of four to six per cent”.

“I anticipate that when the BOJ’s monetary policy committee meets, they will be looking to raise interest rates to try and tame inflation,” he stated.

Were the central bank to take such a decision, Robinson conceded that this would put more pressure on businesses which will have to pay more on their loans, and on consumers, who will have to pay more on their mortgages and the various loans they are carrying.

“We’re far from being in a good position in the economy, we’re actually seeing the highest rates of car repossessions; we’re seeing bad loans at banks at elevated rates. So it indicates that there’s significant consumer pressure being faced, people are struggling to meet their basic obligations,” said Robinson.

Anticipating talk from some quarters that the cost of living pressure is being driven by factors outside Jamaica’s control, such as the higher cost for fuel and electricity as a result of the Middle East war, Robinson said while that is true, there are things within the control of the Government that would lessen the pressure on Jamaicans.

“The Government has the control to determine how much imported oil we use, it has been an absolute failure on the part of this Government to increase the amount of renewables that have been added to the grid,” Robinson argued.

“In the 10-and-a-half years that they have been in office, they have added no renewables to the grid,” he said, adding that what was in fact added since 2016 started under the previous PNP Administration with Phillip Paulwell as energy minister.

Pointing out that it took the Jamaica Labour Party Government eight years to issue a request for proposal for renewables, the Opposition spokesman said those companies that have been selected cannot sign private purchase agreements with Jamaica Public Service Company because the company’s contract is in limbo (its licence expires in July 2027).

He asserted that while we cannot control the price of oil, we can determine how much oil we import by building out more renewables. In this regard, he said the Government has failed; a failure with a direct impact on cost of living.

“Because, if we’re less dependent on oil, it improves our financial position and it means the impact is less on consumers,” he said.

Robinson also argued that the minister pointing out that the economy is recovering faster than projected masks certain uncomfortable realities.

“We’re underspending the capital budget. Our capital budget is required to build out schools, hospitals, roads, etc, we’re underspending that,” he reiterated. He argued that such spend is important to ensuring that there’s growth in the economy “because there’s a direct link between your capital budget and economic growth and for the last five years we have underspent it”.

Robinson pointed out that when the capital budget is underutilised, the money is shifted to recurrent expenditure such as wages and salaries. “This makes the fiscal situation look a little better but it does not account for the fact that we have been woefully underspending the capital budget,” he insisted.

He lamented that the vast majority of Jamaicans most affected by Hurricane Melissa — either at the individual or small business level — have received no assistance from Government. This, he said, has made it difficult for them to recover, resulting in lower tax revenues. He insisted that Government has taken too long to get help to those who are most in need.

In her take on the economy, Williams highlighted that in the quarter following the hurricane, the economy contracted 7.1 per cent, then 4.1 per cent in the next quarter and just 2.9 per cent in the quarter after that. She said the 2.9 per cent projection should be finalised by the Statistical Institute of Jamaica by the end of September.

The finance minister argued that the shrinking year-on-year numbers are themselves proof that the economy is recovering, adding further that “an economy in decline produces deepening figures, not improving ones”.

Williams urged Jamaicans to remember that immediately after the hurricane, PIOJ projected that the country would not get back to its pre-Melissa level of output until the last quarter of 2028. She noted that the PIOJ now expects that the economy will begin to see growth by the second quarter of 2027 — “six quarters earlier, a year-and-a-half earlier”. According to her, the PIOJ “has been able to revise their forecast because the out-turn keeps getting better”.

World.title: Ocho Rios won’t sit out Heroes’ weekend
World.content:
The team behind Republic Weekend 2026 comes together at the official media launch at AC Hotel Kingston. The inaugural four-day, five-event experience takes over Plantation Cove, Ocho Rios, from October 16–19 for Heroes’ weekend.

Organisers have carefully curated an experience they believe will shift between moods, energies, and personalities as they unfold Republic Weekend.

Ocho Rios will be transformed into a four-day playground for Heroes Weekend, as Republic Enterprises Limited mounts the inaugural staging at a time when the north coast and the wider St Ann entertainment belt have increasingly become magnets for major events, giving the resort town fresh momentum as one of Jamaica’s premier entertainment destinations.

For Adam Fernandez, director of finance and commercial strategy at Republic Enterprises, the intention is not simply to pack a calendar with parties, but to create an experience capable of keeping patrons engaged.

“Republic Weekend is not five unrelated events sharing a location; it is one carefully curated experience… ” Fernandez said during the event’s recent media launch at AC Hotel Kingston.

The concept, which he said has been approximately two years in the making, weaves together music, fashion, Carnival, beach, brunch, food, nightlife, friendship, travel, and escape.

It is a formula organisers believe could turn Heroes Weekend into another major destination period for the north coast.

While Kingston prepares for the spectacle of Cardi B, whose highly anticipated Jamaica appearance is expected to pull thousands into the capital, Republic Weekend is presenting an entirely different proposition — leave the city behind and spend four days moving from one experience to another in Ocho Rios.

Representatives of Plantation Cove said the four-day concept has the potential to extend the benefits beyond the venue, generating business for hotels, villas, transportation operators, restaurants, suppliers, and other players across Ocho Rios and the wider parish.

Dr Mikhail “IQ” De Gale, managing director and director of marketing at Republic Enterprises, said: “Marketing can create anticipation. Creative can shape the story… But in this business, the experience has to deliver on the promise.”

For him, that means paying close attention to everything from production and service to entertainment, environment, and the transition between each event.

The takeover begins on Friday, October 16 with Fanatic Festival: EDEN, which will leave Kingston for the first time since its inception in 2022. After 11 stagings, the high-energy dancehall event heads to Plantation Cove, with Fanatic Festival director Justin Campbell making clear that the opening night will not be easing patrons gently into the weekend.

The intention, he said, is to “set the pace”.

By Saturday morning, Republic Weekend is slated to switch gears with Rosé N Roses, which will make its Jamaican début under the theme THINK PINK. Fashion, food, and music will anchor the daytime affair, alongside the event’s signature “Rosé All Day” experience, which includes complimentary rosé during its first two hours.

The weekend will then usher in Night Carnival: Sugar Waist on Saturday, transforming Plantation Cove into a soca and dancehall playground as patrons trade brunch attire for Monday wear, costumes and Carnival energy. The event builds on the Fete Republic concept, which has been staged since 2019, and introduces another dramatic shift in mood as the weekend progresses. By Sunday, the focus moves to the shoreline for Republic Beach Club. Then, after three days of partying, Republic Weekend is promising to finish with #SSS (Secret Soca Society) Republic Bush on Monday, October 19.

The final event will also carry a charitable component, with part proceeds going to the Jamaica Cancer Society in support of breast cancer awareness and research.

— Shereita Grizzle

World.title: FUJITSU POWERS DIGITAL PUSH
World.content:
Fujitsu Caribbean’s Holborn Road offices in St Andrew, where the company has opened its new Digitication Operations Centre, dubbed “The Engine Room”, to process paper-based records into searchable digital data.

Jamaica’s drive to modernise decades of paper-based government and business records is getting a fresh boost, with Fujitsu Caribbean opening a specialised digitisation centre in St Andrew capable of turning old documents into searchable data that can be used in digital systems and artificial intelligence (AI) applications.

The new Digitisation Operations Centre, dubbed “The Engine Room”, is already supporting major public-sector projects, including the conversion of vital records held by the Registrar General’s Department (RGD) and documents linked to the National Land Agency’s e-titling programme.

Mervyn Eyre, CEO of Fujitsu Caribbean, said the facility is designed to go beyond basic document scanning by converting information contained in paper records into structured digital data that can be searched, analysed, and integrated into applications.

“It’s not just the image of the document. It’s all of the data that can then be ingested into applications to support transformation of organisations and ultimately society,” Eyre said during an interview with the Jamaica Observer following the unveiling at the company’s Holborn Road offices on Wednesday.

Pointing to Fujitsu’s work with entities such as the Registrar General’s Department (RGD), Eyre said this provides an example of how the company has helped to digitise vital records, including birth, death, and marriage records dating back to 1935, while converting information contained in the documents into searchable data.

He said the same approach is now being applied to the National Land Agency’s e-titling programme, as Fujitsu digitises records associated with the land-titling process while supporting the development of automated workflows around them.

The St Andrew-based facility utilises high speed scanners capable of processing up to 70 pages per minute, while using technology and AI tools to extract information from typed and handwritten documents.

“These are not easy jobs,” Eyre said, noting that accuracy is critical when dealing with names, property records, and other sensitive personal information.

He said the process also includes quality assurance and contextual checks to ensure that information extracted from documents is accurate and can be trusted before being fed into digital systems.

Identifying trusted digital records as a critical foundation for digital transformation, particularly in the Caribbean where significant amounts of institutional information remain in paper and card-based systems, Fujitsu said digitisation will serve as a starting point for organisations seeking to advance automation, analytics, and AI.

The approach forms part of Fujitsu’s regional strategy, which is built around three core capabilities — platforms, applications, data and AI.

In addition to digitisation, the ICT firm’s operations also span cyber security, business applications, data and AI, among other services.

Declining to comment on the total investment pumped into the firm’s newest operation, Eyre described it only as a “significant undertaking”, with much of the expenditure directed towards specialised technology and personnel.

The centre currently employs about 45 to 50 people, although the CEO said the workforce is not fixed and will be scaled according to the volume and complexity of projects undertaken.

Deliberately targeting complex, high-volume assignments, the facility was unveiled as a shared service that will support both public and private sector customers.

Beyond Jamaica, the multinational company is building a regional pipeline, with work being undertaken or pursued in markets including Barbados, Trinidad and Tobago, and Antigua. Eyre expects demand for the service to increase as organisations seek to modernise their operations and prepare their information for AI applications.

“While the physical scanning of records can be done at Fujitsu facilities in other Caribbean markets, the Jamaican centre will provide a key part of the technology and processing capability needed to convert those records into intelligent digital documents,” he said.

Noting that the push towards digitisation is becoming more urgent with the rise of AI, Eyre said organisations cannot derive meaningful value from the technology without reliable digital information.

“If we really want to leverage AI in the region or in Jamaica, then we need to accelerate getting information, authentic information, sovereign information in the digital form,” he further stated.

Fujitsu, which currently works with technology partners such as Google, Fluent, Check Point, and Digital Office Solutions (DOS), is therefore seeking to support organisations in linking the conversion of legacy records with infrastructure modernisation, applications, data management, and AI.

Minister with responsibility for Efficiency, Innovation and Digital Transformation Audrey Marks, in welcoming the centre’s launch, said the facility represents an important development in Jamaica’s transition towards a more digitally enabled economy.

She said the investment demonstrates confidence in the country’s people and its potential to serve as a regional hub for technology services and innovation.

“For Jamaica, digital transformation is about improving lives. It is about making government services more accessible, making business more productive, creating opportunities for our young people, strengthening governance, and ensuring that every Jamaican can participate meaningfully in a digital economy,” Marks said.

She said that while the country has made progress in modernising public services and transitioning from paper-based processes to digital systems, the new centre will support the next phase of transformation.

“It signals our readiness to move beyond merely digitising documents towards creating an intelligent, secure, and insight-driven information ecosystem. It signals our readiness to embrace responsible innovation and to build stronger foundations for AI, digital government, and future economic growth. Most importantly, it signals our commitment to ensuring that technology serves people, improves lives, and creates opportunities for all Jamaicans,” Marks also said in her remarks during the launch.

World.title: ‘VERY SPECIAL’
World.content:
Maaz Sadaqat of Jamaica Kingsmen celebrates his century during the Republic Bank Caribbean Premier League Eliminator match against Barbados Tridents at Kensington Oval in Bridgetown, Barbados, on Wednesday. (Photo: CPL T20)

Captain Rovman Powell described his team’s exciting run-chase as “very special” after Jamaica Kingsmen demolished Barbados Tridents by nine wickets to stay alive in the Republic Bank Caribbean Premier League (CPL) at Kensington Oval in Bridgetown on Wednesday.

Chasing 145 for victory, the Kingsmen cantered to the target with the loss of just one wicket in just 14.1 overs on the back of a brutal century from Maaz Sadaqat, booking a spot against the loser of Qualifier 1 between Guyana Amazon Warriors and Antigua & Barbuda Falcons this evening for a place in Sunday’s final.

Guyana Amazon Warriors and Antigua & Barbuda Falcons were scheduled to clash in Qualifier 2 on Thursday.

When asked how special that run chase was, the Kingsmen skipper said the win was no accident but the execution of a clear team plan to let the top order set the table for the big hitters.

“It was very special. Something we sat down as a team and discussed. If our top two, top three batters can give us a very good start, a very good platform, then it allows myself, Andre Russell, and Hassan, those power-hitters, with a platform being laid, to come out and express ourselves a little bit more,” Powell said in a televised interview.

Earlier, the Tridents had been rescued from the brink of collapse. Sent in to bat, they slumped to 30-5 in 6.5 overs before half-centuries from Quinton de Kock, 71 off 49 balls, and captain Chris Green, 57 not out off 44 balls, added 114 for the sixth wicket to push them to 144-6.

Andre Russell took 2-36 from 3.5 overs, with Powell bowling the final ball of his spell, while Hassan Khan, Saim Ayub and Husain Shah took one apiece.

The reply was all Sadaqat. The left-hander hammered 112 off 49 balls with eight sixes and nine fours, sharing an opening stand of 138 with Kirk McKenzie, 22 not out off 34 balls.

Saim Ayub finished on two not out as Daniel Sams took the only wicket.

Despite dominating the Powerplay, Powell admitted his side was relieved to restrict the Tridents after de Kock and Green wrested back momentum.

“At the halfway stage, we were very, very pleased. If at the start of the day you had given us 144 to chase, we would have taken it. Having said that, even though they were four wickets down in the powerplay, credit has to be given to de Kock and their Captain Chris Green, and I think they batted really well,” Powell applauded.

Explaining why he has given young spin bowler Vital Lawes rather than bowling him out, Powell said it was about learning his patterns and protecting his confidence.

“I think it’s a case of we have realised some patterns with our team. It’s a case of myself also learning as a captain. I want to give him a lot of confidence, a lot of know-how to go out and bowl. But we have seen a trend where if he bowls back-to-back overs, he generally gets scored off,” Powell revealed.

“The last game he played, he bowled two, three good overs, and then in the last over they take him down just a bit. So it’s a case of me just trying to make some matchups as a captain and see how best I can come up with 20 overs instead of having somebody who hasn’t bowled or over-bowled the last over,” Powell further said.

Quizzed about Russell’s fitness after the all-rounder appeared jaded in the field, Powell moved quickly to allay any fears and praised his match-winning burst with the ball.

“He’s good. He was also fit for us to bat tonight. He’s just a little bit jaded. Obviously, Andre is closer to 40 than he is to 30, so he’s somebody that we have to keep on taking care of. But tonight he was special,” Powell said.

“We talked about getting early wickets, something he hadn’t really done for us all season. But in a play-off game, we know that our big players have to stand up. Showing the ball to him tonight and telling him to get me one or two in the powerplay — he did exactly that,” Powell stated.

Looking ahead to the do-or-die Qualifier 2, Powell insisted there will be no complacency and demanded a 10-15 per cent improvement, especially in the field.

“I think it’s a case of us replicating our performance. Tonight was good. We didn’t field as well as we wanted, so that is also something for us to work on. If we can also as a group improve 10-15 per cent, I’m very big on that, if we can keep on improving as a group, now is the time for us to rack up those very good performances,” he affirmed.

World.title: Evergo EV Link Up… 5 years strong
World.content:
Flash Motors was keen for interested EV buyers to experience the Geely brand through the EX2 and EX5 model. (Photo: Rory Daley)

Things remain strong for Evergo EV Link Up as the event celebrated its fifth anniversary on Saturday, September 5 at Police Officers’ Club in St Andrew.

“I can’t believe it is five years already, but what I’ve recognised in those five years is the transformation. We only had plug-in hybrid at that first event and grey market EVs [electric vehicles]. Today, in our convoy, we had 22 vehicles, and within those 22 we had 11 different models of EVs,” Dr Wayne McKenzie, president and CEO, Evergo, told the Jamaica Observer’s weekly Auto magazine.

That increase in options and variety was instantly reflected at the event as the automotive vendors displayed their wide model range.

On hand for attendees was the ATL Automotive Group, representing BYD, BMW, MINI, Audi, Kia, Porsche, and Jaecoo.

The Chinese brands were heavily represented, as Flash Motors was on hand with their Geely brand, as was Fidelity with GAC.

There were a few new faces, as Jetcon showed off their BAIC Arcfox EV models, and Affinity Motors had the JMEV ELIGHT on display at the Evergo booth.

“We at Jetcon have always believed that EVs were the future. With all the energy crises we have had over the decades, the combination of EV and solar is good for Jamaica. So we started with used EVs, and that didn’t do very well. Now, we’re into brand new EVs with the Arcfox, and so far the response to them has been awesome,” explained Andrew Jackson, CEO, Jetcon.

McKenzie indicated that he has been impressed not just by the range of models, but by the pricing that has seen many EVs now costing below their combustion equivalents. This, along with the increase in range, were both initial concerns from the buying public.

“We have so many dealers, not just the legacy dealers, popping up and bringing in very good EVs at affordable prices, because initially that was what everyone was talking about… But now you have cars that are competing with ICE models that are one-third or 50 per cent of the price. And then you compare the range,” he said.

Along with the ever-increasing adoption of EVs by the Jamaican automotive public, McKenzie sees Evergo’s role as more than just a charging network, but one of environmental and economic impact, serving to reduce the island’s carbon footprint and its reliance on fossil fuels.

“Evergo is contributing to the decarbonisation of Jamaica. It’s contributing to the energy transition of Jamaica, and we’re not just a partner to the Government of Jamaica, but to its people as well,” he said.

McKenzie further added that the transition from educating Jamaicans on e-mobility has moved on to one of explosive growth due to natural consumer interest.

“When you look at the crowd, how big it has become, this is going to be a legacy event,” said McKenzie.

— Rory Daley

World.title: Holness elected CPA vice-chair, first Jamaican in 33 years
World.content:
Speaker of the House of Representatives, Juliet Holness

CAPE TOWN, South Africa — Speaker of the House of Representatives Juliet Holness has been elected vice-chairperson of the Commonwealth Parliamentary Association (CPA), becoming the first Jamaican to do so in 33 years.

Holness was elected on Thursday during the 69th Commonwealth Parliamentary Conference in Cape Town, South Africa.

Her election marks Jamaica’s return to the vice-chairpersonship for the first time since former Speaker of the House of Representatives Headley Cunningham served in the office from 1992 to 1993.

Holness previously served as chair of the CPA Caribbean, Americas and the Atlantic (CAA) Region and her tenure as regional chair culminated in Jamaica’s hosting of the 48th CPA Caribbean, Americas and the Atlantic Regional Conference from August 30 to September 5, 2026.

Reflecting on her election, Holness said she was deeply honoured.

“For Jamaica to return to this office after 33 years is a proud and significant moment for our Parliament and our country. I accept this responsibility with humility and with a clear sense of purpose. Leadership in the CPA is ultimately about service — strengthening the institutions through which we represent our people,” she said.

Holness gave special recognition to the presiding officers and other delegates of the CAA Region who worked actively in support of her candidacy.

“This achievement was not the work of one person or one Parliament. It was a tremendous regional effort, and I carry that support with me into this new responsibility. I remain committed to ensuring that the experiences and perspectives of our region, particularly those of small states and smaller jurisdictions, continue to inform and enrich the work of the CPA,” she noted.

Holness will serve as CPA vice-chairperson for a one-year term.

She assumes the vice-chairpersonship as the CPA advances its Strategic Plan 2026–2029 and transitioning to a new international legal status, following legislative measures in the United Kingdom designed to recognise the CPA in a manner more consistent with its character as an international interparliamentary organisation.

The 69th Commonwealth Parliamentary Conference is being held in Cape Town, South Africa, from September 13 to 19, 2026 under the theme “Strengthening International Law and Parliamentary Democracy in a Changing World Order: Commonwealth Leadership”.

World.title: Far-right Zemmour lets slip French presidential bid
World.content:
Eric Zemmour after his closing speech during the Summer university of the Reconquête political party in Port Marly, France on September 13, 2026. | Bastien Ohier/Hans Lucas/AFP via Getty Images

PARIS — Anti-immigration firebrand Eric Zemmour let slip Thursday that he plans to run in next year’s presidential election, seemingly ending speculation that he might step aside to make way for his partner, MEP Sarah Knafo.

The leader of the far-right party Reconquest — who advocated in the past for the mass deportation of immigrants, state spending cuts and banning Muslim headscarves in public spaces — told BFMTV: “I am a candidate for the presidency of the Republic,” before adding, “you know what I mean, I will be a candidate.”

Zemmour’s popularity in France peaked in the early days of his first campaign for the presidency in 2022, as his incendiary anti-immigrant remarks and promotion of the great replacement conspiracy theory — which asserts that immigrants are being let into Western countries like France to deliberately dilute the white population— earned him worldwide notoriety.

He even seemed to pose a threat to Marine Le Pen, the longtime face of the French far right. But his campaign eventually lost momentum, only scoring 7% of the vote in the first round of voting.

Zemmour’s partner, whose political star has been rising despite an unsuccessful bid for Paris mayor in March, has fueled speculation that she may be considering a presidential run of her own. Earlier this month, Knafo published a book accusing the state of mismanaging public finances, and it quickly became a bestseller.

World.title: Slovakia’s Fico casts doubt over NATO mutual defense clause
World.content:
Under NATO’s Article 5, an armed attack against one ally is seen as an attack against all 32 members. If that ally requests or consents to a collective response, others must come to its defense, triggering a political process that can end with military action. Article 5 has only been activated once, after the Sept. 11, 2001 terror attacks in the U.S.

The comments underscore growing anxiety in Europe as tensions with Russia soar amid an escalating campaign of sabotage attempts, airspace violations and cyberattacks across the continent.

Fico, seen as one of Europe’s most Kremlin-friendly leaders, has also long argued that Western countries’ approach to Russia and continued support for Ukraine risks war with Moscow.

“Sometimes there’s a tendency to mask our inability to solve problems such as illegal migration, competitiveness, and high energy prices by resorting to this bellicose talk: ‘Come on, let’s fight.’ For heaven’s sake, who do we want to fight? Who?” Fico told students at a university hospital in a ceremony marking the start of the academic year.

“Can you imagine, ladies and gentlemen, that Article 5 of the NATO treaty would be invoked?” he said. “Can anyone imagine that they would tell us: ‘Prepare 5,000 soldiers, 10,000 soldiers,’ and they will go to war somewhere? And we will not even know with whom, why and for what.”

Fico is set to join leaders including Poland’s Donald Tusk and representatives from Austria, the Czech Republic, Romania, Serbia and Hungary in western Ukraine on Friday for a regional economic summit dubbed the Carpathian Integration Initiative.

NATO declined to comment.

World.title: EU warns Turkey to clean up waste treatment or face trade ban
World.content:
While a suspension would be in line with EU rules on the shipment of waste, it would also jeopardize the bloc’s most important market for trash. Last year, Turkey received a third of the EU’s exported plastic waste.

The Commission assessment, dated Sept. 1 and obtained by POLITICO, reported a long list of concerns over Turkey’s treatment of EU waste, including the fact that only around 10% of plastic waste is recycled in the country, while the majority goes to landfills, is mismanaged or leaks into the environment.

The Commission official said the report pointed to “several instances” of plastic waste mismanagement, generating “serious pollution problems.”

Despite evidence of practices that could breach EU rules, the report said the Commission would hold off on suspending exports and instead engage with the Turkish authorities on these concerns.

The bloc’s Waste Shipment Regulation — which restricts exports of certain types of EU waste to third countries to curb pollution — says the EU can stop the export of waste to OECD countries that fail to show the waste is managed in an “environmentally sound manner.”

The law specifically requires the Commission to assess whether OECD countries importing large volumes of plastic waste are managing it without causing significant environmental or health damage.

World.content:
Ein teures Symbol der Abhängigkeit: In Texas nimmt Verteidigungsminister Boris Pistorius den ersten F-35-Kampfjet für die Bundeswehr entgegen. World.title: Week Ender: Can Europe patch up the world in disorder?
World.content:
The old global order is breaking down. Ursula von der Leyen thinks Europe may have to start building something new around it.

In her State of the European Union speech, she floated closer ties with Canada — even “associate membership” — and a new European Security Council, as Europe looks for new ways to work with like-minded powers in an increasingly chaotic world. But both ideas immediately raised questions about whether von der Leyen was getting ahead of her own allies.

Host Sarah Wheaton is joined by POLITICO Executive Editor Carrie Budoff Brown, senior EU climate reporter Zia Weise and AI and technology reporter Pieter Haeck to unpack what von der Leyen’s speech tells us about Europe’s search for a role in this new global “unorder.”

They also look at her climate message — heavy on adaptation to heat, drought and fires, but lighter on new answers to Europe’s energy problems — and at her attempt to square AI regulation with the need to keep Europe in the global tech race.

World.title: Germany and Spain go head-to-head in EU budget fight
World.content:
They are pressuring Ireland, in its position at the helm of the six-month rotating presidency of the Council of the EU, which is steering the talks, to cut hundreds of billions of euros in their next negotiating document due in October.

Officials involved in the negotiations who spoke to POLITICO and were granted anonymity because the discussions are confidential see more moderate cuts as the most likely outcome.

Debt time bomb

The EU’s seven-year budget, the multiannual financial framework, which governs EU spending from farmers’ subsidies to student exchange programs, is the subject of some of the fiercest negotiations in Brussels and pits different groups of countries against one another.

To try to bring their positions closer together, European Council President António Costa toured 25 EU countries in the past month to sound out leaders on the most sensitive questions facing the negotiations. He continued the trip in Dublin on Thursday.



In his bid to free up more budget funding, Cuerpo said he wants to delay repayment of joint debt issued in 2021 to tackle the economic fallout from the Covid-19 pandemic.

Around €300 billion must be repaid from 2028 to 2058. While interest repayments are set in stone, governments have more leeway to set the timeline for repaying the principal.

The current plan compels EU governments to front-load repayments and cough up €25 billion a year over the next budget cycle. Critics say this limits the funds available for other areas of spending and further constrains negotiations.

World.title: Germany’s Merz girds for a post-election fight for political survival
World.content:
It’s for this reason that Merz has arranged a meeting with CDU leaders to take place Sunday, just before polls close, at which he’s expected to gauge their support and attempt to convince them that he has a plan to turn things around. Merz has also canceled a planned speech at the United Nations General Assembly scheduled for Wednesday to remain in Berlin and address the domestic fallout from the CDU’s performance.

In an effort to rally support, Merz is emphasizing the importance of avoiding turbulence in Berlin during volatile times for Europe.

“All eyes are on Germany, on Berlin, on our role in the world,” Merz said at a CDU campaign event in Berlin on Thursday evening. “Expectations are placed on us to contribute to keeping this European continent stable.”

‘Hell breaks loose’

Despite his efforts to remain at the helm, Merz’s fate could be sealed by as little as a few percentage point shifts on Sunday in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania. Polls show Merz’s conservatives collapsing to just 7% in the state, as its center-left premier takes on the leading AfD in an increasingly two-way contest between the strongest centrist force and the far right.

Hendrik Wüst, Minister President of North Rhine-Westphalia and seen as Merz’s most likely replacement, speaking during the 2026 Digital X at Rheinauhafen in Cologne on Sept. 8, 2026. | Thomas Lohnes/Getty Images

Should the CDU fall further, it would put the party at risk of failing to meet the 5% vote threshold required to enter the state parliament — a result that one conservative official, speaking on condition of anonymity to frankly discuss the mood inside the party, said would mean “all hell breaks loose.”

In Berlin, where the other regional election will be held this Sunday, the chancellor’s party is polling better — but things could still go poorly. The CDU is narrowly trailing the far-left Die Linke, or Left Party, at around 20% support, according to polls. That is still 8 percentage points below the CDU’s result in the last Berlin election — a decline that could see the conservatives ousted from the city government they currently lead and replaced by a coalition of left-wing parties.

World.title: Five EU leaders: Europe must spend better, not just more
World.content:
Budgets are where political priorities become real. Speeches, declarations and summit conclusions matter, but ultimately it is the allocation of money that reveals what governments are genuinely prepared to prioritize. Europe needs to become more competitive, more sovereign and better able to defend itself. There is no other choice.

Our budget must reflect that new reality.

The status quo of the current MFF cannot be the starting point. It is too focused on subsidies and transfers allocated largely in advance, leaving too little room for what Europe urgently needs: common investment in security and defense, competitiveness, innovation, and the fight against irregular migration. The next MFF will be the test of whether Europe has understood the message of Mario Draghi’s landmark report on European competitiveness. It will show whether our promises of more common European investment are real — or just rhetoric.

Mario Draghi addresses the audience during the conference ‘One Year After the Draghi Report’ at the EU Charlemagne building on September 16, 2025 in Brussels. | Omar Havana/Getty Images

That requires choices. And choices require political courage. This does not mean abandoning traditional policies, but we cannot just add every new priority to every old one and send the bill to taxpayers.

Almost every EU member country is making painful efforts to consolidate its public finances. Those that are not should concern us even more. There will be no European sovereignty without sound public finances.

We are doing our part: The group of net contributors that recently met in Berlin stands for almost 40% of the financing of the EU budget and provides around 70% of EU member countries’ bilateral support for Ukraine. We are investing heavily in our common security and defense. We are not tight-fisted. Nor are we hiding behind the label “frugal.” In fact, when it comes to supporting Ukraine, greater engagement by other member states is both reasonable and urgently needed.

World.title: "Iris" and "Weeping Willow": unseen Monet paintings go on sale in Paris
World.content:
Between 22 and 30 million euros, the highest estimate ever placed on a painting sold in France. That is what a buyer could spend to obtain "Iris" by Claude Monet.

 

On 22 October, the auction house Sotheby's will be offering it for sale, alongside other works from the Schlumberger family's private collection.

A monumental painting created by Monet at the end of his life, the canvas is, according to curators, in remarkable condition. "It has no varnish, it is on its original canvas and has never been restored. They are exactly as Monet painted them 100 years ago," explains Thomas Bompard, co-director of the Modern and Contemporary Department at Sotheby's France.

Canvases preserved in the Schlumberger living room

Every detail counts. Varnish alters the chromatic tones of a painting, according to art historian Marianne Mathieu. But restoration could damage the texture of the paint on the canvas. "Late Monet is a Monet who works the material. So to truly discover and understand him, that material has to be preserved. And we still have these thick impastos."

Hung in a Schlumberger family sitting room for a century, "Iris", like "Weeping Willow", also up for sale and valued at between nine and ten million euros, has never been moved.

Above all, it has never been seen in colour by the general public. It was acquired by Jeanne Schlumberger (1889-1983), "a brilliant art collector", from the painter's family through "the visionary gallerist" Katia Granoff, according to Thomas Bompard, without going through an auction room.

"Many people knew the story, or at least knew of the existence of this collection; people whispered that these were the finest Monets in Paris, but very few had actually seen them. That is also what is fuelling today's excitement," he notes.

A collection valued at 40 million euros

Another factor that has pushed prices higher is the centenary of the death of the Impressionist artist, who died on 5 December 1926. Two exhibitions on the painter's life open in Paris at the end of September: "Monet, Painting Time" and "Stories of Landscapes, from Monet to Hockney".

In all, 28 works are being offered for sale at Sotheby's, in a sale expected to raise more than 40 million euros. Among them are four Monets, as well as a sculpture by Camille Claudel and several paintings by Gustave Moreau.

Also being sold on this occasion is a wall composition of three works by Paul Cézanne. "La Ferme", the central painting, is "the largest work by the artist ever to be offered at auction" and is estimated at between 600,000 and 800,000 euros.

The three paintings have been designated as "national treasures", a measure intended to give the state 30 months in which to arrange a possible acquisition.

World.title: Russia seizes control over assets of Nestle, French firms
World.content:
A little-known Russian company called L.E.V. Management has been handed temporary control of 16 businesses linked to Nestlé, Auchan and several other Western groups.

 

President Vladimir Putin signed a decree on Thursday placing the management of stakes and shares in the 16 Russian companies under the control of the firm.

The move tightens Moscow’s control over Western-owned assets amid its confrontation with Western countries over sanctions imposed following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.

"Of course, one of the factors taken into account when making this decision was that these are unfriendly countries, which are currently most actively involved in military operations against our country," Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said at a press conference on Friday.

The businesses concerned include Nestlé Russia, Nestlé Kuban, French retailer Auchan’s Russian subsidiary, two local FM Logistic entities and Le Monlid, which operates the former Leroy Merlin DIY chain under the Lemana Pro brand.

The measure does not formally confiscate the businesses or change their ownership, according to Russian lawyers cited by business newspaper Kommersant. However, temporary administration has previously preceded the sale or transfer of Western-owned assets to Russian buyers.

L.E.V. Management was registered in Moscow in October 2024, and its shareholders are not publicly disclosed. According to Kommersant, the company showed no active business operations in its publicly available 2025 accounts.

Andrei Krayushkin was appointed its general director on 10 September, one week before the decree was issued. Independent outlet Novaya Gazeta Europe reported that his name and date of birth match those of a Russian interior ministry major general. This has not been independently confirmed.

Most Western companies quickly sold or ring-fenced their Russian businesses after Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Russia has since made it increasingly difficult for foreign companies to leave, requiring presidential approval for deals and placing some assets under temporary administration.

In a statement, Nestlé said it was “assessing the situation and its options”.

“Nestlé is committed to taking all necessary steps to protect its rights and ensure continuity of business operations in the interests of all stakeholders, particularly its employees,” it said.

Nestlé has around 7,000 employees and six factories in Russia. It has suspended most non-essential sales, imports and exports, as well as advertising and capital investment, while continuing to supply products it considers essential.

Jean-Philippe Bertschy of Swiss investment bank Vontobel said the financial impact was expected to be limited because Russia now accounts for around 1% of Nestlé’s group sales, down from approximately 2% before the war.

Auchan Retail Russia told Russian business news outlet RBC that it had asked the authorities to clarify the decree and would comment further after receiving more information. It said its stores and other facilities continued to operate normally.

Auchan employs around 30,000 people and operates approximately 230 stores and an online business in Russia.

Lemana Pro told Kommersant that it had not yet received official information from the authorities and continued to operate normally.

Leroy Merlin’s French parent company, Adeo, transferred control of its Russian business to local management in 2023. The operation was subsequently rebranded as Lemana Pro and now has 112 stores.

FM Logistic had not publicly commented at the time of publication.

The move echoes Moscow’s 2023 takeover of Danone’s Russian business. It was initially placed under the management of Yakub Zakriev, a nephew of Chechen leader Ramzan Kadyrov, before Danone sold the operation at a substantial discount in 2024.

World.title: Barcelona has a bold plan to protect its vulnerable coastline – and it could be prize-winning
World.content:
This summer, Barcelona recorded its highest temperature in more than a century.

 

It’s part of a worrying trend: the Mediterranean is warming around 20 per cent faster than the global average, while record-warm waters are fuelling stronger storms, sea level rise and coastal erosion.

The collapse of a stretch of a storm-hit promenade on Barcelona’s northeast coast in 2023 underlined the need for climate resilient infrastructure. Around 70 per cent of the artificial sand added in 2010 has since disappeared.

“Cities like ours must learn to live with climate change while protecting the places and communities that define them,” says Jaume Collboni, Mayor of Barcelona.

The Spanish city’s ambitious coastal resilience project is now in the running for a prestigious environmental award.

Barcelona is a finalist for The Earthshot Prize

Barcelona has been announced as a finalist for The Earthshot Prize in the Revive Our Oceans category. First launched in 2020 by Prince William, the awards recognise environmental solutions to “repair” the planet.

The Spanish city is pouring €150 million into restoring one of Europe’s most intensively used urban coastlines. The project will create 22 hectares – roughly the size of 31 football pitches – of climate- and heat-adapted public space along the Sant Martí seafront, integrating restored marine habitats, natural coastal protection and waterfront access.

It is hoped that it will become a blueprint for coastal cities around the world facing increasingly severe sea-level rise, stronger storms, flooding, biodiversity loss and extreme heat – something The Earthshot Prize will help with by boosting visibility and knowledge-sharing opportunities.

“Every year, our Finalists give me renewed optimism,” says Prince William, President and Founder of The Earthshot Prize. “They show us that, even as the environmental challenges remain urgent, extraordinary people around the world are already proving that progress is possible.”

‘Climate-resilient infrastructure designed for everyone to enjoy’

Instead of repeatedly rebuilding its vulnerable northeast shoreline, Barcelona is intentionally moving parts of the waterfront inland, including relocating a popular seafront football pitch, and moving the sea walls back.

This will allow for wider beaches that act as natural buffers, absorbing wave energy and creating more space for storms, erosion and rising sea levels, as well as providing a vital refuge during increasingly severe heatwaves.

Scheduled for completion in spring 2027, Passeig Marítim de la Mar Bella will encourage sustainable use of the coastline while boosting air quality and biodiversity with a 15,000-square-metre linear park.

Visitors will be able to stroll along a 12-metre-wide pedestrian path or cycle down bike lanes – stretching all the way to the Fòrum – resting at energy-producing solar pergolas along the way.

“The choice facing coastal cities is no longer whether to adapt, but how,” says María Buhigas, Chief City Architect of Barcelona. “This is not a defensive structure added to the edge of the city; it is a new piece of climate-resilient public infrastructure designed for everyone to enjoy.”

Who else is in the running for The Earthshot Prize 2026?

From nearly 7,000 nominations across 169 countries, 15 finalists have been selected for The Earthshot Prize.

Each is aligned with one of the five ‘Earthshots’: Protect and Restore Nature, Clean Our Air, Revive Our Oceans, Build a Waste-Free World and Fix Our Climate – with winners in each category poised to receive a £1 million (€1.17m) prize.

For the first time, positive tipping points were part of the selection process, rewarding innovations where progress builds on itself, costs fall with scale and recovery becomes self-propelling.

Other European finalists include Ørsted (Fix Our Climate) – the Danish renewable energy company behind some of the world’s largest offshore wind projects – and PFAS-Free France (Build a Waste-Free World), the policy and civil-society campaign that helped securing, and is now implementing, France’s ‘forever chemical’ phaseout in everyday products.

Further afield, Argentina’s Satellites on Fire is being recognised for its AI-powered wildfire detection and alert platform, alongside zero-emission shipping alliance ZEMBA, and India’s electric three-wheeler pioneer Mahindra Last Mile Mobility.

Reconnecting a vast mountain landscape across Canada and the US so wildlife can move freely once again, conservation collaboration Yellowstone to Yukon is among the contenders for the Protect and Restore Nature prize.

“Seeing solutions work gives us all confidence to act. When they succeed, they inspire others and accelerate change,” says Prince William.

The five winners of The Earthshot Prize 2026 will be announced at an awards night in Mumbai, India, on 17 November.

World.title: Turkish actor and World Cup star among 16 held in Istanbul drug raids
World.content:
A Turkish actor and a footballer who helped the national football team finish third at the 2002 World Cup were among 16 people detained in anti-drug raids across Istanbul on Friday as part of a probe into celebrities, venue operators and social media influencers.

 

Hasan Şaş, who earned 40 caps for the Turkish national team and played for Galatasaray during its most successful European period, and actor Aras Bulut İynemli, known abroad for Netflix Turkey productions, were detained alongside actor Melis Sezen, rapper Sefo and 12 others.

Authorities had not located two further suspects by the time of publication.

Bakırköy Chief Public Prosecutor's Office said the investigation concerns allegations of using narcotic and psychotropic substances, facilitating their use and mediating their supply.

Authorities ordered biological examinations alongside the searches and detentions.

Others detained include actors Nilperi Şahinkaya, Melisa Şenolsun and Afra Saraçoğlu, YouTuber Melis İşiten, sports journalist Yağız Sabuncuoğlu, model Yeliz Yeşilçimen, content creator Aydan Osmanlı, singer Anıl Durmuş and businesswoman Hande Demir.

Friday's operation is the latest in a series of similar anti-narcotics raids targeting well-known figures in Istanbul since late 2025.

In December 2025, singer Aleyna Tilki, actor İrem Sak and influencer Danla Bilic were among those taken into custody and later released after biological samples were collected.

In May of this year, authorities detained 20 people from a list of 25 suspects that included actors Serenay Sarıkaya and Onur Tuna, singer Mabel Matiz, and television presenter Mirgün Cabas.

In July, searches and biological sampling were carried out on a further 25 suspects including singers Sıla Gençoğlu and İlyas Yalçıntaş and producer Fatih Aksoy. Yalçıntaş was subsequently arrested.

World.title: Portugal prepares for rising temperatures and likely heatwave
World.content:
Portugal is set to experience a gradual rise in temperatures from this Saturday, with weather conditions hotter than usual for this time of year. The warning comes from the Portuguese Institute for Sea and Atmosphere (IPMA) (source in Portuguese), which is even pointing to the likelihood of a heatwave.

 

"This spell of hot weather will be defined mainly by how long it lasts, with a high probability that it will develop into a heatwave across much of the country," the IPMA said in a statement.

The document explains that a heatwave occurs when, "over a period of six consecutive days, the maximum air temperature is 5 °C above the average value of the daily maximum temperatures".

Temperatures are therefore expected to reach above 30 °C in mainland Portugal. In some areas, such as Lisbon and the Tagus valley, they could even approach 38 °C.

Minimum temperatures will also rise, staying above 20 °C in some parts of Alto Alentejo, Beira Baixa, the Tagus valley and the eastern Algarve.

"Although the forecast maximum temperatures are lower than those recorded during some episodes this summer, they will be substantially higher than the average for the second half of September," the statement adds.

The hot weather is due to the "influence of an anticyclone located to the north of the Azores, extending in a ridge as far as the Bay of Biscay". This system will transport "a mass of continental air (hot and dry) over the Iberian Peninsula".

In July, Portugal had already recorded anomalous temperatures, with red warnings in most of the country and the government declaring a state of alert. The same situation extended to the rest of mainland Europe during the month of July.

A report by the non-profit organisation Climate Central concluded that the continent had been "the most abnormally warm region on the planet". Almost nine in ten Europeans lived through an entire month of "dangerous heat".

Before Gaza became synonymous with conflict, it was a place where merchants sold wine from local vineyards, pilgrims crossed continents, fishermen set out before dawn, and generations of families lived between sea and desert. RFI explores its deep history.

Advertising

Sitting on the coastal corridor linking Egypt, the Levant, the Arabian Peninsula and the Mediterranean, the port city has always been a strategic crossroads.

Like many places around the Mediterranean, Gaza's identity wasn't built by a single people or culture. It was shaped by generations of arrivals, departures and exchanges.

As the Mid-East Junction podcast returns from a six-year hiatus, we'll trace the city's history from the age of the Philistines until the creation of Israel in 1948.

In this first episode of season 3, a Gazan archaeologist, a historian, and a professor of contemporary Arab people shed light on Gaza’s little-known yet fascinating ancient history.

World.title: Bolivia: New cat species discovered by scientists
World.content:
Genetic data confirmed that the small feline, called "tilcayo" by locals, is a new species of cat. It's the first such discovery in more than 100 years.

Scientists in Bolivia have identified a small wild cat with a leopard-like coat as a previously unknown species.

Local communities call the feline "tilcayo," a nickname that inspired the cat's new scientific designation: Leopardus tilcayo.

Biologist and National Geographic explorer Paola Nogales-Ascarrunz described the discovery as a "remarkable event, because a new wild cat species hasn't been described in 100 years."

The last feline species to be discovered was the Uruguayan pampas cat in 1923.

The animal is around 18 inches (46 centimeters) long and weighs some 3 pounds (1.4 kilograms) Image: Fernando Faciole/National Geographic/Handout/REUTERS

What do we know about Leopardus tilcayo?

The cat was found in Bolivia's Yungas forest, a remote region on the eastern slope of the Andes mountains.

The animal measures around 18 inches (46 centimeters) long and weighs around 3 pounds (1.4 kilograms), making it smaller than the average domestic cat.

"Its fur is light brown ... with irregularly shaped rosettes across its body," Nogales-Ascarrunz said.

According to National Geographic, Nogales-Ascarrunz first came upon the animal in 2016 after receiving a call from a local wildlife sanctuary.

The organization said at the time that it had been handed "a weird cat."

"I took a hundred pictures of it," Nogales-Ascarrunz told National Geographic. "I was so fascinated."

It was a few years later that she realized the cat she had photographed was unlike any previously seen.

National Geographic Explorer Paola Nogales-Ascarrunz led the research that identified Leopardus tilcayo Image: Fernando Faciole/National Geographic/Handout/REUTERS

Species finds its place in cat family tree

Research on the new species was published this week in the journal Current Biology.

Using genetic analysis in collaboration with geneticist Eduardo Eizirik, co-lead authors Nogales-Ascarrunz and the University of Antwerp's Jonas Lescroart were able to place the feline in its specific category in the cat family tree.

Nogales-Ascarrunz said that a pair of tilcayos have undergone whole-genome sequencing and are the only such creatures found so far.

"So far, it's only been detected in Bolivia" and not "anywhere else on the planet," Nogales-Ascarrunz said.

"Showing the general public that even in a flagship group such as cats ... there are still new species to be discovered may transmit an important message," said Eizirik, who is an evolutionary biologist at the Pontifical Catholic University of Rio Grande do Sul in Brazil.

"There are many undiscovered species out there in the world, and they are at risk of disappearing before we even discover them."
