World.title: FACT CHECK: Poa remains VP Sara’s counsel, defense spokesperson in impeachment trial
World.content:
Lawyer Michael Poa serves as Duterte's legal counsel and defense team spokesperson in her impeachment trial. He stepped down as the Office of the Vice President’s spokesperson in 2024.

Claim: Lawyer Michael Wesley Poa has vacated his post as Vice President Sara Duterte’s spokesperson.

Rating: MISSING CONTEXT

Why we fact-checked this: The claim was posted on September 9 by the Facebook page “Balita at Kaalaman,” which has more than 219,000 followers. The post has reached over 1,800 reactions as of writing.

The post, labeled as “breaking news,” reads, “Atty Michael Poa binitawan na ni #SaraDuterte after kawawain sa harap ng publiko. Grabe ginagawa sayo niyang praning na amo mo atty.”

(Sara Duterte dropped Atty. Michael Poa after being humiliated in public. That paranoid boss of yours is really putting you through a lot, attorney.)

Two other posts, uploaded on September 2 and 7 respectively, mention that Poa has resigned as Duterte’s spokesperson.

A YouTuber by the channel name “Mike Cervera Vlog” also posted a live stream commentary on August 29 with the title “Atty. Michael Poa nag resign na?!” As of writing, it has reached over 180,000 views and 400 comments.

The posts circulated following reports on September 9 that Duterte appointed lawyer Paolo Panelo as the new spokesperson for the Office of the Vice President (OVP).

The facts: Poa already stepped down as Duterte’s spokesperson on November 5, 2024. However, he remains Duterte’s legal counsel and her defense team’s spokesperson in her impeachment trial. He himself confirmed this in a message to the media on the day Panelo’s appointment was announced.

In a September 10 interview on Bilyonaryo News Channel, Poa clarified his role as he addressed social media speculation that he had been replaced or removed from Duterte’s team.

In November 2024, Poa said the OVP pre-terminated his consultancy contract as spokesperson, describing the move as a “mutual decision.” He added that he could not fulfill his contract as spokesperson because he deemed it difficult to face the media without losing objectivity. At the time, Poa was a resource person in a House panel probe into the OVP’s alleged misuse of funds.

In appointing Panelo as its new spokesperson, the OVP said he will “serve as the official point of communication, representing the views and positions of the Vice President and engaging with the media and public on relevant matters.”

Prosecution’s hostile witness: On September 1, Poa temporarily stepped aside as counsel and spokesperson for the Vice President’s defense team to take the witness stand in the impeachment trial.

He became one of the prosecution’s hostile witnesses, called to testify on Article I of the impeachment articles concerning Duterte’s alleged misuse of confidential funds.

During the trial, Poa faced questions around the use of P112.5 million in confidential funds of the Department of Education (DepEd). In his testimony, Poa said that during his time as DepEd undersecretary and chief of staff, he prepared the agency’s response to the 2024 Commission on Audit findings on DepEd’s use of confidential funds.

However, he said that he was unaware that Duterte’s security officer Colonel Dennis Nolasco handled the funds.

He clarified that his involvement in the confidential funds issue only began when he received the audit memorandum, and that he relied on other officials’ reports to respond to COA’s inquiries on the use of the funds. – Lourence Angelo Marcellana/Rappler.com

World.title: Villar family faces graft complaints over PrimeWater contracts
World.content:
(1st UPDATE) In a statement, Manny Villar says they respect the legal process and will respond to the complaints at the proper time and forum

MANILA, Philippines – The Office of the Ombudsman confirmed on Friday, September 18, that graft complaints are now pending against members of the Villar family due to allegations related to PrimeWater Infrastructure Corporation.

Assistant Ombudsman Mico Clavano confirmed that the Ombudsman filed criminal and administrative complaints against Senators Mark and Camille, former senators Manny and Cynthia Villar, and businessman Paolo Villar for preliminary investigation.

Also included in the complaints are officers of PWIC, as well as local water district officials.

Preliminary investigation is the step of criminal proceedings where prosecutors decide if there’s enough evidence against the respondents. If there is, the prosecutors will indict the respondents and file cases with courts.

“[This is] for violation, of section 3(e) and 3(g) of [Republic Act No.] 3019, otherwise known as the Anti-Graft and Corrupt Practices Act. This is the initial list, and there are still more water districts under investigation, and expectantly more cases in the pipelines,” Clavano said.

In a statement, Manny Villar said they respect the legal process and will respond to the complaints at the proper time and forum.

“We are confident that, once given the opportunity to examine the allegations and the evidence supporting them, we will be able to fully and properly defend our rights and address the matters raised against us,” Villar said.

“In the meantime, we ask that the legal process be allowed to take its course and that conclusions not be drawn before the parties have been afforded the opportunity to be heard,” he added.

Also included in the complaints are the following PrimeWater and local water district officials:

Fe Rebancos, PrimeWater president

Romeo Sabater, PrimeWater vice president

Enrico Pasumbal, Quezon Metropolitan Water district general manager

Guillermo Pili Jr., San Pedro Water District general manager

Juliet Ocampo, Trece Martires Water District general manager

According to the Ombudsman, the investigations stemmed from a report from the Office of the Government Corporate Counsel that showed that a total of 75 local water districts (LWDs) entered into joint venture agreements (JVA) with PrimeWater.

However, a report revealed that PrimeWater failed to supply uninterrupted water service and instead provided water that “allegedly failed to meet drinking water standards, among other complaints against the company.”

Other concerns also include questions on JVAs itself and PrimeWater’s deficient service, and how these happened under Mark Villar’s term as Department of Public Works and Highways secretary and Local Water Utilities Administration board of trustees Member.

The Ombudsman also noted that the Commission on Audit had flagged PrimeWater’s “non-payment for the utilization or consumption of materials and supplies inventory of the local water districts.”

“Considering the three (Quezon Metro, Trece Martires, and San Pedro, Laguna) areas, the total unpaid obligations of PWIC have reached P65,650,708.07,” said the Ombudsman.

The Villars are also facing a separate complaint with the Department of Justice for alleged violations of the Securities Regulation Code. The complaint, filed on January 30, is currently at the preliminary investigation level. – Rappler.com

World.title: At least 3 dead, 6 wounded in South Cotabato school shooting
World.content:
(1st UPDATE) Students are sent home, and South Cotabato Governor Reynaldo Tamayo Jr. calls for calm following the school shooting in his province

Trigger warning: This article contains references to violence and weapons.

MANILA, Philippines – At least three children were killed and six others wounded after a minor opened fire at Banga National High School in Banga town, South Cotabato, on Friday, September 18, Governor Reynaldo Tamayo Jr. said.

Tamayo, quoting the provincial disaster risk reduction and management council, said the dead included two girls and the alleged shooter as of 4:10 pm.

“Ang suspek ay nagbaril din ng kanyang sarili after niya binaril ‘yong apat,” Tamayo said in an earlier video statement.

“Ngayon ay nando’n lahat sa ospital pero medyo delikado ang kalagayan ng iilan sa kanila,” he said.

(The suspect also shot himself after he opened fire. Now, all of them are in the hospital, but some of them are in critical condition.)

The police investigation is still ongoing.

Tamayo said the incident was an “isolated case,” and authorities have sent the students home to “control their emotions.”

“Sa ngayon, manatili lang tayong kalmado. Alam kong mabigat ito sa munisipyo ng Banga at sa mga magulang na nandito, pero wala tayong choice kung hindi pakalmahin muna natin ang ating mga sarili,” he said.

(For now, we must remain calm. I know this is a serious issue for the municipality of Banga and the parents here, but we have no choice but to calm ourselves for now.)

In a statement, the Department of Education (DepEd) said it was deeply concerned by the reported shooting incident, adding that its immediate priority was the safety and well-being of students, teachers, and school personnel.

It said it is ready to provide psychological first aid and mental health and psychosocial support.

“We urge everyone to remain calm and refrain from sharing unverified information as authorities continue their investigation,” the DepEd said.

In June, three students were killed after their two schoolmates opened fire at the San Jose National High School in Tacloban City.

In August, two students died in the shooting incident at Ateneo de Zamboanga’s junior high school campus in Zamboanga City, including the alleged shooter himself.

This is a developing story, and will be updated. – Rappler.com

World.title: [OPINION] BARMM post-elections: Building a coalition that needs to govern
World.content:
A healthy parliamentary democracy requires a credible opposition. The BFP should resist the temptation to create an oversized coalition simply to eliminate opposition.

After generally peaceful and democratic parliamentary elections, the region now faces a different — and perhaps more difficult — political challenge: how to govern after the votes have been counted.

Based on unofficial results, four political parties out of 13 appear poised to cross the 2.5% threshold for regional political party representation. The Bangsamoro Federalist Party (BFP) leads with 16 party seats, followed by the Moro Islamic Liberation Front-led United Bangsamoro Justice Party (UBJP) with 15, the clan alliance under the Bangsamoro Grand Coalition (BGC) with 8, and the Bangsamoro People’s Democratic (Raayat) Party with 1.

For the 32 district representatives, incumbent chief minister Abdulraof Macacua of BFP won in Maguindanao del Norte while MILF chairman Ebrahim Murad’s son, Mansor, won the seat in the Special Geographic Area. BFP won a total of 13 district seats, UBJP had 10, and the Adiong-led local party SIAP of Lanao del sur got six. Three other local parties got one seat each.

The six elected sectoral seats all went to the UBJP, thus affirming the sectoral and territorial dominance of the MILF’s UBJP. Two representatives from the indigenous peoples in BARMM were elected by them prior to September 14.

Overall, the 80-member parliament is now comprised of the following: a total of 30 seats for the BFP, 29 seats for UBJP, and 19 seats for the clan-led political parties. This parliament will govern for the next five years.

Many analysts would always equate the BARMM to the national government’s interests which is a given. The Bangsamoro Organic Law ties those interests due to national security risk management, natural resource management, devolution imperatives, and political economy. But that is another matter to discuss.

The numbers in votes tell only part of the story. No party has a majority. And that means the first elected Bangsamoro government will have to be built through coalition, negotiation, compromise, and trust. It also should not lead to a super majority coalition where there is no credible opposition.

What is needed is for a coalition to govern and not just forming a government. The former is difficult, the latter is easy.

Building a unity government

With no party dominating the elections, the arithmetic is straightforward. The transition party incumbent BFP’s 30 party seats are not enough to govern alone. An alliance with the UBJP’s 29 seats would produce a dominant majority. But that would leave out the clan-led political parties which is critical for governance.

This is where the real politics begins.

The Bangsamoro parliamentary system was designed to encourage representation and negotiation. Unlike a presidential system where the executive derives a separate electoral mandate, a parliamentary government depends on the ability of political forces inside Parliament to construct a stable governing majority.

A government that survives by one or two votes on every major issue will be unstable. The new governing coalition should be dominant enough to survive disagreements, defections, political shocks, and difficult budget negotiations. The objective should be a stable parliamentary majority, not merely the minimum number needed to elect a chief minister.

Coalition governments inevitably require some distribution of executive responsibility.

But there is a danger. If Cabinet positions become rewards for delivering votes, the new government could reproduce the worst features of traditional Philippine politics.

The BFP-led coalition should instead adopt three principles: representation, competence, and accountability. Coalition partners should have meaningful representation in government. But ministers must also be competent to manage public institutions.

With the elections of the chief minister happening on the first day of convening parliament, a coalition government needs to be formed prior to that. In reality, the incumbent government under the BFP can initiate the formation. The goal should not merely be to find 41 votes to elect a chief minister. The goal should be to build a majority that can govern for five years.

But the first substantive agenda in coalition negotiations would be a governance agenda for a coalition government. The BFP could propose a Bangsamoro Governance Compact 2026–2031, signed by coalition partners before the election of the Chief Minister. The compact could establish a common agenda around on peace, development and governance.

This would shift coalition formation from “What position do I get?” to “What government are we going to build?” That distinction is crucial.

The UBJP question

There is another delicate issue. The electoral transition should not be interpreted as the end of the MILF’s political relevance. The Bangsamoro Parliament itself is a product of the peace process.

The presence of former MILF leaders and representatives associated with the movement inside the elected political system is therefore not an anomaly. It is part of the transition from armed struggle to democratic politics.

The challenge is to institutionalize that transition.

The most consequential negotiation may be between the BFP and UBJP. With 30 party seats between them, the two parties could form the nucleus of the next government. But the relationship would carry a significance beyond parliamentary arithmetic. The UBJP represents a political tradition deeply connected to the Bangsamoro peace process and the transition that produced the BARMM.

A BFP-UBJP coalition could therefore symbolize an important political transition: from the politics of the peace process to the politics of democratic parliamentary government, without abandoning the gains of the peace process itself.

The two should not be framed as competing sources of legitimacy. The Bangsamoro needs both.

The future government can draw legitimacy from the peace process, the ballot box, and the communities represented by elected district and sectoral leaders. The challenge is to bring these sources of legitimacy together. That would be a genuine measure of the success of the peace process.

Don’t dismiss the clans

The new parliament is likely to include representatives associated with powerful political families and local networks, including the Adiongs, Ampatuans, Gandamras, Hatamans, Mangundadatus, Midtimbangs, Sinsuat, etc.

These representatives should not automatically be dismissed as “clan politicians.”

They represent real constituencies. Their voters have concerns about roads, schools, hospitals, agriculture, fisheries, livelihood, security, local government, and access to public services.

The question is not whether these representatives have local political interests. Of course they do. The question is how those interests are incorporated into a transparent regional development agenda. The new government should establish transparent criteria for allocating public resources, while giving district representatives a legitimate role in setting regional priorities.

Representation must also mean geographic balance. The Bangsamoro is geographically and politically diverse. The composition of the executive should reflect this diversity. This is especially important for communities that historically have felt distant from the regional government like the Special Geographic Area carved out from the North Cotabato Province. A coalition government that promises inclusion but remains concentrated around the region’s established political centers will quickly lose credibility.

Credible opposition matters

There is another important principle. Not everyone should be brought into the government.

A healthy parliamentary democracy requires a credible opposition. The BFP should resist the temptation to create an oversized coalition simply to eliminate opposition. This is what happened at the national level that should not be replicated.

An opposition can strengthen government. It can expose weaknesses, question expenditures, scrutinize appointments, challenge policies, and force ministers to explain their decisions. A Parliament in which everyone is part of the government risks becoming a Parliament where nobody is accountable.

The ideal arrangement is therefore: a broad governing coalition, a legitimate opposition, strong parliamentary committees, and active civil society. That is how parliamentary democracy becomes more than an institutional design. It becomes a political culture.

The 2026 parliamentary election should ultimately be judged not only by whether it was peaceful. It should also be judged by what happens after the election. The most important question of all: can the government be seen, felt, and deliver tangible improvements in the lives of ordinary Bangsamoro?. – Rappler.com

Tom Villarin is a political science professor at the Ateneo de Manila University. He served in the 17th Congress as Akbayan Party List representative. He also was former local government undersecretary under the Noynoy Aquino administration.

World.title: ‘Intentional ramming’: China Coast Guard damages Philippine ship in West PH Sea
World.content:
The BRP Datu Magat Salamat is en route back to Coron to assess its seaworthiness

MANILA, Philippines — A Bureau of Fisheries and Aquatic Resources (BFAR) vessel sustained damage to its main railings, metal stanchions and supports, as well as deck fixtures and equipment, after a China Coast Guard (CCG) ship rammed it on Friday, September 18, the Philippine Coast Guard (PCG) said.

In an online briefing with reporters, PCG spokesperson for the West Philippine Sea Rear Admiral Jay Tarriela said it was a case of “intentional ramming” by the CCG vessel. A day earlier, the Philippine vessel ran aground at Hasa-Hasa (Half Moon) Shoal.

The BRP Datu Magat Salamat has since decided to cut short its mission and was en route back to Coron to assess if it was still sea-worthy, said Tarriela.

Play Video

The BRP Datu Magat Salamat was supposed to bring fuel to Filipino fisherfolk in Abad Santos (Bombay) Shoal when the CCG ship (CCG-21585) used dangerous manuevers on the smaller BFAR ship — cutting across her stern before “striking” or ramming the slightly smaller BFAR vessel.

No injuries were reported from the BRP Datu Magat Salamat, which is manned by a mix of PCG and BFAR personnel.

Tarriela said the 21-series CCG ships are the smallest in the fleet, at under 50 meters long, and are the most agile. In the past, Tarriela said, vessels in this class have been involved in incidents of harassment in the West Philippine Sea, including during resupply missions to Ayungin (Second Thomas) Shoal, a Philippine Navy outpost in the West Philippine Sea.

Abad Santos Shoal is just around 54 nautical miles away from Palawan and is within the Philippines’ exclusive economic zone (EEZ) in an area Manila calls the West Philippine Sea.

In a statement, the National Task Force for the West Philippine Sea condemned China for a “reckless act” that breached the 1972 Convention on the International Regulations for Preventing Collisions at Sea (COLREGs), the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), and the 2016 Arbitral Award.

“The NTF-WPS calls on China to cease dangerous and unlawful actions that endanger lives at sea. We will continue to exercise our rights under international law with restraint, professionalism, and firm commitment to the security and dignity of the Filipino people,” said the inter-agency NTF-WPS.

China claims almost all of the South China Sea to include the Philippines’ EEZ. China has also refused to accept the landmark 2016 Arbitral Award, which affirmed the Philippines’ 200 nautical mile EEZ and deemed China’s sweeping “historical” claim invalid. – Rappler.com

World.title: Kazakhstan Reshapes Investment Model to Attract More Private Capital
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan is restructuring its investment policy to increase private and foreign capital, strengthen domestic production and infrastructure, and shift state support toward mobilizing additional business investment.

The Investment Policy Concept until 2030 was adopted in December 2025, while Baiterek Holding was transformed into a national investment holding. Through its instruments, the government plans to attract an additional $150 billion in investment by 2029, reported the Prime Minister’s press service on Sept. 18.

From investor attraction to targeted investment

Kazakhstan is moving toward proactive investor targeting, with regions identifying priority sectors and preparing investment proposals. Investor support is being reorganized across external, central and regional levels, while the Fast Track mechanism is used to accelerate project implementation.

The Investment Headquarters under the government has expanded its role, alongside stronger investor protection mechanisms, including a prosecutorial filter, a unified register of investor complaints and improved pre-trial settlement procedures.

In 2025, 30 investment agreements were concluded. This year, another 26 agreements worth approximately 5.2 trillion tenge (US$11.7 billion) have been signed.

The new digital architecture includes the National Digital Investment Platform and an integrated analytical system for monitoring investment projects, incorporating data analytics and artificial intelligence.

Investment reaches 23.5 trillion tenge in 2025

Investment activity has maintained positive momentum. Investment in fixed capital exceeded 19.4 trillion tenge (US$43.6 billion) in 2024, with real growth of 8%. In 2025, it rose to approximately 23.5 trillion tenge (US$52.8 billion), with real growth accelerating to 16.7%.

In January-August 2026, more than 13.5 trillion tenge was invested in fixed capital, up 8.1% year on year. The share of fixed-capital investment in GDP increased from 14.2% in 2024 to 14.7% in 2025.

Some 667 projects worth $162.5 billion have been selected, alongside an additional $42.6 billion portfolio focused on developing the resource base.

Greater focus on manufacturing and the real economy

Investment growth has increasingly shifted toward sectors beyond traditional extractive industries. In January-August, real investment growth reached 49.3% in energy, 45.3% in information and communications, 39.9% in manufacturing and 17.6% in agriculture.

Manufacturing’s share of total investment increased from 10.7% in 2024 to 14.1% in January-August, while agriculture rose to 5.6% and energy to 9.7%. Meanwhile, mining’s share fell from 18.7% in 2024 to 13.9%.

The manufacturing sector’s contribution to GDP reached 14% in the first half of this year, up from 12.4% in 2024.

State funding increasingly mobilizes private resources

The structure of investment financing is also changing. The share of budget funding fell from 21.5% in 2025 to 14% in January-August, while non-budget sources accounted for 86%. Enterprises’ own funds represented 66.7%, bank loans 5.6% and other borrowed funds 13.7%.

Baiterek plans to maintain 8 trillion tenge (US$18 billion) in real-sector financing this year, including 1 trillion tenge (US$2.2 billion) through its capitalization.

Since the beginning of the year, Baiterek instruments have provided 7.4 trillion tenge (US$16.6 billion) in support, including 5.4 trillion tenge (US$12.1 billion) for entrepreneurship. Around 5,000 SME projects received 1.4 trillion tenge (US$3.1 billion) through Damu Fund, while more than 1 trillion tenge (US$2.2 billion) was directed to agriculture.

Digital tools expand access to financing

Support for SMEs includes guarantees covering up to 85% of financing for loans of up to 7 billion tenge (US$15.7 million), as well as preferential lending and leasing programs.

A unified front office, contact center 1408, CRM system and AI assistant have been introduced to simplify interaction with development institutions.

Investment mechanisms are also being applied to infrastructure and agriculture. Some 346 utility infrastructure projects worth 884.6 billion tenge (US$2 billion) have been approved, while agricultural leasing reached 250.5 billion tenge (US$563 million) in the first half of this year, almost twice the level recorded a year earlier.

Overall, Baiterek’s support through its instruments amounted to 10.4 trillion tenge (US$23.4 billion) in 2025, with the 2026 focus remaining on the real sector, new production, infrastructure, entrepreneurship, agriculture and exports.

World.title: Turkic States Discuss Strengthening Cooperation in Digital Security
World.content:
ASTANA – Turkic states discussed ways to strengthen cooperation on digital security, including developing artificial intelligence capabilities and coordinating more closely among relevant agencies.

Kazakhstan’s Deputy Chairperson of the Security Council Aida Balayeva highlighted the importance of closer cooperation among Turkic states amid growing geopolitical instability and emerging international security challenges during the fifth meeting of the secretaries of security councils of the Organization of Turkic States (OTS) on Sept. 17 in Baku.

The meeting addressed current security threats, the impact of developments in the Middle East on the security environment of OTS member states, and the development of national artificial intelligence capabilities in the context of national security, reported Kazinform.

They paid particular attention to Kazakhstan’s initiatives to establish a council on cybersecurity and a network of artificial intelligence centers of Turkic states. Participants stressed the need to develop practical mechanisms for cooperation, including direct interaction between relevant government agencies.

The heads of the OTS delegations also met with Azerbaijan’s President Ilham Aliyev. The meeting reaffirmed the importance of continued dialogue and deeper cooperation to promote regional stability and security.

World.title: ‘Our Relationship With Kazakhstan Has Never Been Stronger,’ US Consul General Says
World.content:
ALMATY – The relationship between Kazakhstan and the United States has reached a period of “unprecedented momentum,” U.S. Consul General Peter Kaufman said at a Sept. 17 press briefing in Almaty, as Kazakhstan prepares for President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev’s participation in the G20 Summit in Miami in December and the two sides deepen cooperation on critical minerals and other strategic areas.

Tokayev is expected to attend the G20 Summit at the invitation of U.S. President Donald Trump, with Kazakhstan’s participation in the December meeting adding a high-level dimension to an already active period in bilateral relations. Kazakhstan and the U.S. have also been expanding cooperation through the C5+1 framework, including the first C5+1 Critical Minerals Dialogue held in Astana in June.

“The U.S. was the first to establish diplomatic ties with Kazakhstan, and since that moment, our relationship, our ties, have only grown stronger. We remain committed to Kazakhstan’s independence, sovereignty, and territorial integrity,” Kaufman said.

The consul general, who began his assignment in Almaty in July, said his priority is to build on the existing momentum.

“My work here is to build on that momentum. My main message is, this relationship has never been stronger. We’re seeing tremendous momentum across all of these sectors,” he said.

The timing also places economic cooperation at the center of the bilateral agenda. According to Kaufman, agreements between U.S. and Kazakh companies reached $17 billion over the past year, while bilateral trade reached $7 billion, doubling since 2020. American companies have invested more than $100 billion in Kazakhstan over the past 35 years.

“Transportation, logistics, AI, minerals, Kazakhstan’s mineral wealth, of course. That’s where we’ve seen the most tremendous commercial successes in recent years. But I wouldn’t limit it to those sectors,” he said.

Critical minerals gain strategic importance

Critical minerals have emerged as one of the most significant areas of potential cooperation, particularly as Kazakhstan seeks to develop its resource base beyond raw material extraction and attract investment and technology for processing. Kaufman said U.S. companies are increasingly interested in Kazakhstan’s mineral potential.

He also said U.S. investment can bring technology and expertise while creating economic opportunities in Kazakhstan.

“U.S. companies bring top-notch equipment and technology. They bring the highest standards of corporate governance and environmental protection. And, of course, they bring economic opportunities for Kazakh citizens. They have the creation of jobs, the creation of training opportunities, the creation of professional development opportunities. So I think critical minerals in particular are a good example of a sector in which we’ll see prosperity on both sides,” Kaufman added.

G20 to provide another high-level platform

The upcoming G20 Summit in Miami will provide another opportunity for Kazakhstan and the U.S. to discuss their expanding partnership. Kazakhstan’s Foreign Ministry has said Tokayev’s participation in the December summit will be accompanied by preparations for a substantive agenda at the highest level. Kaufman described the relationship as having reached a particularly strong point and linked its momentum to growing contacts at both the government and business levels.

He also pointed to Kazakhstan’s broader regional role and the C5+1 framework, which has expanded from regional integration into economic cooperation, AI and critical minerals.

“What began primarily as a platform for regional integration, one that would connect the Central Asian countries with the U.S., and on that we’ve, I think, very successfully built to expand it into other areas,” he said.

The consul general said Kazakhstan has played a significant role in developing contacts between Washington and Central Asia.

AI, trade and regional connectivity

Beyond critical minerals, Kaufman highlighted AI, transportation and logistics as other areas where the relationship is expanding.

“What I’ll say on AI is that the U.S. brings world-class AI technology to the world. We’re extraordinarily proud of our AI companies, our AI industry, and our AI technology,” he said, noting that AI is also becoming part of the C5+1 agenda, with a dedicated meeting planned within the framework.

Speaking to The Astana Times about Pax Silica, a U.S.-led initiative focused on strengthening cooperation around artificial intelligence, semiconductors and resilient technology supply chains, Kaufman said the initiative is closely connected to the broader strategic partnership between the U.S. and Kazakhstan.

“What you asked about is the State Department-originated platform for building consensus on how to take AI into the future and also to make sure that we are building the resilience of our supply chains. And so on that, I would say that it is at the very core of the strength of our relationship with Kazakhstan,” he said.

“I think I mentioned earlier that there is actually an AI meeting in the C5+1 framework at the end of this month, where I think those questions will be very much at the center of those discussions,” he added.

Visa applicants urged to rely on official information

Kaufman also addressed the continuing interest among Kazakh citizens in traveling to and studying in the U.S., urging applicants to rely exclusively on official sources for visa information.

“Our main advice, our main message is for visa applicants to rely exclusively on official sources of information, such as travel.state.gov, the official State Department website on visa issues, and of course on our embassy website and our consulate website, to make sure that they are receiving the most accurate information on these issues.” he said.

He said the U.S. continues to issue visas to tourists, business people and students in large numbers, while warning applicants about agencies that claim to facilitate or guarantee visa issuance.

“There is a lot of inaccurate, unofficial information out there, a lot of rumors out there. There are agencies that charge money for facilitating the visa process, and even in some cases, trying to guarantee the issuance of a visa,” Kaufman said.

‘I hope so’ on potential Trump visit

Asked whether U.S. President Donald Trump could visit Kazakhstan following invitations from Tokayev, Kaufman responded briefly but positively.

“I hope so. I hope so,” he said.

He also added that the relationship between the two presidents reflected the broader momentum in bilateral ties.

“President Tokayev and President Trump speak frequently. They have a very strong relationship, and I think that’s really emblematic of the momentum, the extraordinary, unprecedented momentum we’re seeing currently in the relationship,” he said.

For Kaufman, the current period represents an opportunity to build on three decades of diplomatic relations through stronger commercial ties, investment, technological cooperation and closer people-to-people connections.

“And my main priority is to make sure that we can preserve this momentum and build on it so that we can develop this relationship even further. That’s what I look forward to doing, especially as I get started in my new capacity here,” he said.

World.title: Foreign Minister Tileuberdi Reviews Ties With China, Russia and Kyrgyz Republic
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan reviewed the current state and prospects of bilateral cooperation with China, the Kyrgyz Republic and Russia during separate meetings between Foreign Minister Mukhtar Tileuberdi and the countries’ ambassadors on Sept. 17.

With Kyrgyz Ambassador Kudaibergen Bazarbaev, Tileuberdi discussed political, trade and economic, water and energy, and cultural and humanitarian cooperation. The officials reaffirmed their commitment to strengthening allied relations and exchanged views on regional and international issues, reported the ministry’s press service.

During talks with Chinese Ambassador Han Chunlin, the officials focused on implementing agreements reached by the leaders of Kazakhstan and China and preparing for upcoming high-level bilateral and multilateral events.

Tileuberdi and Russian Ambassador Alexey Borodavkin discussed bilateral cooperation, the implementation of agreements reached at the highest levels, and the schedule of upcoming mutual visits and joint events.

The meeting participants also exchanged views on regional and international developments and cooperation within multilateral formats.

World.title: Beyond Seoul Summit: Can Kazakhstan Turn Korean Investment Into Industrial Capacity?
World.content:
The first Korea–Central Asia Summit in Seoul has ended. The agreements have been signed, the Seoul Declaration adopted, and a relationship that began nearly two decades ago at the vice-ministerial level has now reached the presidential table.

But for Kazakhstan, the most important question begins after the summit.

Before the meeting, much of the discussion centered on why South Korea was becoming more interested in Central Asia: critical minerals, energy, supply-chain diversification and access to new markets. These interests remain important. Yet the outcome in Seoul suggests that the relationship could develop into something more ambitious.

The language has shifted from access to resources toward value chains; from individual projects toward industrial capacity; and, in Kazakhstan’s case, from attracting investment toward localization, technology transfer and production for third markets.

That shift matters.

Kazakhstan now has an opportunity to test a proposition that extends well beyond its relationship with South Korea: Can growing international demand for its resources become a catalyst for industrial development, rather than simply another cycle of raw-material exports?

Seoul changed the terms of the conversation

The summit on Sept. 16 brought together South Korean President Lee Jae Myung and the presidents of all five Central Asian states for the first leaders-level meeting in the history of the Korea–Central Asia format.

The institutional result was significant. The six countries adopted the Seoul Declaration, agreed to continue meetings at the leaders’ level, and Kazakhstan is set to host the next summit in 2028.

But the economic language of the meeting may prove more consequential.

Lee argued that cooperation should move beyond individual projects and infrastructure construction toward jointly developing industrial capabilities and mutually beneficial value chains. The logic is clear: Central Asia possesses critical minerals, energy resources and growing markets, while South Korea brings manufacturing capacity, technology and industrial expertise.

The countries backed this vision with an agreement on industrial and supply-chain cooperation covering manufacturing, infrastructure, critical minerals, energy and digital transformation. They also established a consultative mechanism among industry ministers to help translate political commitments into implementation.

This is precisely where the summit begins to differ from many conventional “Central Asia plus” meetings.

The question is no longer only what South Korea wants to buy from Central Asia. Increasingly, it is what the two sides can produce together.

Kazakhstan brought an industrial proposition

Kazakhstan used the summit to make that distinction explicit.

President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev proposed developing a Central Asia–Korea industrial and technological partnership built around localization, technology transfer, stronger regional supply chains and exports of finished products to third-country markets.

That is an important formulation because it addresses the central dilemma facing Kazakhstan in the current global competition for critical minerals.

International demand for uranium, lithium, rare earths and other strategic resources gives Kazakhstan geopolitical and commercial leverage. But demand alone does not guarantee industrialization.

A country can diversify its buyers while leaving its economic model largely unchanged.

If resources are extracted domestically but most processing, technological development and manufacturing take place elsewhere, Kazakhstan remains primarily at the lower end of the value chain.

The objective should therefore not be simply to export more minerals to more destinations.

It should be to capture more value before those resources leave the country.

The agreements reached around President Tokayev’s visit indicate that this transition is at least beginning to enter practical discussions.

Among the projects announced were cooperation on joint drilling at the Bakennoye lithium deposit involving Tau-Ken Samruk and the Korea Institute of Geoscience and Mineral Resources, as well as cooperation involving POSCO Holdings on rare-earth processing and refining.

Beyond minerals, QazaqGaz and Hyundai Engineering agreed on a gas-processing project at Karachaganak, while KazMunayGas and Samsung E&A reached an agreement connected with expansion of the Pavlodar refinery.

Taken together, the broader package of announced Kazakhstan–Korea projects and agreements was valued at approximately $19 billion, although these initiatives are at different stages of development.

The headline number is impressive. But it should not become the principal measure of success.

What matters is what kind of economic capacity those investments leave behind.

From investment volume to investment quality

For Kazakhstan, the next stage should therefore focus less on how much investment is announced and more on what that investment does.

A successful project should ideally generate several layers of value.

The first is obvious: capital, production and jobs.

The second is more important over time: local suppliers, engineering expertise, workforce development and technological capabilities.

The third is the most difficult: integrating Kazakh enterprises into international production networks so that they can eventually compete beyond the domestic market.

This is where South Korea is particularly relevant.

Korea’s economic strength does not come from natural resources. It comes from its ability to transform imported inputs into sophisticated manufactured products through technology, engineering, skills and export-oriented industrial ecosystems.

That experience makes Korea a potentially different kind of partner for Kazakhstan.

The relationship should therefore not be framed simply around Korean investment in individual Kazakh projects. The more ambitious objective should be the gradual creation of industrial ecosystems around those investments.

A Korean-backed processing facility, for example, becomes significantly more valuable to Kazakhstan if local engineering companies can supply it, universities train specialists for it, research institutions work with it and domestic companies eventually enter its supply chain.

That is how foreign investment becomes industrial capacity.

Critical minerals should be the beginning, not the entire relationship

Critical minerals will remain one of the strongest drivers of Korea–Central Asia cooperation. The Seoul Declaration reflects a shared interest in combining Central Asia’s mineral resources with Korean technology and expertise.

But Kazakhstan should resist allowing minerals to define the entire partnership.

The summit also produced an initiative on artificial intelligence and science and technology. Cooperation covers digital transformation, energy and other advanced sectors.

These areas matter because the next stage of Kazakhstan’s development cannot depend only on extracting different commodities more efficiently.

The country needs engineering capability, applied research, digital infrastructure, advanced manufacturing and human capital.

This is also where cooperation with Korea could acquire greater strategic depth.

South Korea’s experience in electronics, automotive manufacturing, energy infrastructure, digital technologies and research-intensive industries provides potential areas for cooperation that are not dependent on commodity cycles.

Education should be part of the same conversation.

Technology transfer does not happen merely because a memorandum contains the phrase. It requires engineers, technicians, researchers and managers capable of absorbing and eventually improving imported technologies.

Industrial agreements should therefore increasingly be accompanied by partnerships between Korean companies and Kazakh universities, technical training programs, joint laboratories and applied research initiatives.

The ultimate objective should be not only technology transfer, but technology absorption.

Kazakhstan can connect industrialization with connectivity

There is another reason why the partnership should move beyond resources.

Kazakhstan’s value to South Korea is geographic as well as geological.

Seoul is seeking greater diversification of markets and supply chains at a time when economic security and national security are becoming increasingly interconnected.

Kazakhstan sits at the center of emerging transport routes connecting China and Central Asia with the Caspian Sea, the South Caucasus and Europe.

This creates an opportunity to connect two agendas that are often discussed separately: industrialization and the Middle Corridor.

Transport routes become considerably more valuable when they do not merely move goods through a country but carry goods produced there.

If Kazakhstan can combine Korean investment, domestic resources, processing capacity and improved trans-Caspian connectivity, its role changes.

It becomes not simply a transit state or a resource supplier, but a production and logistics platform linking Asian industrial networks with European markets.

That is a much more ambitious proposition.

A regional opportunity

The Seoul summit also demonstrated that this transformation does not need to stop at Kazakhstan’s borders.

South Korea and Central Asia increasingly speak in terms of regional value chains.

That approach makes economic sense because no single Central Asian country possesses every resource, industrial capability, energy source or transport connection required for a complete production chain.

Kazakhstan brings significant mineral resources, energy, industrial capacity and transport infrastructure. Uzbekistan offers a large market and expanding manufacturing base. The Kyrgyz Republic and Tajikistan possess important hydropower and mineral potential, while Turkmenistan brings major energy resources and a strategic position toward the Caspian.

Greater regional complementarity could allow Central Asia to offer external partners something larger than five separate markets.

For Korea, that could mean access to an emerging regional production platform.

For Central Asia, it could mean stronger negotiating power and a greater ability to retain value within the region.

The summit’s regional format is therefore important not simply because five presidents sat at the same table in Seoul. It matters because the format can gradually encourage the region to think about what it can offer — and demand — collectively.

CFive Analysis: Astana 2028 should be the deadline

The most important outcome of the Seoul summit may ultimately be that it created a clock.

Kazakhstan is expected to host the next Korea–Central Asia Summit in 2028.

That gives Astana roughly two years to demonstrate whether the language of industrial partnership can produce measurable results.

By the next summit, the relevant questions should be concrete.

How many of the projects announced in Seoul have moved into implementation?

How much Korean investment has entered processing and manufacturing rather than extraction alone?

Have local suppliers entered Korean-led projects?

Have joint laboratories, engineering programs or training centers been established?

Has cooperation on critical minerals produced processed materials or higher-value exports from Kazakhstan?

And have any Kazakh enterprises become part of Korean or wider international supply chains?

These indicators would tell us considerably more than another headline investment figure.

The Seoul summit has already provided the political framework. It established leaders-level cooperation, adopted the Seoul Declaration, created an industrial consultation mechanism and placed value chains, technology and industrial capacity at the center of the relationship.

Kazakhstan now has to convert that framework into economic structure.

Before the summit, the central question was whether Kazakhstan would remain primarily a resource supplier or use Korean engagement to become an industrial partner.

Seoul did not resolve that question. But it produced a clearer pathway toward the second option.

The next two years will determine whether that pathway becomes reality.

By the time the leaders meet again in Kazakhstan in 2028, success should not be measured by how many new memorandums are ready to be signed.

It should be visible in what Kazakhstan and Korea have already begun to build together.

The author is Alisher Amangeldinov, a senior research analyst at CFive analytical firm, Kazakhstan.

The article is published as part of the partnership between The Astana Times and CFive think tank.

World.title: Astana to Host UEFA Super Cup in 2028
World.content:
ASTANA – Astana will host the UEFA Super Cup in 2028, marking the first time the prestigious European club football match will be held in Kazakhstan.

The decision was approved by the UEFA Executive Committee on Sept. 15. The match will take place at Astana Arena, which will become the venue for the annual meeting between the winners of the UEFA Champions League and UEFA Europa League.

The UEFA Super Cup has traditionally brought together the winners of Europe’s two major club competitions in a single match at the start of the new season. The fixture has been held at different European venues since 2013.

Astana Arena has previously hosted major international football events. In 2015, FC Astana became the first Kazakh club to reach the UEFA Champions League group stage, with its home matches played at the stadium. The club’s historic European campaign was covered here.

The stadium has continued to host European club competitions, including Champions League fixtures involving FC Astana and FC Kairat.

Preparations for the 2028 Super Cup will include infrastructure upgrades to ensure the stadium meets UEFA’s requirements for hosting the event.

The 2027 UEFA Super Cup will be played at Johan Cruyff ArenA in Amsterdam, while Astana Arena will host the following year’s edition. The exact date and the participating teams for the 2028 match will be determined after the corresponding European club competitions are completed.

The decision adds Kazakhstan to the list of countries that have hosted one of UEFA’s major annual club fixtures and brings a high-profile European football event to Astana.

World.title: Expert: Investment Headquarters Highlights Gaps in Kazakhstan’s Investment Infrastructure
World.content:
ASTANA – The Investment Headquarters is an important mechanism for resolving investors’ problems, but its continued role also shows where Kazakhstan’s investment infrastructure still has “rough edges,” financial analyst Rassul Rysmambetov told The Astana Times.

He described the Investment Headquarters as a useful “diagnostic” tool, saying that its cases could provide insight into which regions and sectors resolve investor issues more quickly and where decisions take longer.

“If we collect all the data from the Investment Headquarters and understand in which regions or sectors decisions are made faster and where they take longer, we need to understand which regions are working poorly and in which sectors we have poor legislation,” Rysmambetov said.

From resolving individual problems to identifying systemic barriers

Over the past three years, the Investment Headquarters has held 69 meetings, addressing issues related to 309 projects with a combined value of more than $154 billion, reported the Prime Minister’s press service on Sept. 16.

Its work covers different stages of project implementation, including land allocation, infrastructure connections, permits, raw material supplies, financing and preparation for construction.

In 2025, decisions by the Investment Headquarters enabled 12 projects in nine regions to proceed to construction and installation works, representing more than $1.5 billion in invested capital.

Rysmambetov said the mechanism is particularly relevant because investors can face difficulties when moving from central government institutions to regional authorities. He identified coordination between central and regional authorities as a key challenge, noting that central-level decisions can face delays when investors move to the regional level.

Investment agreements expand the pipeline

The Government has also increased its use of investment agreements, intended to give investors greater predictability about the conditions for implementing large projects.

In 2025, 41 investment agreements worth $29.8 billion were signed, compared with six agreements worth $2.2 billion in 2024. Since the beginning of this year, another 25 agreements worth about $11 billion have been concluded.

The figures indicate a substantial expansion in the number and value of projects receiving this form of state support. The more important measure, however, is how many of these projects progress from agreements and investment decisions to construction and eventually operational production.

Several projects already moving through the implementation process illustrate the potential economic impact.

From raw materials to higher-value production

The projects illustrate how investment support can translate into new production and jobs. In Balkhash, the $1.5 billion Qazaq Smelter project is expected to produce 300,000 tons of cathode copper annually, process up to 1.5 million tons of concentrate and create nearly 1,600 jobs.

In the Mangystau Region, a $287.6 million multifunctional terminal at the Port of Kuryk is planned to handle 15 million tons and create around 500 jobs, adding capacity to the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route.

Other projects focus on domestic processing. Advanced Processing is developing a $100 million ammonia and ammonium nitrate plant in the Atyrau Region, while QazCoilPro is investing nearly $256.8 million in a full-cycle aluminum plant in the Turkistan Region, with more than 1,000 jobs expected across the project and related facilities.

Measuring implementation, not only commitments

These projects also highlight why resolving administrative barriers matters: investment agreements and announcements must ultimately translate into construction, production and jobs.

Rysmambetov said the Investment Headquarters helps “break through this ice” and reach the core of issues at the regional and ministerial levels. But its continued role also indicates that Kazakhstan’s investment infrastructure still has gaps.

“The fact that there is still work for such things as the Investment Headquarters means that the investment infrastructure is not yet fully developed,” he said.

Tracking the problems brought before the headquarters could help identify recurring regulatory and regional barriers and show where systemic reforms are needed.

Rysmambetov expects the Investment Headquarters to remain necessary for at least the next five years. Its longer-term value, he suggested, will depend on whether the problems it now solves project by project can eventually be addressed through improvements to the broader investment system.

World.title: Kazakhstan Expands International Air Connectivity With New Routes to Türkiye and UAE
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan is set to expand international air connectivity with new and resumed passenger and cargo services linking the country with Türkiye and the United Arab Emirates (UAE), as airlines increase capacity on key routes.

Turkish airline SunExpress plans to launch regular flights between Astana and Izmir with flights scheduled twice a week on Wednesdays and Saturdays using Boeing 737 aircraft, while increasing the frequency of its existing Almaty–Izmir service.

The plans were discussed during a Sept. 15 meeting between the Chairman of Kazakhstan’s Civil Aviation Committee and representatives of SunExpress, according to Kazakhstan’s Ministry of Transport.

Meanwhile, Air Astana plans to resume regular flights between Kazakhstan and Dubai in October. The Almaty–Dubai service is scheduled to restart on Oct. 1, followed by the Astana–Dubai route on Oct. 2. The airline plans to gradually increase frequencies during the month, with Almaty–Dubai flights rising from four to 12 per week and Astana–Dubai flights from three to 10 per week by the end of October. The airline said the schedule could be adjusted depending on developments in the Middle East.

The expansion also includes air cargo connectivity between Kazakhstan and the UAE. FlyDubai plans to launch weekly cargo flights on the Almaty–Dubai route from Oct. 2 using Boeing 737 aircraft. The service will transport both import and export cargo between the two countries, according to Kazakhstan’s Civil Aviation Committee.

The new cargo route is expected to provide additional logistics options for Kazakh businesses and support trade and economic ties between Kazakhstan and the UAE. Kazakhstan’s Transport Ministry has identified the development of air cargo transportation as a priority for strengthening the country’s transport and logistics potential, increasing its transit attractiveness and supporting the development of aviation hubs.

World.title: Opinion: Abolition of Georgia’s state grants agency contradicts pledges to ‘support good causes’
World.content:
Abolition of Georgia’s state grants agency

“The Georgian authorities’ decision to abolish the state grants management agency has confirmed how superficial officials’ claims were when they established it in 2025,” Tamar Oniani, chair of the Georgian Young Lawyers’ Association (GYLA), said, commenting on the decision.

“When the agency was established, the authorities said its purpose was to strengthen democratic institutions, combat corruption, support people with disabilities, protect the environment and minority rights, and carry out other ‘good deeds’ funded from the state budget,” Oniani recalled.

The Grants Management Agency was established in February 2025. Its stated purpose was to “support civil society organisations operating in Georgia, using funding from the Georgian state budget, whose activities are aligned with the country’s development priorities”. The government said state grants would be available only to organisations that complied with the “Transparent Financing” law and registered as “agents of foreign influence”.

On 17 September 2026, Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze announced that the Grants Management Agency would be abolished by the end of the year.

“NGOs are artificial entities created for foreign political interference,” Kobakhidze said. He also claimed that “100 years ago, there were no non-governmental organisations“.

Tamar Oniani: “A hundred years ago, it was not only NGOs that did not exist. Neither did the Strasbourg court or the modern international system for the protection of human rights.

At the time, human rights were regarded as an ‘internal matter’ for states. But without human rights organisations, no human rights treaty could function effectively. That is why these organisations were given a recognised status and powers.

If anyone finds comfort in the claim that civil society organisations did not exist 100 years ago, it is both historically inaccurate and politically dangerous.

In fact, history provides an example in the Society for the Spreading of Literacy among Georgians, founded by educator Ilia Chavchavadze. It is precisely an example of a civil society organisation.

It is worth paying attention to the narrative being used to justify the agency’s closure.

It is through this prism that the current regime views people – as powerless, subordinate and, consequently, deprived of their rights.

The phrase ‘NGOs did not exist 100 years ago’ means that the system is fighting those who have the organisational and institutional capacity to demand that people’s rights be upheld.

In other words, the regime is fighting genuine human rights organisations.

The decision to abolish the state Grants Management Agency has confirmed how superficial officials’ claims were when they established it – that they intended to strengthen democratic institutions, combat corruption, support people with disabilities, protect the environment and minority rights, and carry out other ‘good deeds’ funded from the state budget.”

World.title: Armenians to be able to fund media directly through their income tax payments
World.content:
Citizens of Armenia will be able to fund quality media

In the near future, citizens of Armenia will be able to direct part of the income tax they pay towards funding media outlets, NGOs and political parties. The government has approved a decision to expand the list of “social expenses”, a category introduced as part of the personal income declaration system.

Under the current regulations, anyone who submits an annual tax declaration to the State Revenue Committee can receive a refund for part of the money they have “spent on social needs”. These expenses include education and medical costs. The compensation amounts to up to 100,000 drams ($276). Once the amendments come into force, social expenses will also include money that citizens donate to media outlets, NGOs and political parties.

The government will determine the procedure for transferring these funds and set the maximum amount in a separate decision.

“We are moving to the next stage of democratic reforms, under which NGOs, media outlets and political parties will be able to receive public funding,” Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan said.

Political analyst Robert Ghevondyan told JAMnews that even after the changes take effect, it will be difficult to imagine media outlets or NGOs achieving complete financial independence.

“But changes will certainly follow. Even if they receive funding from domestic sources, both media outlets and NGOs will continue to seek funds and build certain relationships. Nevertheless, a situation will clearly emerge that is much more aligned with Armenia’s interests,” he stressed.

The deadline for submitting income declarations for 2025 is 1 November this year. According to the head of the State Revenue Committee, as of 1 September, 92,000 people had already applied for and received compensation for social expenses. The total amount reached 7.5 billion drams [more than $20 million].

Finance ministry proposal

The Ministry of Finance has presented a draft law entitled “On Amendments and Additions to the Tax Code”. Under the ministry’s proposal, social expenses would also include funds that individuals transfer to:

public organisations;

legal entities and individual entrepreneurs engaged in media activities;

political parties.

“Stable operations by public organisations, legal entities and individual entrepreneurs engaged in media activities, as well as political parties, are important for developing independent parties and civil society, and for protecting freedom of speech,” the draft’s explanatory note says.

Before the decision comes into force, the government will determine not only the maximum amount of social expenses, but also:

which NGOs, media outlets and political parties will qualify;

the criteria they must meet;

the information they must submit to the tax authority;

the procedure for submitting and publishing this information.

“We are creating mechanisms to protect public interests impartially”

According to Armenian Finance Minister Vahe Hovhannisyan, the changes aim to create mechanisms that will increase the financial independence and transparency of NGOs, media outlets and political parties. The amendments are also expected to promote freedom and impartiality in public statements and strengthen ties with the public.

“NGOs, media outlets and political parties have a responsibility to protect the interests of different sections of society. Therefore, we are creating independent funding mechanisms to ensure the most impartial protection of these interests and, in doing so, strengthen Armenia’s democratic institutions,” the minister stressed.

Hovhannisyan presented details of the draft. He said that, first, the tax authority would compile and publish lists of NGOs, media outlets and political parties that meet the government’s criteria and have submitted reports on their financial activities.

“When filing their declarations, citizens will choose an organisation and specify the amount they wish to transfer through an electronic system. State agencies will then ensure that the funds are transferred,” he explained.

Political analyst Robert Ghevondyan’s comment

“The amendments to the Tax Code could significantly improve the position of civil society in Armenia. For years, civil society has had to rely on external funding and has naturally operated under the influence of those foundations. In many cases, NGOs’ activities, programmes and level of engagement have been limited.

We are now seeing a situation in which Armenia’s residents will be able to help fund civil society organisations using their own money. As a result, they will be entitled to expect these organisations to take a more active role in addressing the problems that matter to them.

At the same time, NGOs will be able to worry less about their financial stability and avoid dependence on geopolitical fluctuations. The situation with USAID is a case in point. They will be able to plan their work properly and defend interests that align with their own programmes and approaches, rather than being forced to serve other people’s interests simply to resolve their financial problems, at least partially.

There is no doubt that we will see greater transparency and accountability, as well as the ‘cleansing’ of the sector. Qualitative changes will be a secondary effect of this process of improvement.

Short-lived organisations with unclear goals often emerge. In the course of their activities, they frequently create problems for the state.

Now we will see a situation in which these organisations’ activities become transparent, primarily to the state but also to society. They will no longer be able to conceal their true intentions behind contrived ideas.”

Citizens of Armenia will be able to fund quality media

World.title: ‘NGOs are artificial phenomenon’ — Georgia to shut down grants management agency
World.content:
Prime Minister of Georgia Irakli Kobakhidze announced on 17 September that the state agency responsible for managing grants would close by the end of the year. He said the agency was already “on standby”. Its head, Tamar Zodelava, will become a deputy justice minister.

The agency was established in February 2025. Its stated aim was to “support, through the state budget, public organisations operating in Georgia whose activities align with the country’s development priorities”.

“The very concept of this structure — a non-governmental organisation — is an artificial phenomenon. The only possible purpose of an NGO is to interfere in the affairs of another state. That is why they were originally created.

There were no organisations of this kind 100 years ago. They were later established and began to be used as the main tool of foreign interference. We have seen many examples of this in Georgia. Therefore, it is wrong for us to finance such activities, which is why we made this decision,” Irakli Kobakhidze said.

Georgia’s PM Kobakhidze takes aim at NGOs

World.title: US court orders Georgia to pay $350m over halted Namakhvani HPP project
World.content:
Georgia to pay $350m over Namakhvani HPP

A US federal court has granted a request by Turkish company ENKA Renewables in its arbitration dispute with the Georgian authorities over the abandoned Namakhvani hydropower plant project.

US District Judge Amit Mehta authorised the enforcement of an international arbitration award.

This means Georgia will have to pay ENKA about $350m, plus accrued interest, bringing the total to approximately $400m.

Interest will continue to accrue daily and will be compounded monthly.

ENKA, one of Turkey’s largest construction companies, began work on the Namakhvani cascade hydropower project in Georgia in October 2020. It was set to become the country’s largest energy project since Georgia gained independence from the Soviet Union. However, the project faced strong opposition from local residents and civil society activists. They argued that the hydropower plant would flood the valley, threaten 18 villages and pose risks to the nearby city of Kutaisi. Local residents dubbed the project the “dam of death”, set up protest camps at the construction site in the Tskaltubo district and demanded an immediate halt to the works and the removal of equipment from the valley. They also filed a lawsuit challenging the permit issued for the construction of the hydropower plant.

The judge rejected all of Georgia’s arguments, including its request to dismiss or stay the case until the Paris Court of Appeal had reached a final decision on ENKA’s arbitration claim.

The court ordered ENKA to submit its final claim by 18 September, including interest accrued since the court’s ruling on 11 September.

How Namakhvani HPP dispute ended up in international arbitration

Local opposition to the Namakhvani HPP project was so intense that it delayed its implementation, and ENKA eventually terminated its agreement with the Georgian government.

The Turkish company argued that Georgia had materially breached its obligations under the agreement, including by failing to provide adequate access to the construction site.

The Georgian government disputed this assessment.

After terminating the agreement, ENKA transferred project-related assets to Georgia and sought compensation based on their fair market value. The two sides failed to agree on the amount, prompting the company to take the dispute to international arbitration.

The case was heard by an arbitration tribunal of the International Chamber of Commerce (ICC), which convened in Paris in May 2022.

After about two years of proceedings, the tribunal found that Georgia had materially breached the terms of its agreement with ENKA.

It also found that ENKA had been entitled to terminate the agreement and that Georgia was required to compensate the company for the fair market value of the assets transferred to the state following the termination, as well as interest.

Interest was initially calculated using the international LIBOR benchmark plus an additional four percentage points. The parties later agreed to use SOFR instead.

In January 2025, the tribunal also issued an additional document correcting a technical error in its decision.

The dispute, however, did not end there.

Paris appeal and Washington court ruling

Both Georgia and the Turkish company subsequently took further legal action.

Georgia appealed to the Paris Court of Appeal, challenging, among other things, the amount sought by ENKA. It asked the court to annul the arbitration award and reconsider the case.

ENKA, meanwhile, applied to a US court seeking recognition and enforcement of the international arbitration award. The company relied on the 1958 New York Convention, which sets out rules for the recognition and enforcement of foreign arbitral awards.

Georgia argued that the US proceedings should be put on hold pending a final ruling by the Paris court. Judge Mehta rejected this argument.

In his ruling, he said one of the main purposes of arbitration was the prompt resolution of disputes and that staying the case indefinitely would be inconsistent with that objective.

The court noted that the arbitration proceedings had begun nearly four years earlier and that, although the final hearing before the Paris court took place in October 2025, no ruling had yet been issued.

Given these circumstances, the Washington court found that waiting for the Paris proceedings to conclude would be inconsistent with the objectives of the New York Convention.

Georgia fails to convince court over damages calculation

One of Georgia’s main arguments concerned the calculation of damages. The parties disagreed over the interest rate to be applied, which could result in a difference of more than $100m in the final compensation amount.

Georgia argued that the tribunal had not given the parties a full opportunity to present their positions. The US court rejected this argument.

According to Judge Mehta’s ruling, Georgia had participated in discussions over the procedure used by the tribunal and had an opportunity to raise its fundamental objection during the proceedings.

The court said Georgia’s representative had not expressed any “strong objection” to the preparation of a joint expert report. It therefore found that Georgia did not have sufficient grounds to have the arbitration award set aside.

Court also rejects Georgia’s procedural argument

Georgia argued that the procedure used by the arbitration tribunal did not comply with the rules agreed by the parties. The Washington court rejected this argument as well.

According to the ruling, the tribunal discussed the methodology for calculating damages with the parties and gave them an opportunity to submit additional arguments on the model prepared by experts. Georgia failed to demonstrate that the tribunal had breached any arbitration rules previously agreed by the parties.

Court rejects Georgia’s argument over sovereign right to control natural resources

Another argument put forward by Georgia was that ENKA’s demand for compensation infringed on states’ sovereign right to determine how natural resources within their territory should be used.

Georgia linked this argument to public protests against the Namakhvani HPP project.

Judge Mehta rejected this argument as well. His ruling said that refusing to enforce a foreign arbitration award on public policy grounds was a narrow exception under US law and applied only in clear-cut cases.

The court considered an example cited by Georgia: a 2018 case in which enforcement of an arbitration award requiring the continued extraction of natural gas in a foreign country was found to be incompatible with public policy.

However, the court found the ENKA case to be fundamentally different. The arbitration award did not require Georgia to take any specific action. It only required the state to pay monetary compensation.

The court found that such a “purely compensatory award” did not violate US public policy.

How much will Georgia ultimately have to pay?

The approximately $350m awarded to ENKA is not the final amount Georgia may have to pay. The US court ruled that interest would continue to accrue after the judgment in accordance with the terms of the agreement.

The court found that the relevant provision was clear and that SOFR plus four percentage points should therefore apply instead of the standard interest rate.

The final amount should become clearer on 18 September, when ENKA is due to submit a proposed final judgment to the court, also reflecting interest accrued since 11 September.

What happens next?

The Washington court’s ruling allows ENKA to seek enforcement of the arbitration award. However, the legal dispute is not yet over.

Georgia’s application to have the arbitration award annulled remains pending before the Paris Court of Appeal. If the French court ultimately sets aside the award, this could provide grounds for refusing its enforcement in the US under Article V(1)(e) of the New York Convention.

World.title: Pre-election mood in South Ossetia: ‘So calm it’s almost boring’
World.content:
Presidential election in South Ossetia

Early presidential elections will be held in South Ossetia on 18 September, with four candidates standing.

However, the contest can only loosely be described as a race, as there has been a clear frontrunner from the outset – acting president and Prime Minister Marat Kambolov, who was sent from Russia in May 2026.

Between May and August, Kambolov, who was immediately granted South Ossetian citizenship, rose from adviser to then-President Alan Gagloyev to prime minister. Following Gagloyev’s resignation, he became acting president and soon afterwards a presidential candidate.

Kambolov’s candidacy is backed even by much of the opposition, while the Kremlin is also seen as standing firmly behind him.

Unlike Kambolov, an outsider to South Ossetia, the other three candidates were born in the region. But that appears to be where their advantages end. Most experts describe them as token candidates who have made little attempt to seriously compete for the presidency.

They are:

Zurab Kokoyev, leader of the Unity party;

Kazbek Kodoyev, an independent candidate and adviser to the rector of South Ossetian State University;

Murat Valiyev, a state security officer and candidate for the Patriots of Alania party.

None of the three has campaigned among voters, limiting their election activities to outlining their vision for South Ossetia’s development during live televised debates.

Campaign with little excitement

Marat Kambolov, by contrast, has been notably active. In less than four months since arriving in South Ossetia, he has addressed a significant number of problems that had been building up for years.

For example, he has:

simplified the cumbersome, hours-long process of checking documents at the Nizhny Zaramag checkpoint on the border with Russia;

overseen the recalculation and increase of pensions;

raised salaries for some categories of military personnel and Emergencies Ministry staff;

begun addressing problems in healthcare and the social sector.

And he has done all this not as part of his election campaign, but ostensibly simply in the course of carrying out his duties as prime minister.

It is therefore unsurprising that a large proportion of voters intend to cast their ballots for him.

Marat Kambolov during an “evening stroll through Tskhinval”

Such certainty has done little to enliven the pre-election atmosphere, with local experts and politically engaged residents describing it as not merely “calm”, but “dull”.

“Everything is stable. There are no conflicts, incidents, mud-slinging or fierce political confrontation,” one Tskhinval resident said, noting the stark contrast with previous election campaigns, each of which had turned into something of a political blockbuster.

Even Kambolov’s rival backs him

In addition to South Ossetia, polling stations will open in Russia – four in Vladikavkaz and one in Moscow.

Unlike during previous presidential and parliamentary elections, there has been no campaigning in North Ossetia this time either. A campaign banner featuring Kambolov has appeared at just one location in Vladikavkaz – outside the regional office of the A Just Russia party, whose representatives support him.

One of them, North Ossetian MP Dzambolat Tedeyev, is also chairman of the South Ossetian Patriots of Alania party – the same party that nominated its own presidential candidate, Murat Valiyev. Yet Tedeyev has openly endorsed Kambolov and urged voters to back him. Valiyev, a young politician, appears to have been put forward largely to gain political experience.

There are, incidentally, no election campaign banners at all in South Ossetia itself.

‘Personnel purge’ already under way

Of course, surprises on election day cannot be ruled out.
