In the past, a significant proportion of South Ossetian voters have shown their independence by backing underdogs rather than candidates favoured by the Kremlin. According to the author, however, such choices have repeatedly led to disappointment among voters.

The most recent example cited is former President Alan Gagloyev, who was elected in 2022. His presidency was marked by a deepening social and political crisis, concerns over crime and a series of corruption scandals. Public discontent grew, while questions were raised over the use of Russian loans. The author argues that this ultimately prompted Moscow to send Marat Kambolov to Tskhinval to “restore order”.

Since stepping down, Gagloyev has occasionally appeared at official events and has sought to retain political influence through allies who continue to hold key positions. But that may not last long. Kambolov has already begun making personnel changes, starting with the dismissal of KGB First Deputy Chairman Aleksandr Tuayev, who, among other things, has been suspected of involvement in smuggling fuel and cigarettes to the Georgian-controlled side.

How far Kambolov might go with this “purge” if he becomes South Ossetia’s de jure leader remains unclear. Some local residents, at least, hope he will remove officials they regard as particularly corrupt or abusive of their positions.

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

World.title: ‘How much money do you need each month to live comfortably?’ Street poll in Tbilisi. Video
World.content:
We asked passers-by on the streets of Tbilisi how much money they need each month to live a normal life. We also asked what they actually mean by “a normal life”.

The answers vary widely. Some young people believe the amount should be at least 5,000–8,000 lari around $1,900–3,000 per person. Middle-aged and older respondents, meanwhile, say that 2,000 lari around $769 is enough for one person.

Meanwhile, the subsistence minimum for the average consumer in Georgia is 250.9 lari around $97.

Responses to the question of what constitutes a normal life also vary by age. For middle-aged and older people, having enough money for food, medication and utility bills already amounts to a normal life.

Here are several examples of the answers we received:

“No excessive comfort, no leisure, just food and medication.”

“The basics, at least food, right? Proper food. Children need clothes and shoes. Basic school supplies.”

“To be able to go into a shop without worrying that if you buy this, you won’t have enough money left. Because absolutely everything is very expensive.”

Cafés and restaurants, trips out of town, shopping, leisure activities and travelling at least once a year, meanwhile, are all seen as part of a “luxurious life” among this age group.

We also asked our randomly selected respondents whether they had ever had to give something up because they lacked the money. It turned out to be a very common experience.

Cost of living in Georgia

World.title: Preferential regime for Armenian exports to EU in response to Russian restrictions
World.content:
Preferential trade regime with the EU for Armenia

Customs duties on a wide range of goods exported from Armenia to the European Union will be temporarily suspended. The preferential trade regime is expected to remain in place for two years. The European Parliament approved the European Commission’s proposal the previous day.

A total of 583 MEPs supported the application of Autonomous Trade Measures to Armenian goods. Forty-nine voted against, while 39 abstained.

“This step is prompted by the restrictions that Russia has imposed since May 2026 on several key Armenian export goods,” the decision says.

The EU Council must now approve the regulation. It will enter into force afterwards.

The EU initiative aims to support Armenia’s economy and create additional opportunities for local exporters to access the EU market.

The Armenian Centre for Socio-Economic Research (ACSES) analysed the potential implications of the decision. The centre’s experts described the scale of trade liberalisation with the European Union as significant. At the same time, they believe further developments will depend on several key factors:

“Can Armenia overcome entrenched perceptions of dependence and restructure its export profile? Much will depend on the next steps taken by Armenian businesses and the government. Creating new, comprehensive logistics infrastructure is a necessity of the times.”

Armenia’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs and International Trade believes the temporary trade preferences “will help diversify Armenia’s foreign trade, expand Armenian goods’ access to the EU market, and further deepen trade and economic cooperation with the European Union”.

Context

In early July 2026, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen announced in Yerevan that the EU could introduce autonomous trade measures for Armenia.

“I am here today to state clearly: if Russia closes its market to Armenian products, the EU will open the doors to its consumer market of 450 million people,” she said.

Since May, Russia has banned imports of Armenian fruit, vegetables, fish products, alcohol and many other goods. Russian authorities cited their alleged failure to meet quality standards. Meanwhile, the European Union, which has stricter standards, has decided to help Armenia.

Ursula von der Leyen said the autonomous trade measures would liberalise around 80% of Armenian exports. In other words, that share of goods would become exempt from customs duties.оло 80% армянского экспорта. То есть такой объем товаров будет освобожден от таможенных пошлин.

Details of the European Parliament’s decision

European lawmakers approved a proposal to liberalise exports of goods marked “Made in Armenia”. The decision will cover 324 product categories. According to EU estimates, Armenian businesses will save a total of €5.4 million over two years. This is the amount they would otherwise have had to pay in customs duties.

To benefit from the preferential terms:

Armenian products must comply with EU regulations on the origin of goods and customs procedures;

Armenia must cooperate with EU authorities to verify the origin of goods and prevent possible fraud.

In addition, the EU plans to introduce duty-free import quotas for eight types of Armenian agricultural products. The list includes apricots, grapes, plums, peaches, cherries, strawberries, cucumbers and pears.

The European Union believes that Russia’s restrictions have significantly limited Armenian goods’ access to their established market:

“The situation has had a severe impact on small and medium-sized enterprises, including agricultural producers, threatening Armenia’s economic resilience.”

The preferential regime will cover 99% of fresh agricultural exports and 91% of beverage exports.

Against the backdrop of these changes, the EU also intends to introduce safeguards for its own market:

“These mechanisms will allow the European Union to intervene if a rise in imports from Armenia negatively affects European producers.”

The European Commission may fully or partially suspend the regime if an increase in imports from Armenia destabilises the EU market. It may also do so if Yerevan fails to meet the agreed requirements.

Expert opinion

Experts at the Armenian Centre for Socio-Economic Research say the project approved by the European Parliament aims to reduce pressure on Armenia’s economy. According to their calculations, potential export losses in 2026 could reach $260 million.

However, goods that will receive temporary exemptions from customs duties account for a significant share of Armenia’s total exports:

“In 2025, Armenia exported around $3.5 billion worth of goods. More than two-thirds of this amount falls under the proposed preferential regime.”

The experts believe that the EU’s preferential trade regime, combined with business support programmes implemented by the Armenian government, could change the structure of the country’s exports. Exporters that previously supplied goods to Russia may redirect their products to the EU.

However, after analysing the tariff quotas that will apply to agricultural products, economists noted that some quotas are lower than actual export figures:

“For example, the quota for plums amounts to only 13% of actual exports, while the quota for apricots stands at 16%.”

In their view, these low quotas are due less to the EU’s desire to protect its own market than to the methodology used to calculate them.

In particular, the quotas were determined using export data from companies registered in Armenia. The information comes from the UN Comtrade database. However, the calculation did not account for the fact that individuals carry out a significant share of fruit and vegetable exports.

“Perhaps our government should have defended the interests of Armenian exporters of fresh fruit and vegetables more consistently,” the publication says.

Preferential trade regime with the EU for Armenia

World.title: Former Georgian security chief Grigol Liluashvili jailed for 13 years for corruption
World.content:
Georgia’s ex-security chief jailed

Former head of Georgia’s State Security Service Grigol Liluashvili was sentenced to 13 years in prison on 16 September on corruption charges. The ruling was handed down by Tbilisi City Court judge Nino Tarashvili.

Liluashvili headed the State Security Service for more than five years, from October 2019 to December 2025. He was found guilty on all four charges. Liluashvili denied the charges.

Charges against Grigol Liluashvili

Grigol Liluashvili was arrested on 23 December 2025.

He was accused of “accepting particularly large bribes as part of a group acting by prior agreement”.

Prosecutors charged Liluashvili over four separate bribery cases.

● The first dates back to October 2022. According to prosecutors, Liluashvili received $1m from Turkish investor Cagatay Ulker through then Deputy Economy Minister Romeo Mikautadze, who is also in custody. Prosecutors said the money was paid in exchange for lobbying for a wind farm construction project.

● According to the second case, in February 2022 Liluashvili, again through Romeo Mikautadze, demanded and received 1.5m lari (about $580,000) from Giorgi Khazhalia, founder of Express Service 2008, in exchange for helping the company secure tenders for household gasification projects.

● The third case concerned call centres operating in Georgia between 2021 and 2023. According to prosecutors, Liluashvili took bribes from “a small number of call centres that remained in Georgia” through his relative Sandro Liluashvili.

Prosecutors allege that Liluashvili received about $1.365m in connection with the call centres, with Sandro Liluashvili acting as an intermediary.

● The fourth case involved Kakha Gvantseladze, former director of the Tbilisi City Hall agency responsible for managing kindergartens.

According to prosecutors, Liluashvili used his official position to protect Gvantseladze’s alleged corrupt activities in exchange for payment. Prosecutors said Gvantseladze received particularly large sums in kickbacks from private companies in return for awarding them procurement contracts for kindergartens.

Georgia’s ex-security chief jailed

World.title: MOL commissions new solar park and battery storage facility in Hungary
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 18. Hungary-based energy company MOL Group has commissioned a 37.4 MWp solar park and a 20 MW battery energy storage facility with a storage capacity of 40 MWh at its Algyő site in Hungary, the company said.

The new facilities are expected to strengthen the energy independence of MOL’s operations, improve electricity supply flexibility and cut CO2 emissions by around 13,000 tonnes annually.

“Recent experience has highlighted the importance of managing intraday fluctuations in electricity generation. This is what we are achieving by commissioning our latest energy storage facility. The investment simultaneously promotes sustainability, security of supply and economic competitiveness: green electricity generated from our own sources reduces our reliance on external energy supplies, while the battery storage system contributes to the stability of the national power grid,” said György Bacsa, Group Chief Strategic Officer of MOL Group.

The new solar park, combined with MOL’s existing power generation facilities at Algyő, can fully cover the electricity demand of the company’s operations in the region. Its annual output is equivalent to the electricity consumption of around 22,500 households in Hungary’s Csongrád-Csanád County.

The 20 MW battery storage system is designed to help balance fluctuations in electricity generation from weather-dependent renewable sources. Its 40 MWh storage capacity is equivalent to the annual electricity consumption of approximately 7,300 average households in the county.

MOL said the project forms part of its long-term SHAPE TOMORROW strategy, under which the company is expanding renewable generation and energy storage capacity as part of its decarbonization efforts.

The solar park was built by ALTEO Plc., in which MOL and its partners hold a 73.8% stake. ALTEO operates around 115 MW of renewable generation capacity from wind, solar, hydropower and biogas facilities.

Following the commissioning of the new project, MOL operates nine solar parks in Hungary with a combined capacity of 405 MW. The company also operates two energy storage facilities with total capacity of 80 MWh and plans to reach 500 MWh of storage capacity in Hungary by 2030.

In Croatia, MOL currently operates two solar parks with a combined capacity of 10 MW, while a third facility planned for next year is expected to bring the country’s total capacity to 23 MW.

Overall, MOL Group’s photovoltaic capacity in the region has reached 415 MWp, with the company estimating that its solar facilities contribute to an annual reduction of around 160,000 tonnes of CO2 emissions.

MOL Group’s expansion of renewable generation and energy storage is part of its SHAPE TOMORROW strategy, which targets carbon neutrality across all scopes by 2050 and calls for low-carbon projects to account for 30–40% of total capital expenditure between 2025 and 2030. The company has been expanding its photovoltaic portfolio in Hungary through both new developments and acquisitions, while also increasing the use of renewable electricity and developing other low-carbon technologies.

World.title: Kyrgyzstan continues asphalt paving on road in Jalal-Abad region
World.content:
Photo: Press Service of the Ministry of Transport and Communications of Kyrgyzstan

BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 18. Asphalt paving works are continuing on the Kashka-Terek - Katranky road in Suzak district of Jalal-Abad region of Kyrgyzstan.

According to the press service of the Ministry of Transport and Communications of Kyrgyzstan, the 2026 title list provides for asphalt paving of a 5-kilometer section of the road.

"Active asphalt paving works are continuing on the Kashka-Terek – Katranky road in Suzak district of Jalal-Abad region," the statement said.

At present, the works are being carried out by Road Maintenance Facility No. 22 in accordance with the established schedule. Asphalt paving of a 1-kilometer section has been completed to date.

The repair of the road is expected to provide safer and more convenient travel conditions for the local population and improve transport links between settlements in the district.

Road construction and repair works are being carried out under the supervision of the Ministry of Transport and Communications of Kyrgyzstan.

Meanwhile, Kyrgyzstan has been carrying out road construction and rehabilitation projects as part of efforts to improve domestic transport connectivity and road infrastructure. Road maintenance and rehabilitation activities are implemented across the country under state programs and annual infrastructure plans.

Jalal-Abad region is located in the western part of Kyrgyzstan and has an extensive network of roads connecting its districts and settlements. The condition of local roads is relevant to the movement of residents and the transportation of goods between populated areas.

The rehabilitation of local road sections is aimed at maintaining transport links between settlements and improving road conditions. Such projects are generally implemented by specialized road maintenance organizations under the supervision of the Ministry of Transport and Communications.

World.title: Kyrgyzstan and Iraq discuss development of international road transport
World.content:
Photo: Press Service of the Ministry of Transport and Communications of Kyrgyzstan

BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 18. Kyrgyzstan and Iraq discussed the development of cooperation in the field of international road transport.

This was reported in a statement issued by the Ministry of Transport and Communications of Kyrgyzstan following a meeting on September 17 between Deputy Minister Kubanychbek Turganbaev and Chargé d’Affaires of the Republic of Iraq in Kazakhstan Jaber Al-Tamimi.

"During the meeting, the parties discussed issues related to the development of cooperation between Kyrgyzstan and Iraq in the field of international road transport," the statement said.

As noted, Kyrgyzstan and Iraq currently do not have a bilateral agreement regulating international road transport.

In this regard, the Kyrgyz side prepared a draft of the relevant agreement and sent it to the Iraqi side for consideration.

The parties also considered opportunities to develop international transport routes connecting Kyrgyzstan and Iraq through Uzbekistan, Turkmenistan and Iran.

Particular attention was paid to visa-related issues. Kyrgyz citizens currently obtain Iraqi visas in Astana. In view of the complexity of the visa procedure and the single-entry nature of the visas, the Kyrgyz side proposed considering the possibility of issuing one-year multiple-entry driver visas to international freight carriers.

Following the meeting, the parties expressed readiness to intensify cooperation in the transport sector, expand international freight transportation and jointly develop practical steps in the relevant areas.

World.title: Kazakhstan’s Tokayev receives credentials from new ambassadors
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 18. President of Kazakhstan Kassym-Jomart Tokayev received credentials from the newly appointed ambassadors, the presedential press service announced.

The ceremony was held at the Palace of Independence in Astana and brought together representatives of the eight countries newly appointed to diplomatic posts in Kazakhstan.

The credentials were presented by Egyptian Ambassador Sameh Shehata, Swiss Ambassador Christine Honegger Zolotukhin, Estonian Ambassador Marje Luup, Omani Ambassador Salah Salim Jaboub, Hungarian Ambassador Ferenc Csombos , Guinea-Bissau Ambassador Braima Embalo, Nigerian Ambassador Joseph Olusola Iji and Danish Ambassador Lars Thuesen.

In his welcoming remarks, Tokayev reaffirmed Kazakhstan's commitment to a peaceful foreign policy.

"Today is indeed an important day - both for you, as representatives of your respective countries, and for the Republic of Kazakhstan. I am convinced that we should work together, as Kazakhstan is a peace-loving state. We pursue a balanced and constructive foreign policy. We seek to create favorable conditions for carrying out reforms in the country. I would like to assure you that the doors of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and state bodies, including the President's residence, will always be open to you, as we need to stand together in this very unsettled and turbulent world," Tokayev said.

World.title: Azerbaijan, Turkmenistan explore new frontiers for energy cooperation
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 18. Azerbaijan and Turkmenistan discussed energy cooperation, joint international exhibitions and events, as well as opportunities to exchange expertise.

This was stated in a post by Azerbaijani Ambassador to Turkmenistan Gismat Gozalov following his meeting with Nazar Atajanov, Director of the Turkmen Energy Forum.

"Turkmen Energy Forum organizes Turkmenistan's annual Oil & Gas of Turkmenistan (OGT) International Exhibition and Conference," the publication says.

According to the information, in the course of the meeting, the sides also exchanged views on opportunities to share experience and expertise in the energy sector.

Meanwhile, Azerbaijan and Turkmenistan have been expanding practical cooperation in the energy, transport and Caspian Sea sectors, with the relationship increasingly focused on commercial and infrastructure projects. The two countries have also been strengthening contacts between their energy companies and institutions, while cooperation in the Caspian is creating additional opportunities for trade and transportation links between Central Asia, Azerbaijan and European markets.

Energy cooperation is also reflected in the growing participation of Azerbaijani companies in Turkmenistan's international energy events. Azerbaijan's state oil company SOCAR will serve as the Premier Partner of the 31st International Conference and Exhibition “Oil & Gas of Turkmenistan - OGT 2026,” scheduled for October 21-23 in Ashgabat. The event will bring together energy companies, investors, financial institutions and technology providers, with the 2026 agenda covering investment opportunities in Turkmenistan's energy sector, the Galkynysh gas field, gas export routes, the TAPI pipeline, Caspian offshore projects, gas processing, digitalization and methane reduction. SOCAR's role highlights the company's participation in Turkmenistan's international energy dialogue and the broader development of commercial ties between the two Caspian countries.

Maritime cooperation provides another practical dimension to bilateral relations. On June 22, 2026, Azerbaijan presented the “Dostlug” oil tanker to Turkmenistan in a ceremony attended online by Presidents Ilham Aliyev and Serdar Berdimuhamedov. Built at Baku Shipyard, the 141-meter vessel has a deadweight of 7,875 tons and is designed to transport petroleum products. The tanker also complements broader efforts to develop transport and logistics links across the Caspian, including routes connecting Turkmenistan with Azerbaijan and onward markets.

World.title: Uzbekistan, SparkLabs sign deal to accelerate startups in South Korea
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 18. On September 18, Uzbekistan and South Korean venture firm SparkLabs Inc. signed an agreement in Uzbekistan to launch an acceleration program for Uzbek startups seeking to enter the South Korean market.

This was reflected in the statement by the Ministry of Digital Technologies of Uzbekistan, following talks between Uzbek Deputy Digital Technologies Minister Jamol Makhsudov, IT Park Uzbekistan Executive Director Jahongir Rajabov and SparkLabs co-founder Bernard Moon.

The joint acceleration program is scheduled to launch in the fourth quarter of 2026 and will focus on selecting and preparing promising Uzbek technology startups for expansion into South Korea.

“The program will create additional opportunities for Uzbek startups to gain international expertise, connect with investors and venture organizations, and enter the South Korean market,” IT Park said.

The sides discussed the startup selection process, the format of the acceleration program and opportunities for participants to establish connections with South Korea’s broader venture ecosystem.

Under the program, Uzbek startups will receive support in entering the Korean market and gain access to potential investors and venture capital organizations, including TIPS and Mirae Asset, as well as other participants in the country’s investment ecosystem.

The agreement provides for cooperation in identifying promising technology projects, preparing startups for international expansion and facilitating their entry into the South Korean market.

The parties also discussed expanding cooperation through international technology events. Moon is expected to participate in ICT Week Uzbekistan 2026.

The partnership with SparkLabs is intended to give Uzbek startups access to international expertise, mentoring and business contacts while creating additional opportunities to attract investment and expand into foreign markets.

SparkLabs, founded in Seoul in 2012, is a South Korean startup accelerator and venture capital firm focused on seed- and early-stage companies. The firm provides investment, acceleration and mentorship and supports startups seeking to enter international markets. According to the company, SparkLabs has supported and invested in more than 320 startups and operates inbound and outbound programs connecting international technology projects with the South Korean market and Korean startups with overseas markets.

World.title: North Melbourne's 1020-day winning streak over after shock loss to Hawthorn
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

North Melbourne's record 32-matchwinning streak is over after Hawthorn pulled off a massive AFLW upset.

The Hawks' 4.8 (32) to 3.7 (25) win on Friday night in Cairns is their greatest win since they joined the women's league in 2022.

The Kangaroos' sequence of straight wins is the longest in AFL, VFL and AFLW history. They had not been beaten since 2023, going undefeated in their 2024 and 2025 premiership runs.

Hawthorn's Jacqueline Dupuy said the feeling was "unreal".

"In my head, I was just panicking, thinking, 'How long have we got?' I reckon I looked at the bench three or four times in the last 90 seconds, just praying for the siren," Dupuy told ABC Sport.

"It was pretty unreal when it finally went. And to be able to look around at these girls I love so much and just see the sheer joy and feel that myself was amazing."

Hawthorn's win was made even more impressive given the absence of captain Emily Bates, who went down with an ACL rupture last weekend.

The triumph came off the back of relentless pressure.

North led by 10 points at the main break in blustery and humid Cairns conditions, but Hawthorn's Mikayla Williamson kicked the only goal of the third term, pulling the match to within three points.

Four straight behinds gave Hawthorn the lead in the last term for the first time since the first quarter. Cairns native Jacqueline Dupuy then kicked a goal to give Hawthorn a seven-point buffer at nine minutes.

Jacqueline Dupuy of the Hawks said the win was unreal. (Getty: Emily Barker)

But North was not done, with Blaithin Bogue kicking a goal against the run of play.

Inside the last two minutes, Hawks ruck Lucy Wales snapped the sealing goal.

"It's just a credit to the kind of player Lucy is. She's clutch. She is one of the most consistent players for us and I just feel like it was very fitting that she was able to kick that winning goal," Dupuy said.

North's last loss was the 2023 grand final against Brisbane. The Kangaroos then started the 2024 season with a win and a draw, before starting their historic streak.

Friday night's tally was also their lowest score since 2023.

It is a great start to the weekend for the Hawks, ahead of Saturday's AFL preliminary final against Brisbane, when they will also start as underdogs against the two-time defending premiers.

The AFLW victory puts the team just outside the top four.

"It's always tough to go to sleep after a game, and certainly feeling pretty jacked right now," Dupuy said.

"But I'm sure we'll get a rest and go up again in six days, which would be exciting to head down to Geelong."

With AAP

World.title: Australian finalists for Prince William's Earthshot Prize 'nervous but excited'
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Indigenous rangers responsible for one of the largest cultural burning programs in the world have been named finalists for Prince William's Earthshot Prize.

The prize, which comes with $1.9 million to support each winner's work, aims to reward environmental projects "that will drive significant progress towards repairing the planet".

The alliance celebrated its 10th anniversary with a conference at Uluru in 2024. (Supplied: IDA/ Salty Davenport)

Samantha Murray, CEO of the Indigenous Desert Alliance (IDA), said she was proud the network of 70 ranger teams across Central Australia had been given global recognition.

"To be recognised on such a massive scale is something that we work really hard at, to make sure that desert rangers are known, they're heard, they're seen."

More than 150 judges selected the IDA from among 7,000 nominations from 169 countries, with Ms Murray admitting she was "slightly nervous, but really excited" about the alliance's prospects.

In the past four years the alliance has engaged 1,300 Indigenous participants, trained 885 rangers and managed fuel loads and restored biodiversity across 145 million hectares of land — an area four times the size of Germany.

Sam Murray says desert rangers are integral to climate talks. (ABC: Nicholas Martyr)

Ms Murray, a proud Yilka, Wongutha and Nyoongar woman, said the Right Way Fire program, which combines cultural and Western ways of burning, was key to their nomination for the prize.

The rangers conduct targeted burns to create a mosaic of vegetation which reduces fuel loads, improves native habitats and lessens the risk of large, destructive bushfires.

"Those ways of reading country are when to burn, who to burn by the right people, what times, what weather, what country," Ms Murray said.

She said alliance, formed more than a decade ago, relied on land management practices developed and passed down over tens of thousands of years.

"It really just helped to elevate the way my desert people have been connecting for a very, very long time across different country," she said.

"It's really big about making sure we're continuing that caring for country from our ancestors and our elders, for ourselves and our children."

Nyikina Mangala Rangers from the Kimberley region conduct burning. (Supplied: IDA/ Ewan Noakes)

Prince impressed by 'scale' of IDA's work: CEO

Rangers across the desert carry out culturally informed fire management. (Supplied: IDA/ Ngurrara Rangers)

Prince William created the Earthshot Prize in 2020, saying he wanted to reward new ideas and technologies for tackling climate change.

Earthshot Prize CEO Jason Knauf said the prince would be among those who decided who would win in Mumbai in November.

"I think he was absolutely amazed by just the scale [of IDA's work]," he said.

"To have one initiative that is protecting 2.7 million square kilometres — we haven't seen anything like that in the previous six years."

The first Earthshot award ceremony was held in 2021 in London. (Supplied: Reuters/ Henry Nicholls)

The IDA is one of three finalists in Earthshot's "protect and restore nature" category.

It is up against the Himalayan country Bhutan, which has enshrined environmental protection in its constitution, and the Yellowstone to Yukon Conservation Initiative which protects habitats along the Rocky Mountains on the Canada-US border.

Jason Knauf says there is strong competition for the 2026 prize. (ABC: Scott Preston)

Mr Knauf said investing in the knowledge of Indigenous people was key to meeting the global commitment of protecting and conserving 30 per cent of land and sea by 2030.

"Indigenous communities right around the world who are protecting a disproportionate share of the land that we all rely on for our economy … have the deep knowledge about what is going to work in the face of climate change."

Earthshot Prize announcement The Earthshot Prize is an ambitious environmental program that aims to find new ideas and technologies around the world to tackle climate change.

If the IDA won, Ms Murray said the funds would boost the alliance's fire protection work, as well as increase the grants available for projects such as trips on country for intergenerational knowledge transfer or ranger exchanges.

She would like to see more desert communities having a "visible presence" in global conversations about climate change.

"We can't ignore the impacts of climate change and how it's impacting and shaping country a little bit differently and making it much harder for desert rangers out there," she said.

'Loudest voice in any room'

The Queensland Indigenous Womens Ranger Network protects the Great Barrier Reef. (Supplied: BBC)

Australia has been a strong contender for the prize in the past, with the Indigenous Women Rangers Network in Queensland winning the "revive our oceans" category in 2022.

Local finalists have also included the world's first fully upcycled skyscraper Quay Quarter Tower, the Sydney Institute of Marine Science's living seawalls project, and an Australian-owned cattle and sheep feed supplement which used seaweed.

The great desert skink is being protected. (Supplied: IDA/Karenza Sunfly)

Mr Knauf said he hoped the recognition would mean the work of the Indigenous Desert Alliance would be shared worldwide.

"We get our whole global network behind them to scale, replicate their work and really champion what they're doing on a global stage," he said.

"We say that we want our finalist to be the loudest voice in any room that they walk into and we help them to achieve that."

World.title: Adelaide workers expected to bear brunt of Bendigo Bank cuts
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

A union says 137 workers at the Bendigo and Adelaide Bank are slated for redundancy as part of an ongoing company restructure, but the company says its plans are "yet to be finalised".

They would form part of a total of 299 job changes across the bank's Consumer Lending Operations and Customer Care divisions.

ABC News understands that the bank's Adelaide staff would be impacted more than its other city and regional workforces.

That restructure began in April, when Bendigo Bank announced partnerships with two international companies: IT service provider Infosys, and agentic AI company Genpact.

In a statement the union said about 445 Bendigo Bank positions had been "lost or reduced through restructures" since January 2025 and that forthcoming losses had "a strong documented relationship to AI, automation or broader technological change".

"The bank has told us that as a partnership with an offshore technological company, that it's making efficiencies through these redundancies," ASU SA-NT branch secretary Ella Waters said.

"We're yet to see what that means for whether or not these workers are going to be completely replaced by AI, but we're extremely concerned that, in the name of technological advancement, hundreds of jobs are being cut."

Ella Waters is concerned Bendigo Bank jobs will be sent offshore. (ABC News )

A Bendigo Bank spokesperson referred ABC News to an April statement announcing the partnerships with Infosys and Genpact, saying the bank "continues to review its business operations and processes".

The spokesperson did not confirm whether AI would replace workers.

"The detailed design for all impacted areas is yet to be finalised," the spokesperson said.

"The process and operational improvements expected to be delivered will lead to workforce changes that will impact our people.

"The bank is committed to supporting all employees through this period of change, including exploring opportunities for redeployment for those whose roles will no longer be required, where possible."

World.title: At least three dead in Philippines school shooting
World.content:
At least three students are dead and eight others injured following a shooting at a high school in the southern Philippines, authorities have confirmed.

The announcement came after the country's education department revealed the incident occurred at Banga National High School in Banga in the province of South Cotabato.

Provincial Governor Reynaldo Tamayo told Reuters that the shooter was among the three people killed.

Banga Mayor Albert Palencia later confirmed the shooter was 16 years old and that four of the eight people injured were in a critical condition. The victims were aged between 14 and 17.

"The suspect supposedly sat beside his friends and told them to go home, 'Because after lunch, I will be executing my plan,'" Mr Palencia told Reuters.

"His friends laughed because the shooter was a known joker."

In a video posted to Facebook and verified by AFP, a man can be seen carrying what appears to be an injured child from the school, rushing him into the sidecar of a waiting motorbike.

In another, a teacher speaking in a local dialect could be heard saying there were two shooters and a student insisting they were outsiders.

The local Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Office said school classes had been suspended across the Banga municipality.

The incident follows two shootings since June at schools in the south of the country.

School shootings were previously rare in the Philippines, but the incidents led to nationwide live shooter drills being conducted this month.

The incident marks the third school shooting in the south-east Asian country since June. (AFP: Philippe Turping/PhotoNonStop)

Last month a student live-streamed himself shooting and killing another student in a classroom in Zamboanga before taking ‌his own life.

In June, at least three students were killed and about 20 others injured an attack at a public high school in Tacloban when two classmates opened fire on campus.

The latest incident came just days after three other people were killed and 15 injured in a separate shooting in Cotabato during the first parliamentary election held in the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao.

The Philippines has relatively strict gun ownership regulations, including background checks and psychological evaluation requirements, although illegal firearms remain in circulation.

Mr Tamayo urged parents to ensure guns were kept out of reach of minors.

"We need to be responsible in storing firearms. Gun owners, in particular, must make sure that minors do not have access to them," he told Reuters.

"We cannot expect a handful of security personnel to monitor thousands of students. We need to work together because otherwise this will be very difficult for us to address."

AFP/Reuters

World.title: Federal finance minister threatens to bypass NT government on funding
World.content:
Federal Finance Minister Katy Gallagher has met with the Northern Territory's acting chief minister over concerns the NT government is not spending Commonwealth money where it is needed.

With more than 70 per cent of the NT government's revenue coming from the Commonwealth, Ms Gallagher travelled to Darwin today to take issue with how some of the funding was being distributed.

Ms Gallagher said she and Indigenous Australians Minister Malarndirri McCarthy had initially organised to meet with Chief Minister Lia Finocchiaro, who is now on leave, and instead met with Acting Chief Minister Gerard Maley.

"We had hoped to meet with the Chief Minister," she said.

"We made that appointment some two weeks ago and the reason behind that was we were certainly, from the Commonwealth's point of view, experiencing some concerns about how particular programs are being run."

Malarndirri McCarthy and Katy Gallagher met with Gerard Maley this week after Lia Finocchiaro went on leave. (ABC News: Pete Garnish)

Ms Gallagher pointed to areas such as disaster relief, domestic violence service provision and housing, where she believed the tough-on-crime NT government had dropped the ball.

The federal parliament heard last month that $330 million allocated under a Commonwealth housing agreement had not been spent, and the NT government was seeking to reduce its 10-year housing target from 2,700 to 1,800.

Ms Gallagher also said the federal government was concerned a lack of money hitting the ground was exacerbating social dysfunction, as the NT goes backwards on seven Closing the Gap targets — the worst performance of any jurisdiction.

NT goes backwards on Closing the Gap targets The NT government has released its Aboriginal Affairs framework as the territory goes backwards on several Closing the Gap targets.

A string of serious crime incidents have occurred in the territory this month, including one where two boys, aged eight and 11, allegedly held up two Darwin businesses at knifepoint while wearing balaclavas.

"The money that we are investing is to reach the outcome that we want, which is to provide better services and better supports in housing, in particular in relation to overcrowding, in domestic, family and sexual violence, to make sure the service system is able to cope with the level of violence that exists right across the country," Ms Gallagher said.

"So when we're seeing delays or reductions in the Northern Territory's own expenditure, that concerns us.

"That was why we wanted to put it on the table — we wanted to come up to the chief minister and say 'Look, these are all of our concerns, it's across a number of portfolios'."

Ms Gallagher said if the NT government did not act, the Commonwealth would bypass it and deliver more funding directly to frontline services.

"If we are going to ... not see the money getting to where it's needed ... we would look to directly fund those organisations," she said.

Katy Gallagher says the federal government isn't afraid to pull funding from the NT government and give it directly to service providers. (ABC News: Pete Garnish)

"The Commonwealth is serious that we are not going to see our investments sit there and not get progressed.

"In housing, we want the houses built, in domestic, family and sexual violence, we want the service system supported."

Before the meeting, Mr Maley said it was "a bit rich" for Ms Gallagher to "come up here and tell us what to do".

"They need to have a good, hard look at themselves in relation to the non-government organisations they fund and the funding that they put in to the Northern Territory and where that money is spent," he said.

Gerard Maley says the federal government should look more closely at the services it funds directly. (ABC News: Pete Garnish)

"We have asked for a full audit in relation to that money many times and it has fallen on deaf ears.

" They need to have a good, hard look at themselves because they are spending money in my view where it should not be spent. "

Disaster funding not applied for

The Northern Territory experienced a series of natural disasters over the most recent wet season, including Cyclone Fina and floods which caused the displacement of hundreds of people.

Ms Gallagher said the NT government still had not applied for disaster relief funding for events that occurred last year.

"Some of those disasters happened in November 2025, so it's been some 10 months, and we're still waiting for the paperwork," she said.

"What that means is those communities are still waiting for Commonwealth funds to flow under those arrangements."

NT community still without key services months after floods Months after record flooding, Nauiyu / Daly River remains significantly damaged and without key services.

But Ms Gallagher said "we made some progress in the meeting on that front".

"The Northern Territory government [is] committed to having the paperwork for various projects they want funded under that category in to the Commonwealth by Christmas, but it has taken a long time to get here," she said.

A spokesperson from the Office of the Chief Minister said the meeting was "productive" but "it was clear the federal ministers had come with closed minds and pre-prepared press lines".

"The CLP government will continue to focus on reducing crime, rebuilding the economy and restoring lifestyle and leave the carping and hand-wringing to Canberra," they said.

World.title: Hat-draw to decide mayoral contest ends in confusion
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Imagine deciding who would become prime minister or premier by drawing a name out of a hat.

As unbelievable as the scenario may sound, it can be a reality in local government.

The election of a mayor for the Clarence Valley, in northern NSW, descended into a farce this week when a four-four tied vote led to an attempt to determine the winner by just such a method.

But a problem arose when those involved could not agree whether the name drawn out of the hat was the winner, or the person eliminated.

Dominic O'Sullivan said those involved should have had a clear understanding of the process. (Supplied: Charles Sturt University)

Charles Sturt University political science professor Dominic O'Sullivan said it was an unusual situation, but the confusion could have been avoided.

"It does happen from time to time and that's why this procedure of drawing names from a hat is stipulated," he said.

“In some elections it might be the tossing of a coin.

"A very simple Google search by any member of the public will find the fact sheet from the NSW government that explains how all this is supposed to work.

"I think the confusion arose because the returning officer misinterpreted the regulation and said the name drawn out was the person to be eliminated. That's not correct.

"The fact that neither the general manager, who was acting as returning officer, nor a single councillor seems to have understood the process is slightly odd and unusual.

“People need to be better prepared than obviously was the case in this instance."

Councillor Peter Johnstone, who was installed as Clarence Valley Mayor earlier this week, has now resigned from the position.

The eight councillors who voted in the ballot. (Supplied: Clarence Valley Council)

The council has released a statement saying councillors had "resolved to seek legal advice within 14 days to ensure the process for electing a Mayor to fill the vacant position complies with all procedural and legal requirements".

Dr O'Sullivan had some advice for them to consider before the next round of voting.

"The lesson for that council next time is 'read the rules," he said.

"I think voters in the Clarence Valley are entitled to expect a bit better than that."

World.title: Regional businesses alarmed as Australia limits working holiday visas
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Around a normally lively Far North Queensland backpackers' hostel, an unusually sombre mood lingers in the air.

Irish backpacker Fionnghuala Ni Fheinne feels uncertain about her future in Australia after a shake-up of Australia's working holiday visa program.

"If I'd known about this sooner, I would have looked at a different route," she said.

Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke announced the changes to Australia's migration system last night, including introducing a ballot system for working holiday makers.

Among the changes, third-year working holiday visas would be limited to 5,000 backpackers each year.

The tourism and hospitality sectors in regional Queensland said the change would have devastating impacts.

Ms Ni Fheinne's shock was shared by others on working holiday visas in Cairns.

"It's a little bit scary," German backpacker Philip De Broux said.

Philip De Broux is worried the changes will complicate his hopes of working in Australia for a second year. (ABC Far North: Rosanne Maloney)

Mr De Broux said the change may impact his hopes of a second year working in Australia.

"I love the country and I definitely want to stay here longer, but now it's more serious and there's more competition," he said.

"Now I know there are less places, which makes the competition even harder."

Peter McLeay is the owner of a Cairns backpackers hostel and a local restaurant. He said the announcement had thrown the business into chaos.

Peter McLeay says he feels betrayed by the government. (ABC Far North: Rosanne Maloney)

"To find out last night that a backpacker will have about a one-in-six chance of getting that third year after they do everything right is just devastating for us," he said.

" I've built this hostel business over the last 15 years … it's just basically my life's work up-ended overnight and I don't understand why. "

He said he felt betrayed by the government's decision, with backpackers making up about 90 per cent of his staff.

Peter McLeay says backpackers make up about 90 per cent of his staff. (ABC Far North: Rosanne Maloney)

"These are roles we just can't fill with Australians … we don't get Australians applying to be a hostel manager and [similar roles], so it's going to gut the entire hierarchy of the company," Mr McLeay said.

"Imagine, if in every friendship group, one person gets to stay out of about six [people], it's like an episode of Survivor or something," he said.

"It's just going to be horrible."

Other tourism businesses in Townsville shared the concerns.

Local resort chief executive Tim Richardson said it was hard to employ locals and working holiday makers filled a crucial part of the community's employment structure.

"Hospitality is tough by itself; we are very highly regulated and the hours aren't sexy for young employees anymore," he said.

Tourism Tropical North Queensland chief executive Mark Olsen said he was concerned the visa changes could make Australia less appealing for working holiday makers in general.

Mark Olsen says limiting the number of international workers will devastate the tourism economy. (ABC News: Baz Ruddick)

"We are seeing increasing cost pressures for Australia as a destination … compared to other destinations," he said.

"So to maintain our competitiveness … this is vital for us," he said.

Mr Olsen said the international workforce was a key part of the region's skill base and limiting their numbers would have devastating impacts for the tourism economy.

"Using working holiday makers as a solution to a housing crisis is a really blunt instrument," Mr Olsen said.

"We understand the capital cities are under pressure, but we would call on the federal government to reconsider.

"The downward pressure on second- and third-year numbers will impact the regions more than they impact the capital cities.

"These working holiday makers … play a vital role in our community. They put food on our tables; they're not taking the roofs off our heads."

Agriculture operations were also worried about what the visa changes meant for their industry.

David Groves, field manager at a tropical fruit farm north of Rockhampton, said focusing on backpackers would not solve the housing crisis.

"We don't really have a solution to the problem here, but we are creating some problems," Mr Groves said.

He said there would be a workforce shortfall.

David Groves says the changes will be especially hard on small and medium farms. (ABC Capricornia: Katrina Beavan)

"Obviously, we'll hire as many locals as we can, but it won't be enough to pick our entire crop and, if we can't get enough backpackers, that means fruit will fall on the ground and be wasted," Mr Groves said.

Backpacker Fionnghuala Ni Fheinne is considering other avenues that may allow her to continue working in Australia.

"I'm frantically searching to see if I should [apply for a skilled visa]," she said.

"I have a degree in education if I should go down the skilled visa route instead, but it's kind of leaving it very last minute for me.

"We do a lot for this country; we work very hard. There's a lot of doctors here. There's a lot of nurses that aren't Australian and I just found it very shocking, to be honest, and I'm hoping that they change their mind."

World.title: Mini-Times Square? New digital billboard planned in centre of Queen Street Mall
World.content:
NationalQueenslandBrisbane development Mini-Times Square? New digital billboard planned in centre of Queen Street Mall William Davis September 18, 2026 — 8:14pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The Times Square-ification of Queen Street Mall is set to continue, with plans progressing for another large electronic billboard. An application to install a new roof supporting the advertising feature on a deteriorating building were lodged with Brisbane City Council in September. According to one expert, the proposal raised questions about the future of public spaces in Brisbane and how digital technology should be managed. A new roof with an attached digital billboard for advertising is planned at 136 Queen Street in Queen Street Mall. William Davis The two-storey complex at 136 Queen Street comprises a Telstra Shop, as well as Off Ya Tree tattoos and body piercings and various food and drink outlets including Boost Juice.



According to the application, its roof had deteriorated significantly due to water damage, fungal decay and termite activity. “While the central structural spine continues to provide support, the overall condition indicates that the roof framing is nearing the end of its functional lifespan,” it says. An artist impressing on the plans for the Telstra building at 136 Queen Street in Queen Street Mall. The application requests approval for a replacement, with an artist impression showing a large digital screen erected on the corner opposite Hungry Jacks. The application also seeks approval for a “digital room” to maintain the sign.



Similar electronic billboards are already installed above the KFC and Optus shop, both located on the same intersection. Another large screen also hangs from a steel frame further up the mall outside Uptown shopping centre. Marcus Foth is professor of urban informatics at QUT’s school of design. He has researched the impacts and potential of screens in shared spaces. “The proposed Queen Street Mall screen raises a broader question about public value,” he said. “The problem is that the technology’s possibilities are much broader than the way it is commonly deployed.



“A screen can support digital placemaking and public culture, or it can primarily function as advertising infrastructure.” There are multiple public screens now through Queen Street Mall, above KFC, Optus and next to Uptown. Rhett Hammerton Foth said the fact people using public space couldn’t choose to turn off a billboard or change the channel meant planners had a responsibility to think about how and where they were deployed. “This is particularly important for an ... environment such as Queen Street Mall,” he said. “Large digital displays can add to light pollution and glare, but there are also accessibility and health considerations.



“Excessive brightness, rapid animation and flashing or high-contrast content can make public spaces difficult for people with sensory sensitivities, and particular flashing patterns can trigger seizures in people with photosensitive epilepsy.” He pointed to Melbourne’s Federation Square as an example of how large public screens can support cultural programming and community engagement, rather than functioning solely as advertising infrastructure. “Brisbane will undoubtedly have more digital infrastructure in its public spaces. The challenge is ensuring that we don’t confuse having more screens with becoming a better digital city,” Foth said. Plans for a screen above the Telstra shop were lodged with council in April, 2025. “The sign is in keeping with the character of the local environment and supports its role as a major retail and activity hub,” the application at the time said.



A spokesperson for the lord mayor’s office declined to comment on the merits of the proposal, saying it would be assessed by independent planning officers. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: WA nurses threaten strike action as government delays patient ratio rollout
World.content:
NationalWAIndustrial relations WA nurses threaten strike action as government delays patient ratio rollout Sophie Fenna and and Michael Philipps September 18, 2026 — 8:05pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

WA’s peak nursing union has warned of impending strike action after the organisation was told that nurse and midwife-to-patient ratios, due to be implemented by the state government this month, have been postponed. The proposed rollout of the third phase of ratios was scheduled to be in place by September 21, but Australian Nursing and Midwifery Federation WA state secretary Romina Raschilla said members had recently been told the implementation had been rescheduled. Nurses and Midwives rally at WA Parliament House and Dumas House in 2022. Hamish Hastie “Last Thursday we had a meeting with the chief nurse midwifery officer, and she advised us that the nurse midwife patient ratios that were due to be implemented on the 21st of September have been halted,” she said. “This was going to affect over 90 wards in the metropolitan public hospitals, and it’ll affect a lot of nurses and midwives, and also a lot of patients.



“Our members are really angry. They want to strike right now, but there is a process that needs to take place.” The third phase of the rollout was set to address particular wards, including geriatrics, some pediatrics, neonatal and other specialties, following the completed first two phases. Raschilla said ratios assist with the care that is delivered to the most vulnerable people in the community. “When that doesn’t occur, then the nurses and midwives have got more patients than they should have, and it is very difficult to provide that excellent care that each nurse and midwife wants to provide to their patient,” she said. “If we decide to strike or rally, we will ensure that it is done in accordance with the Industrial Relations Act, and we will also ensure that our patients do not suffer because nurses and midwives do not want a negative impact on their patients.



“However, if this is the only way that the government will pay attention, respect, and not disregard nurses and midwives. We will do whatever we need to do.” Related Article Updated

Hospitals in crisis Perth man suffering painful renal failure had to wait 12 hours to see doctor If industrial action goes ahead, it will be the first time WA nursing staff have committed to a work stoppage since thousands of members went on strike across WA in November 2022, with those at metropolitan hospitals gathering at Parliament House before marching to the health minister’s office at nearby Dumas House. WA Health Minister Meredith Hammat said the government has been delivering landmark nurse and midwife-to-patient ratios and will continue to do so. “I met with the Australian Nursing and Midwifery Federation this week and had a productive discussion about the next phase of the nurse and midwife-to-patient ratio rollout,” she said.



“The next phase will further expand the program to include Peel Health Campus, Murray District Hospital, Bentley Hospital, Kalamunda Hospital and Cockburn Health, and remaining metropolitan speciality medical and surgical wards, rehabilitation wards and emergency departments.” Hammat said the wards represent some of the most complex clinical environments within the hospital system, requiring careful planning. “This is a long-term, system-wide reform and it is important we take the necessary steps to get it right, for patients and for the health workforce,” she said. “Patient safety will always be the highest priority in any decision relating to the rollout of ratios. “It is also important that the needs of the health workforce are at the forefront of decision making, and our nurses and midwives can continue to provide safe care to the community of Western Australia.”



Raschilla said union members have little confidence in the government, and it is diminishing at a rapid rate, which is going to affect the healthcare provided for patients. “We feel that we have been, as nurses and midwives, disrespected and disregarded, and we have not been given priority with the nurse and midwife patient ratios that should have been rolled out,” she said. The proposed strike action comes as the WA Police Union launches a new campaign calling for public holiday penalty rates for officers ahead of the King’s Birthday public holiday on Monday. WAPU spokeswoman Simone Taplin said police officers should not be treated differently when they are required to work on public holidays. “Police officers don’t get to choose whether the community needs them on a public holiday. They turn up, put on the uniform and do the job,” she said.



“For many families, a public holiday means time together, a day trip on our roads, a family lunch or simply a day to switch off. “For our members, it can mean another shift, another road trauma, another day away from their families and another public holiday spent keeping the community safe. “And for doing that, they receive no additional public holiday penalty rate. That’s not the recognition our members deserve.”

World.title: Double delight as Dolphins land two more big fish
World.content:
SportNRLNRL 2026 Double delight as Dolphins land two more big fish Sebastian Tan September 18, 2026 — 7:55pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The Dolphins have pulled off a double signings coup, getting Selwyn Cobbo to commit to the club until the end of 2031 and locking Kulikefu Finefeuiaki in for another two years. With a battle on their hands to retain the current star-studded roster, the Dolphins have at least landed two blows as they prepare for the club’s maiden NRL preliminary final. Selwyn Cobbo scores a try during the Dolphins’ qualifying final win over the Warriors in Auckland. Getty Images Cobbo has found his best football at the Dolphins this season, after initially joining on a one-year deal and then signing a one-year extension in April. But off the back of scoring 18 tries in 19 games this year, the Queensland State of Origin winger is now committed to making the Dolphins his long-term home.



Finefeuiaki was also off-contract at the end of the 2027 season, meaning the second-rower would be free to negotiate with rival teams, including the tax-free PNG Chiefs on November 1. But after a stellar season in which the 22-year-old established himself as a crucial member of the club’s forward pack and earned his State of Origin debut, the Dolphin inked a deal that keeps him at the Redcliffe-based side. Kulikefu Finefeuiaki of the Dolphins runs the ball during NRL Qualifying Final match between New Zealand Warriors and Dolphins at Go Media Stadium on September 12, 2026 in Auckland, New Zealand. (Photo by Phil Walter/Getty Images) Getty Images The Dolphins do have star-studded duo Herbie Farnworth and Hamiso Tabuai-Fidow off contract at the end of next year, and face a battle to fit them both in the salary cap. Jack Bostock is another outside back who will at this stage become a free agent on November 1, and will no doubt have his salary go up after a NSW State of Origin debut.



The re-signings come after the team already locked down star forwards Tom Gilbert, Kurt Donoghoe and Max Plath until at least the end of 2028. Tevita Naufahu and half Brad Schneider also re-signed on Wednesday. Loading Dolphins CEO Terry Reader praised the way Cobbo had hit the ground running at the Dolphins this year, after finding himself on the outer at Brisbane. “Selwyn has made an immediate impact since joining the Dolphins, and what he has been able to produce in his first season at the club has been remarkable,” Reader said. “It is clear the environment has really suited him and he is enjoying his football – and Selwyn’s performances are underlining that.



“At just 24 years of age we know there is still plenty of great football ahead of him, and we’re excited that will be in a Dolphins jersey. Related Article NRL 2026 The boxer, teacher and curse breaker: The coach who shone from Bennett’s shadow “He has quickly become an important part of our team, and to have a player of Selwyn’s calibre committed to the club through until the end of 2031 is a great result.” Meanwhile, after making his NRL debut for North Queensland in 2023, Finefeuiaki moved south in 2025 and has enjoyed regular minutes since. “What I think has been most impressive about Kuli’s rise in our squad has been his transformation as a player,” Reader said.



“His work to turn himself into an 80-minute player on the edge who now plays State of Origin has been extremely impressive. “We see Kuli as one of the cornerstones of our pack and are excited about what he can do for this club, not only in this finals series, but over the next few years.” AAP

World.title: The ‘troubled’ class assignment that changed Lee’s teaching career
World.content:
NationalNSWEducation The ‘troubled’ class assignment that changed Lee’s teaching career Christopher Harris September 18, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

When Lee Casuscelli got her first job out of teachers college in the 1980s, she was given what might be termed a challenging first assignment at The Grange Public School in south-west Sydney. “She just got given the troubled class, I guess they called it, and no teacher really was able to do anything with these kids,” says her daughter Lauren Casuscelli. “They couldn’t really sit still at the start, they were jumping out of the windows and it was a bit chaotic.” Teacher Lee Casuscelli graduated from teachers college in the 1980s and went on to have a career in autism and special education. But Lauren says her mother gave her students 100 per cent of her focus. Attendance soon improved, the class became much more settled, and students were able to learn. “She just saw them as kids, not their disability,” Lauren says. That class at The Grange Public about 40 years ago would become the first step in a long and dedicated career working to improve the lives of students with disabilities and autism.



When Casuscelli died suddenly in a car crash in February, it prompted an outpouring of grief in the Camden community and across the state. Local MP Sally Quinnell told NSW parliament that hundreds of parents had paid their respects to Casuscelli, describing how she had “helped their children to grow and how she supported families with children with additional needs”. That legacy was honoured on Tuesday at Parliament House in Canberra at an event held by Schools Plus, an education not-for-profit, with the inaugural Lee Casuscelli Excellence in Special Education Award. Early in Casuscelli’s career, understanding of autism was much more limited both in schools and the general community. She developed numerous programs and initiatives to support students with autism. One of those programs was called Tool Time, which she established at Our Lady Help of Christians in Rosemeadow in the 2000s. In one-hour classes, she helped equip specific groups – such as teen boys – with practical tools to navigate the world.



The junior group would cover topics such as how to make a friend, how to keep a friend, and the sorts of social skills people with autism might struggle with. There was also advice for their parents. She went on to become the principal of Aspect Western Sydney School and Aspect Macarthur School before joining Schools Plus as its director of education. Dr Dawn Grant-Skiba, principal of Warrah Specialist School. Alex Ellinghausen The inaugural winner of the award is Dr Dawn Grant-Skiba, principal of Warrah Specialist School in Dural. The $50,000 prize includes $20,000 for a teacher fellowship, which is 12 months of professional development, including national networking and master classes. A further $30,000 will enable Warrah Specialist School to expand innovative approaches that improve outcomes for students with disability and diverse learning needs.



Schools Plus chief executive Sherrill Nixon said: “We are delighted to recognise Dawn, whose work reflects so many of the values Lee held so strongly.” Editor's pick Education We looked at staff salaries at 60 private schools. These pay the most Grant-Skiba, who was born in Jamaica, has worked across mainstream and specialist support schools in her 26-year teaching career. She says an early experience as a 12-year-old helping older women in her community learn to write their names and develop basic numeracy skillis has been a strong influence. “The ability to do that has changed their lives,” she says. She said while she was happy to teach students who learnt easily, she got the most joy from students who needed her more. “My creative juices flow, I get excited when they read a word, when before, they couldn’t recognise a letter.



“Those formative years really inspired me when I did come into teaching, to always look for the underdogs that others didn’t see as much.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Mini-Times Square? New digital billboard planned in centre of Queen Street Mall
World.content:
NationalQueenslandBrisbane development Mini-Times Square? New digital billboard planned in centre of Queen Street Mall William Davis September 18, 2026 — 8:14pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The Times Square-ification of Queen Street Mall is set to continue, with plans progressing for another large electronic billboard. An application to install a new roof supporting the advertising feature on a deteriorating building were lodged with Brisbane City Council in September. According to one expert, the proposal raised questions about the future of public spaces in Brisbane and how digital technology should be managed. A new roof with an attached digital billboard for advertising is planned at 136 Queen Street in Queen Street Mall. William Davis The two-storey complex at 136 Queen Street comprises a Telstra Shop, as well as Off Ya Tree tattoos and body piercings and various food and drink outlets including Boost Juice.



According to the application, its roof had deteriorated significantly due to water damage, fungal decay and termite activity. “While the central structural spine continues to provide support, the overall condition indicates that the roof framing is nearing the end of its functional lifespan,” it says. An artist impressing on the plans for the Telstra building at 136 Queen Street in Queen Street Mall. The application requests approval for a replacement, with an artist impression showing a large digital screen erected on the corner opposite Hungry Jacks. The application also seeks approval for a “digital room” to maintain the sign.



Similar electronic billboards are already installed above the KFC and Optus shop, both located on the same intersection. Another large screen also hangs from a steel frame further up the mall outside Uptown shopping centre. Marcus Foth is professor of urban informatics at QUT’s school of design. He has researched the impacts and potential of screens in shared spaces. “The proposed Queen Street Mall screen raises a broader question about public value,” he said. “The problem is that the technology’s possibilities are much broader than the way it is commonly deployed.



“A screen can support digital placemaking and public culture, or it can primarily function as advertising infrastructure.” There are multiple public screens now through Queen Street Mall, above KFC, Optus and next to Uptown. Rhett Hammerton Foth said the fact people using public space couldn’t choose to turn off a billboard or change the channel meant planners had a responsibility to think about how and where they were deployed. “This is particularly important for an ... environment such as Queen Street Mall,” he said. “Large digital displays can add to light pollution and glare, but there are also accessibility and health considerations.



“Excessive brightness, rapid animation and flashing or high-contrast content can make public spaces difficult for people with sensory sensitivities, and particular flashing patterns can trigger seizures in people with photosensitive epilepsy.” He pointed to Melbourne’s Federation Square as an example of how large public screens can support cultural programming and community engagement, rather than functioning solely as advertising infrastructure. “Brisbane will undoubtedly have more digital infrastructure in its public spaces. The challenge is ensuring that we don’t confuse having more screens with becoming a better digital city,” Foth said. Plans for a screen above the Telstra shop were lodged with council in April, 2025. “The sign is in keeping with the character of the local environment and supports its role as a major retail and activity hub,” the application at the time said.



A spokesperson for the lord mayor’s office declined to comment on the merits of the proposal, saying it would be assessed by independent planning officers. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: WA nurses threaten strike action as government delays patient ratio rollout
World.content:
NationalWAIndustrial relations WA nurses threaten strike action as government delays patient ratio rollout Sophie Fenna and and Michael Philipps September 18, 2026 — 8:05pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

WA’s peak nursing union has warned of impending strike action after the organisation was told that nurse and midwife-to-patient ratios, due to be implemented by the state government this month, have been postponed. The proposed rollout of the third phase of ratios was scheduled to be in place by September 21, but Australian Nursing and Midwifery Federation WA state secretary Romina Raschilla said members had recently been told the implementation had been rescheduled. Nurses and Midwives rally at WA Parliament House and Dumas House in 2022. Hamish Hastie “Last Thursday we had a meeting with the chief nurse midwifery officer, and she advised us that the nurse midwife patient ratios that were due to be implemented on the 21st of September have been halted,” she said. “This was going to affect over 90 wards in the metropolitan public hospitals, and it’ll affect a lot of nurses and midwives, and also a lot of patients.



“Our members are really angry. They want to strike right now, but there is a process that needs to take place.” The third phase of the rollout was set to address particular wards, including geriatrics, some pediatrics, neonatal and other specialties, following the completed first two phases. Raschilla said ratios assist with the care that is delivered to the most vulnerable people in the community. “When that doesn’t occur, then the nurses and midwives have got more patients than they should have, and it is very difficult to provide that excellent care that each nurse and midwife wants to provide to their patient,” she said. “If we decide to strike or rally, we will ensure that it is done in accordance with the Industrial Relations Act, and we will also ensure that our patients do not suffer because nurses and midwives do not want a negative impact on their patients.



“However, if this is the only way that the government will pay attention, respect, and not disregard nurses and midwives. We will do whatever we need to do.” Related Article Updated

Hospitals in crisis Perth man suffering painful renal failure had to wait 12 hours to see doctor If industrial action goes ahead, it will be the first time WA nursing staff have committed to a work stoppage since thousands of members went on strike across WA in November 2022, with those at metropolitan hospitals gathering at Parliament House before marching to the health minister’s office at nearby Dumas House. WA Health Minister Meredith Hammat said the government has been delivering landmark nurse and midwife-to-patient ratios and will continue to do so. “I met with the Australian Nursing and Midwifery Federation this week and had a productive discussion about the next phase of the nurse and midwife-to-patient ratio rollout,” she said.



“The next phase will further expand the program to include Peel Health Campus, Murray District Hospital, Bentley Hospital, Kalamunda Hospital and Cockburn Health, and remaining metropolitan speciality medical and surgical wards, rehabilitation wards and emergency departments.” Hammat said the wards represent some of the most complex clinical environments within the hospital system, requiring careful planning. “This is a long-term, system-wide reform and it is important we take the necessary steps to get it right, for patients and for the health workforce,” she said. “Patient safety will always be the highest priority in any decision relating to the rollout of ratios. “It is also important that the needs of the health workforce are at the forefront of decision making, and our nurses and midwives can continue to provide safe care to the community of Western Australia.”



Raschilla said union members have little confidence in the government, and it is diminishing at a rapid rate, which is going to affect the healthcare provided for patients. “We feel that we have been, as nurses and midwives, disrespected and disregarded, and we have not been given priority with the nurse and midwife patient ratios that should have been rolled out,” she said. The proposed strike action comes as the WA Police Union launches a new campaign calling for public holiday penalty rates for officers ahead of the King’s Birthday public holiday on Monday. WAPU spokeswoman Simone Taplin said police officers should not be treated differently when they are required to work on public holidays. “Police officers don’t get to choose whether the community needs them on a public holiday. They turn up, put on the uniform and do the job,” she said.



“For many families, a public holiday means time together, a day trip on our roads, a family lunch or simply a day to switch off. “For our members, it can mean another shift, another road trauma, another day away from their families and another public holiday spent keeping the community safe. “And for doing that, they receive no additional public holiday penalty rate. That’s not the recognition our members deserve.”
